  preparation, because the peer's owner binding is not in place yet. Core then
  logs one WARN per such edge ("a woken member's wiring edge could not be
  prepared; its repair is owed") and repairs the edge on its own, at its first
  retry or once the peer has woken; no message is lost, and later retries log
  at debug. It appears only when a host wakes many members at once, for
  example by materializing every member at boot; with on-demand residency and
  no host pre-materialization it does not occur. A fix is planned for the next
  release.

- `meerkat-mob`: after a member's warm reload completes on an otherwise idle
  mob, its runtime binding is recorded at the mob's next command, so a host's
  first `MobHandle::release_member` in that window can be refused once,
  retryably (`MobError::LifecycleOperationPending`); a retry releases the
  member. A fix is planned for a later release.

- `meerkat-mob`: a host `MemberBuildPreparer` that never returns holds the
  Destroy, Reset, RetireAll and Shutdown of its mob, the post-start steps of a
  Retire of that member, and a Resume issued after a Stop that abandoned the
  member's wake, as a spawn's preparation has held them since 0.9.6. Stop
  itself is not held: it abandons the wake. A bound on the preparer is planned
  for a later release.

- The known limitations listed for 0.9.6 still apply; this release changes
  none of them.

## [0.9.6] - 2026-10-27

### Breaking

- `meerkat-runtime`: `meerkat_runtime::completion::CompletionOutcome` gains
  `OutcomeUnknown { run_id }`, the finalized answer to an input that run
  `run_id` consumed at a boundary a recovery committed without the input's
  receipt, once a cold-predecessor settlement answers it: what the run did
  for that input is not known. `CompletionOutcome` is exhaustive, so a
  downstream exhaustive match needs an arm. Read the new variant as not
  completed, and never resubmit or redeliver the input because of it, since
  its run may have acted on it. Only a terminal-receipt read meets it; a
  live completion waiter never does.

- `meerkat-runtime`, `meerkat-machine-schema`, `meerkat-machine-kernels`: the
  MeerkatMachine completion vocabulary gains
  `RuntimeCompletionObservedOutcome::OutcomeUnknown`,
  `RuntimeCompletionTerminalObservation::OutcomeUnknown` and
  `RuntimeCompletionResultClass::OutcomeUnknown`, each appended last (the
  `meerkat_machine::dsl` bridge copies and the catalog and kernel types).
  The generated runtime kernel (`generated::meerkat`) adds the new
  transitions to `TransitionId`, appended last:
  `ResolveRuntimeCompletionResultOutcomeUnknownInitializing`,
  `ResolveRuntimeCompletionResultOutcomeUnknownIdle`,
  `ResolveRuntimeCompletionResultOutcomeUnknownAttached`,
  `ResolveRuntimeCompletionResultOutcomeUnknownRunning`,
  `ResolveRuntimeCompletionResultOutcomeUnknownRetired`,
  `ResolveRuntimeCompletionResultOutcomeUnknownStopped`.

- `meerkat-auth-core` (pre-registered MCP OAuth clients): `McpOAuthError`
  gains the variant `ClientProfile { server_name, refusal }`, appended last:
  the host-registered client profile of the target's credential slot
  refused the operation (`McpOAuthClientProfileRefusal`, non-exhaustive).
  The semver gate reports it as an enum variant added to an exhaustive enum
  (`McpOAuthError` stays exhaustive); a match outside the crate needs the
  arm. Surfaces map it by its refusal: `RedirectMismatch` to the reason
  `invalid_target`, `Changed` to `attempt_mismatch`, the others to
  `configuration_invalid`.

- `meerkat-core` (pre-registered MCP OAuth clients): `PersistedAuthMode`
  gains the variant `McpOauthClient` (serialized `mcp_oauth_client`),
  appended last: the custody row of an MCP credential slot's client
  profile, under the new key kind `TokenKey::mcp_oauth_client`. The semver
  gate reports it as an enum variant added to an exhaustive enum; a match
  outside the crate needs the arm. It is not a credential: no resolver
  accepts it, it has no AuthMachine lifecycle, and the auth profile
  surfaces cannot create it.

- Not measured by the gate (a signature change): `meerkat` (pre-registered MCP
  OAuth clients): `HostAuthService::mcp_registered_redirect_uri` is now
  `async`: it reads the slot's client profile and answers the exact redirect
  the slot's registered-callback login uses (the profile's, which may be the
  registered base itself, or the derived redirect without a profile), and
  `None` for a slot whose profile is a loopback client. A caller adds
  `.await`; `McpOAuthAuthority::registered_redirect_uri` stays the synchronous
  derived redirect.

- Behaviour-only (not measured by the gate): `meerkat-core`:
  `dispatch_retained_consent_attempt`, which hosts call directly, now
  resolves a retained call afresh when its plan names another dispatcher
  allocation (the session's agent rebuilt in this process), where it refused
  before and left the consent spendable. A fresh plan that is the same
  durable execution is rebound and spent once. One that is not, or a
  re-decision the run's owners refuse or no longer review as R3, now
  withdraws the consent instead of leaving it spendable.

### Added

- `meerkat-runtime`, `meerkat-session`, `meerkat-mob`: a host that takes over
  a durable session whose earlier process ended without unregistering it (a
  crash or a power cut) can settle the runtime work that process left before
  it registers the session, without serving it.
  `PersistentSessionService::settle_cold_predecessor_before(id, claim,
  deadline)` runs under the caller's own cross-process hosting claim of the
  session (`grant_session_hosting`, an OS lock) on a HeadCanonical runtime
  store. It commits the durable tail the earlier process left; ends every
  input that never ended `Abandoned { Stopped }`, publishing the terminal a
  directed input's requester waits for; finalizes every terminal receipt and
  publication still owed; and answers an input a recovered boundary consumed
  without a receipt as outcome unknown. The session is left unregistered and
  registrable. The caller keeps its claim until its own registration has
  published, so that registration joins the claim's lineage and does not
  settle the lost owner's consents a second time. `Ok` is a complete census
  (`meerkat_runtime::ColdPredecessorSettlement`): the tail commit, every
  settled input with its finalized receipt and, for a directed input, the
  sequence of its published terminal, the owner-loss outcome, the number of
  durable input rows read closed, and the rows whose receipt a migration made
  permanently unavailable. A refusal
  (`meerkat_session::ColdPredecessorSettleError`, which the facade re-exports
  with its refusal enum) carries only final evidence; a deadline, a cancelled
  call or an error certifies nothing, and a repeat converges from the store. A
  settlement that stops after its sweep commit can leave an outcome-unknown
  answer owed: until a repeat converges it, an archive or a stop of the
  session refuses, typed, so repeat the settlement first. A host that governs
  consents registers the session only on the owner-loss outcome `Completed` or
  `NotOwed`: `NoConsentOwner` means no issuing consent owner is installed on
  the runtime, a composition defect, so install it and repeat the call.
  Directed work needs the service's event store (`with_event_projection`):
  without one, publishing a directed input's terminal refuses after the input
  ended, and the terminal stays owed until a service with an event store
  repeats the call.
  `MobSessionService::settle_cold_predecessor_with_mob_lifecycle_authority_before`
  is the same call for a mob's session service (the persistent service
  forwards it, as the mob session services of `rkat-rpc` and the CLI do; the
  default refuses `Unsupported`). The service composes the runtime's
  settlement steps, which hosts do not call themselves:
  `MeerkatMachine::begin_predecessor_settlement_before`,
  `settle_predecessor_tail_with_lease`,
  `end_predecessor_work_with_lease_before`,
  `finish_predecessor_settlement_before`, and, for a settlement that stops
  before its drain, `remove_predecessor_settlement_registration_before`.

- `meerkat-runtime`, `meerkat-core`, `meerkat-mob`, SDKs: an input that a run
  consumed at a boundary a recovery committed without the input's receipt is
  answered once a settlement reaches it. Its terminal receipt finalizes with
  `CompletionOutcome::OutcomeUnknown { run_id }` (completion type
  `outcome_unknown`, class `CompletionClass::OutcomeUnknown`), naming that
  run: what the run did for the input is not known. A directed input's
  requester gets `interaction_failed` with the new reason kind
  `outcome_unknown` (`InteractionFailureReason::OutcomeUnknown`), which the
  TypeScript and Python SDKs parse. A turn result that meets it answers an
  error that says not to resubmit the input (RPC `kind: "outcome_unknown"`,
  REST and the facade `TURN_OUTCOME_UNKNOWN`, each with `resumable: false`),
  and a mob's bounded turn answers `BoundedTurnFailure::OutcomeUnknown {
  session_id, run_id }`.

- `meerkat-core`: `HostingClaim::completed_owner_loss` reports the owner-loss
  proof a claim's lineage settled once a registration completed it, and
  `HostingClaim::same_lineage` whether two claims belong to the very same
  live cross-process lineage. Both are read-only observations.

- `meerkat-core`, `meerkat-session`, `meerkat-mob`: a run the runtime
  settles without resuming it has a typed terminal payload,
  `meerkat_core::lifecycle::SettledRunTerminal` (the session id, the run's
  transcript identity under its run id, and a `SettledRunCause`:
  `RequeueExpired`, `ResumeRefused` or `Cancelled`), and its
  `run_failed_event` is the existing `AgentEvent::RunFailed` of class
  `Cancelled`, with no reason or cause kind. `CoreExecutorPublicationHandle`
  gains `publish_settled_run_terminal`, which publishes that event through
  the handle's exact live actor and answers unsupported by default.
  `EphemeralSessionService` and `PersistentSessionService` gain
  `publish_settled_run_terminal_for_actor`, and `MobSessionService` gains the
  same method, unsupported by default. The publication handles of the
  `meerkat` surfaces, `meerkat-rpc` and `meerkat-mob` implement it.

- `meerkat-mob`: `QueuedInputsOnShutdown::Keep` (the enum is
  `#[non_exhaustive]`, so the variant is additive). A mob Shutdown with it
  unregisters each member with the runtime's `UnregisterQueuedInputs::Keep`,
  and changes nothing it finds: a member whose registration served no live
  work keeps every input it recovered as the Shutdown finds it, with no
  requeue mark, and the run its session left open, and an autonomous member's
  kickoff stays open. The boot's ordinary recovery may still normalize a
  staged input whose run cannot continue to queued, as every start does; the
  Keep leaves that as it is. A member whose registration served live work is
  stopped, as under `Stop`. It is meant for a host that boots over a store
  another host serves, holds its members' run starts, and must hand back
  unchanged what it finds. While a member's host holds its run starts, a
  kickoff an earlier Shutdown kept in flight is re-attached at the host's
  release (`MobHandle::release_member_run_starts`) instead of at the member's
  restore, so the restore serves the member no work and a `Keep` Shutdown
  keeps the kickoff open.

- `meerkat-runtime`: `MeerkatMachine::registration_run_start_hold_staged`
  answers whether a run-start hold reason is staged for a session's
  registration, as a host's hold on a member's run starts stays until the
  host releases it.

- `meerkat-mob`: `MobStorage::member_binding_history` reads the member
  binding history of a storage's mob with no running mob and no file path,
  through the storage's own identity member store, so it serves every
  storage that has one, a mob storage kept in a host store included. It
  folds the journal and the identity intent rows as
  `MobStorage::read_member_binding_history` folds a store file, answers an
  empty history for a storage that holds no mob, and refuses a custom store
  composition without the built-in identity member store as
  `MobHandle::member_binding_history` does
  (`MemberBindingHistoryReadError::Read` of
  `MobStoreError::IdentityMemberAtomicPersistenceUnavailable`).

- `meerkat-runtime`: `RuntimeStore::import_whole_blob_session` imports a
  whole-blob session document into a store, create-only, as ordinary
  writes. When the runtime has no committed document, it commits this one
  in one atomic write (one batch on a host store, after the chunk batches of
  a large document) together with its catalog entry and, as pending outbox
  rows, the document's pending compaction projection intents, which
  `commit_session_snapshot` refuses, and answers
  `WholeBlobSessionImport::Created`. The same bytes again answer
  `WholeBlobSessionImport::AlreadyCurrent` and write nothing; other bytes
  are refused with `RuntimeStoreError::SessionPersistenceAuthorityConflict`
  and nothing is written. `InMemoryRuntimeStore` and the host store adapter
  `SpiRuntimeStore` implement it; the provided default answers
  `Unsupported`, so a store decorator forwards it to the store it wraps.

- `meerkat-runtime`: the host store reference and `ScopeFamily` now state
  that Core never uses a scope family tag starting with `x` or `mx`, so a
  layer above Core can keep scopes of its own in a realm without colliding
  with a later Core family. The reference also states how Core settles a
  commit whose outcome is unknown or unavailable (the same batch again, with
  the same commit id, within `SpiRealmConfig::commit_retry_budget`; past it,
  the batch's scopes are poisoned until the realm is opened again), what
  `FenceTiming::max_commit_latency` bounds (the backoff of a session write
  fenced by a mob's identity authority, which waits for every batch of the
  identity scope's commit, chunk batches included, and not for a session
  document's chunk batches), and that Core sets no deadline on a commit.

- `meerkat-core`: `BoundOperationReview::consent_notice_issuer` returns the
  approval owner that issues the review's human consent, present exactly
  when R3 routes to human consent, as `consent_owner_loss_settlement` is. A
  host composes it into its delivery owner's consent notice projection
  (`ConsentNoticeProjector`), so the notices that owner owes are projected
  for exactly the owner that issued the consent.

- `meerkat`: the provided `RetainedJobSource::admission_committed` (by
  default it records nothing). The governed admission of a retained
  completion reports each committed admission (its session and input) to
  the job source that confirmed the job, before the delivery row is
  acknowledged and again on a retry; an error leaves the row unacknowledged
  and retried later. A composed source forwards it to the source that
  confirmed the job, routed as `retained_job`, as the `meerkat-mob-mcp`
  composition now does for a host source's declared namespaces
  (`MobMcpState::with_host_job_source`).

- `meerkat-auth-core`, `meerkat`: pre-registered (fixed, confidential) OAuth
  clients for remote MCP servers whose authorization server offers no
  dynamic client registration. A native host installs a client for one
  configured server's credential slot (the server as configured, the realm
  it serves and the account selection) with
  `HostAuthService::mcp_install_client_profile`, replaces it with
  `mcp_replace_client_profile` (the same facts with a new secret rotate the
  secret and keep everything bound to the profile), removes it with
  `mcp_remove_client_profile`, each also in an `_entered` form that
  re-checks the host's administrator at the update's entry, and reads it
  back without its secret with `mcp_client_profile`
  (`McpOAuthAuthority::install_client_profile_entered`,
  `replace_client_profile_entered`, `remove_client_profile_entered` and
  `client_profile` beneath them). An `McpOAuthClientProfile` names the
  issuer, the client id, the client's exact registered redirect (the
  host's registered base itself, the server's own registered `https`
  callback under it, or a loopback redirect with an explicit port; install
  and replace refuse any other registered redirect, and the authority's
  install and replace take the host's base for that check) and
  `client_secret_basic` or `client_secret_post` with the secret
  (`McpOAuthClientSecret`: no `Display`, `Clone` or serialization, a
  redacted `Debug`, its buffer overwritten when dropped), and optionally
  the scopes to request and the protected resource identifier the server's
  metadata names. A profile that names the base itself gives a central
  callback: every slot of one client (users, realms, account selections)
  logs in on that one exact URI, byte for byte, and the host routes each
  callback by its `state` to the ceremony it retained; a callback for
  another slot is refused without consuming or retiring any attempt
  (`McpOAuthAuthority::registered_login_redirect_uri` and
  `HostAuthService::mcp_registered_redirect_uri` answer the URI a slot
  logs in on). The secret is kept only in the credential store, under
  the new key kind `TokenKey::mcp_oauth_client`, and never appears in
  configuration, errors, events, logs or `Debug`. With a profile installed,
  a login (on the registered callback and the loopback route alike)
  registers nothing and needs no registration endpoint: the resource
  metadata must name the profile's issuer, the authorization request uses
  the profile's client id and redirect with PKCE S256, and the code
  exchange and every refresh authenticate the client by its method; a
  refresh token the server rotates is stored and presented next. Under an
  `https` issuer the token endpoint, where the secret is sent, must use
  `https` too, with no loopback exception: discovery refuses another, and a
  refresh never sends the secret to a stored one that does not fit. Attempts
  and credentials are bound to the profile's facts: a completion whose
  profile was removed or replaced is refused and its attempt retired, and a
  refresh that cannot authenticate (the profile removed or replaced, or its
  secret refused by the server with a standard OAuth error response) ends
  the credential as `ReauthRequired`, never falling back to dynamic
  registration or a public client. A server that reports errors with HTTP
  200 keeps the credential: every use retries and fails with a typed error,
  and status can stay `Authorized`, as with Core's other OAuth refreshes.
  Without a profile nothing changes. `auth_oauth` gains
  `OAuthClientAuthentication` with
  `exchange_authorization_code_with_client_auth` and
  `exchange_refresh_token_with_client_auth` (HTTP Basic sends the
  form-encoded client id and secret, RFC 6749 section 2.3.1). No RPC, REST
  or SDK method installs a profile.

- `meerkat-schedule`: `meerkat_schedule_occurrences` takes optional bounded
  read arguments. `occurrence_id` returns one occurrence with all of its
  delivery receipts and answers not found when it belongs to another
  schedule. `due_after_utc` / `due_before_utc` (inclusive, RFC 3339 with any
  offset) and `phase` filter in the store query. `limit` (default 100 once any
  of these options or `view: "summary"` is given, maximum 500) pages the rows
  in due order with a `page` object (`returned`, `has_more`, `next_cursor`),
  and `cursor` (opaque) continues after the last row, stable while new
  occurrences are planned or a revision supersedes old ones; a cursor page
  reads a bounded number of rows, never the rest of the history.
  `view: "summary"` drops the trigger, the target action and prompt and the
  machine state, in both the list and the exact read (whose receipts are
  summarized too), and adds the due time in a calendar trigger's own
  timezone. A call with only `schedule_id`, or with only `view: "full"`,
  returns exactly what it returned before. `ScheduleService` gains
  `list_occurrences_matching`, `get_schedule_occurrence` and
  `list_occurrence_receipts`, and `ScheduleStore::list_occurrences` now
  documents the `(due_at, schedule_revision, occurrence_ordinal)` order and
  limit it already followed.

- `meerkat-core`: the provided
  `CompactionCommitCoordinator::authorize_committed_projection` authorizes
  finalizing a compaction projection whose transcript rewrite the runtime
  store already committed. It defaults to `authorize_projection`; the
  runtime's coordinator implements it so that a revived mob member finalizes a
  committed intent before its runtime is placed (see Fixed, a compaction with
  durable semantic memory inside a run).

### Changed

- `meerkat-runtime`: an input that a durable-tail recovery consumes at the
  boundary it commits now gets its terminal receipt and, when directed, the
  terminal its requester waits for, at every start where it can. The
  boundary's commit stages the run's terminal-completion batch for its
  contributors when no other run's terminal batch is open, and the runtime
  loop's startup drain finalizes and publishes it before it serves. A
  directed contributor's outbox names the runtime placement the session's
  lifecycle row records; without one, the batch holds the nondirected
  contributors only, and a directed one waits for a settlement's
  outcome-unknown answer. Until now such an input stayed consumed without a
  receipt: its exact receipt read answered corruption, and a directed
  input's requester never got a terminal. A process-local completion waiter
  is unchanged: it still fails `AuthorityUnavailable` when its registration
  adopts the recovered terminal. An archive's own recovery that commits such
  a boundary leaves the batch pending in the archived session: an archive
  drains no run-scoped batch.

### Fixed

- `meerkat-core`, `meerkat-session`: a compaction inside an open run no longer
  folds the run's request or its newest round. Before, a run whose own rows
  exceeded the compactor's retention budget kept only its request, and the
  model, seeing a summary of a tool call it had already made, could make it
  again. Now, at a round boundary after the run's first response, the agent
  finds the run's first row (the input rows before its first response: the
  prompt, injected context and the notices a peer, flow, external or job
  input arrives as, found from the run id its assistant rows carry) and
  compacts in two stages:
  1. While the rows before the run hold a turn, only they are handed to the
     compactor (and to a curator), and the run's own rows follow the summary
     verbatim, for any compactor.
  2. When nothing before the run is left, the run's own completed rounds are
     folded, with any earlier summary, by the runtime itself; the run's
     request and its newest round (its tool calls, their results and any
     rows a tool appended after them) stay verbatim, and the summary ends by
     naming every call the run's earlier rounds made, those an earlier fold
     took out included, as already run (a call whose result was an error as
     ran and failed, so it may still be made again). That list is kept in
     the session metadata key `open_run_folded_calls` for the open run,
     committed with each fold, and never read back from a summary's text;
     each call's outcome comes from its own round, since some providers reuse
     call ids in every round. The line names the newest 200 calls and counts
     older ones by tool name. A long single run therefore keeps compacting,
     one boundary later than before, and always sees the calls it made last.
     A fold that would take out only one row is skipped.

  A run whose newest round is its only one has nothing to fold: the attempt
  is skipped before its summary call and recorded for cadence. A run's first
  boundary, before its first response, compacts as before. Custom compactors:
  inside a run the rows a compactor gets end with a complete turn, so a
  rebuild that keeps the last user row and puts the summary first is now
  refused there (the summary must stand at the first discarded row);
  `CompactionWindow` and `CompactionCurator` document what they get.
  `DefaultCompactor` keeps a newest turn's request verbatim only while that
  turn has no final answer, so an answered turn is kept or folded whole and
  never left reading as pending. `compaction_started` and
  `compaction_completed` keep reporting over the whole transcript. When the
  open run's own tool results push a request past the provider cap (also
  after a model fallback, against the fallback's cap), that request (never
  the stored transcript) carries each oversized result of the run, found
  after the run's first row so a reused call id of an earlier run is never
  cut, with its identity and the head of its text and a marker naming the
  call; the compaction trigger and its post-compaction check still see the
  unbounded size, and a request that still does not fit fails as
  `RequestTooLarge`.

- `meerkat-runtime`, `meerkat-core`: a compaction with durable semantic
  memory inside a run no longer leaves its session unable to start or its
  memory projection lost. The compaction stages its memory projection and
  records its intent in the session; the intent rides in the run's
  provisional tail and reaches the compaction outbox only when the tail
  commits. Four gaps are closed:
  - A run kept by a graceful stop resumes again. The reconciliation at the
    next start (and at an attachment's teardown) asked the agent first: an
    agent seeded from the tail refused with "runtime compaction outbox omits
    a validated session projection intent", failing the startup at every
    start while the tail stood, and an agent not yet materialized aborted
    the intent's memory stage as an orphan. While a run's provisional tail
    stands, the whole reconciliation now waits: no agent check, no memory
    finalization, no orphan clean-up and no refresh. The reconciliation
    after the run's boundary commits the tail finalizes the intent once.
  - A revived or restored mob member with a committed intent not finalized
    yet (a crash after the commit, a stopped run's settled tail) starts
    again. Its startup reconciliation refused the intent with "compaction
    projection coordinator rejected the handoff: session has no
    authoritative runtime binding for compaction commit", because the mob
    binds a member's runtime only after its revival succeeds, so the member
    failed at every start. `CompactionCommitCoordinator` gains
    `authorize_committed_projection` (defaulting to `authorize_projection`):
    the runtime's coordinator authorizes finalizing a committed row under
    the member's live session and epoch before its runtime is placed,
    latching nothing, while staging a new compaction still needs a placement
    and a rotated placement still refuses.
  - A run stopped or interrupted after a round commit had written its
    compaction into the tail no longer deletes the compaction's memory
    stage. The tail is committed as an interrupted run with the intent, so
    once a run checkpoint (or re-base) wrote a pending compaction into the
    tail, an abort leaves the rewrite and the stage to the tail's settlement
    instead of rolling them back, and the next reconciliation finalizes the
    intent once instead of failing with "missing durable compaction stage
    for committed rewrite".
  - A resumed run that compacts again before its boundary commits with the
    intent it carried, instead of refusing finalization because the outbox
    held more intents than its own compaction.

- `meerkat-runtime`: a queued prompt that a graceful stop kept for the next
  start (`UnregisterQueuedInputs::Requeue`, which the graceful shutdowns of
  `rkat-rpc`, the REST server and a mob use by default for durable
  sessions) no longer carries the stop's mark once that start runs it. The
  mark stayed on the prompt while its run was open, so when the process
  then ended without a graceful stop (a crash or a power cut) after the run
  had committed a round, the next start after the stop's max age, counted
  from the prompt's admission, ended the run's inputs as `RequeueExpired`
  and closed the run as interrupted instead of resuming it. The mark is now
  cleared, durably, when the prompt is staged for its run, as it already was
  when a run the stop kept resumes; a kept prompt still queued keeps its
  mark. Once its run has started, such a prompt's row is written as stored
  input state version 7 again, which 0.9.4 reads. Rows 0.9.5 already wrote
  keep the mark: a run that 0.9.5 started from a kept queued prompt and a
  crash cut before the upgrade still has its inputs ended as
  `RequeueExpired`, and is closed as interrupted, by a start past the max
  age.

- `meerkat-runtime`: a run that a graceful stop kept open for the next start
  now tells its callers when it is settled instead of resumed. A kept run is
  settled when the next start finds it past the stop's max age
  (`RequeueExpired`), when its resume is refused, when a stop that keeps no
  work ends it, or when the session is archived. Each of these ended the
  run's inputs but staged no terminal for them, so the caller of a directed
  input (a directed peer message or a tracked flow step) never saw its
  interaction end. The settlement now stages the runtime-termination carrier
  for the run's inputs in the same durable commit that ends them, as a stop
  already does for the queued inputs it ends: a directed input's interaction
  fails exactly once with an `InteractionFailed`. A nondirected kept input
  now carries a runtime-termination receipt too: its receipt reads move from
  pending to finalized with the runtime-terminated outcome and the
  settlement's reason, where they used to read as a terminal without a
  receipt (rows 0.9.5 settled still read that way). A start that settles an
  expired kept run publishes after it releases the session, through the
  attachment's publication capability, so a crash in between, or a surface
  without that capability, leaves the committed carrier for the next stop or
  start to publish.

- `meerkat-runtime`: a run left open across a restart (kept by a graceful
  stop, or cut by a crash after a round commit) that the runtime settles
  instead of resuming now ends on the session's event stream: its live
  actor publishes one `RunFailed` of class `Cancelled` under the run's id
  and the transcript identity its rounds carry (its interaction, merged
  from its inputs as its resume would have merged them). The run's
  execution ended in an earlier process, which published no terminal, so a
  client that followed the run by its events never saw it end, whether its
  input was directed or a plain prompt. This covers a start that finds the
  run past its stop's max age, a refused resume, and a stop that keeps no
  work. The event is published after the settlement commits and is not
  part of it. A start that settles an expired run retries it for up to a
  minute while its attachment comes to serve. A crash in between, or a
  start whose tail repair leaves a tail standing (so the session reloads
  instead of serving), loses it, and no later start publishes it. The event
  needs the attachment's publication capability: a surface without one, or
  one that does not support the publication, publishes none. An archive
  that settles a kept run publishes no run terminal, since it serves no live
  actor; nor do a retire, a destroy or a reset, which end a kept run without
  settling it; nor does a suspension the runtime refuses.

- `meerkat-runtime`: a run left open across a restart (kept by a graceful
  stop, or cut by a crash after a round commit) now resumes when a run-start
  hold on its session is released after the session registered. A host that
  holds a restored member's run starts until it is ready
  (`MobBuilder::hold_restored_member_run_starts`, released with
  `MobHandle::release_member_run_starts`) left the open run waiting for the
  member's next input: the registration's wake for the run came while the
  hold stood, and `MeerkatMachine::release_run_starts` woke the runtime
  loop only for queued input, while the open run's inputs are bound to the
  run. The release now also wakes the loop when it leaves no hold and the
  session keeps a resumable run.

- `meerkat-runtime`: an executor attachment whose startup fails keeps the
  inputs its registration recovered from the store, as the cleanup of a
  failed startup has asked since 0.9.5. The runtime loop's own teardown
  could act on the failed attachment before the owner that started it
  retired it, and stopped those inputs: a queued prompt that a crash left
  behind ended as stopped, and the next start ran without it. In rare cases
  the race stalled the failed attachment's teardown instead. The loop's
  teardown now leaves an attachment that never served to that owner, whose
  unregister keeps every input the registration recovered for the next
  start, unless the registration served live work. A retire or an archive
  that meets an unserved attachment still stops every input.

- `meerkat`: consent notices now record their delivery receipts. The
  governed admission of an Approved, Denied or Withdrawn notice records
  `Admitted` for its session and input (reported through
  `RetainedJobSource::admission_committed`), so delivered notices no longer
  stay owed forever, and approved parked consent moves into the resumed run
  its notice starts. A notice whose delivery was settled as refused records
  `Failed`, which withdraws approved parked consent. A round also records
  the receipt of a notice whose admission applied without one.

- `meerkat-core`: a resumed run now spends, once, the human consent the
  approval owner moved into it by the receipt of one of its staged notice
  inputs: a boundary of the run attempts the exact retained call, as for
  consent the run requested itself, and its `consent_attempt` notice also
  names that input (`resumed_input_id`). A receipt that commits after the
  run's first boundary read the consent moved into it can let the model
  call the operation again first, which asks for fresh consent once more
  (approving it runs the operation again); the moved consent still runs
  once, at the run's next boundary. An approval owner held when a boundary
  reads the moved consent makes that boundary look again; held later in the
  boundary, it acts as for consent the run requested itself. Moved consent
  the run never spends (it has no later boundary, or its attempt was
  refused) is withdrawn unspent at the run's close.

- `meerkat-core`: a decided consent moved into a resumed run is now spent
  once even when the session's agent was rebuilt in the same process (for
  example a session unregistered with its queued inputs kept, then resumed).
  The retained call is resolved afresh against the rebuilt dispatcher, the
  fresh plan passes the checks every call passes after its resolution, and
  the approval owner rebinds the consent to that plan only as the same
  durable execution: the same call, tool declaration digest, execution mode
  and durable operation targets, decided R3 again by the run's owners. A
  plan that is not the same durable execution (a hybrid tool that selects
  another mode included), and a re-decision the run's owners refuse or no
  longer review as R3, refuse before entry and withdraw the consent. A tool
  the rebuilt agent has not published yet does not use up the run's one
  attempt: the run's next boundary attempts it again, and a failure that is
  in fact permanent but reads as not ready is attempted once per boundary
  until the run's close withdraws the consent. Accepted limits: an MCP
  server is compared by its configured name, so a name re-pointed to another
  endpoint compares equal when the account does not name the endpoint, and
  an account the owner cannot state compares equal to another such account.
  A process restart still ends the consent, and the next call asks for fresh
  consent.

- `meerkat-session`: the terminals an archive publishes for a session with no
  live actor (the stored-only publisher) take their event sequences from the
  session's event line in the service. When an earlier actor of the session
  had run in the same service, the archive's rows could reuse sequences that
  actor had allocated, and a later actor of the session could allocate at or
  below them. They now land above every sequence the line holds, a later
  actor allocates above them, and a repeated publication inserts nothing.

- `meerkat-schedule`: the `meerkat_schedule_list` description said deleted
  schedules are included; the tool lists active and paused schedules only, and
  the description now says so.

### Upgrade notes

- No storage migration: 0.9.6 opens every 0.9.5 store as it is. No SQLite
  schema or record format changed, and outside the two opt-in paths below
  every row 0.9.6 writes has a shape and version that 0.9.5 reads. Take a
  WAL-complete backup before upgrading: after a graceful stop, copy each
  SQLite file with `sqlite3 <db> ".backup <copy>"` or `VACUUM INTO`, or
  together with its `-wal` and `-shm` files, and keep the rest of the realm
  root (event logs, blobs) with it.

- Rolling back to 0.9.5 in place is safe for ordinary use, but not after
  either of two opt-in paths:
  - The cold-predecessor settlement is one-way for a session where it answers
    an input as outcome unknown: 0.9.5 cannot read those answers (the next
    three entries give the details). A settlement that stopped half way makes
    0.9.5 refuse that session until 0.9.6 repeats the settlement.
  - Pre-registered MCP OAuth client profiles: 0.9.5 ignores the profile file,
    and the credential of a server that logged in through a profile needs a
    new login there, which 0.9.5 makes only by dynamic registration. Remove a
    profile on 0.9.6 first to delete its stored client secret.

  A rollback also brings back the 0.9.5 defects this release fixes.

- A cold-predecessor settlement that stops between its internal registration
  and its sweep commit can leave the session's runtime lifecycle row at
  record version 7, carrying the session's last runtime placement. A binary
  without this release reads that row as an unsupported record version:
  registering, archiving or recovering the session is refused typed, and
  nothing is written. Repeat the settlement with this release before a
  downgrade; its sweep commit writes the row back at version 5 or 6. No other
  row changes version.

- An input that a settlement answers as outcome unknown carries a new
  terminal candidate (until its terminal is published) and a new finalized
  outcome (completion type `outcome_unknown`) in its input row. A binary
  without this release cannot decode that row: while the terminal is pending
  it refuses to register the session; once the terminal is published it no
  longer reads the row to register, but its exact receipt read of that input
  fails (as it already did for that input before the settlement), and a full
  row scan reports the row corrupt.

- The published terminal of such an input is an `interaction_failed` event
  with reason kind `outcome_unknown`. A binary without this release fails to
  decode that event when it reads the session's events; an SDK without this
  release reads the reason as an unknown kind with its raw kind.

- Wrappers and decorators outside this repository must forward the new
  provided methods, whose defaults refuse or do nothing:
  - a `MobSessionService` wrapper:
    `settle_cold_predecessor_with_mob_lifecycle_authority_before` (its default
    refuses `Unsupported`, touching nothing) and
    `publish_settled_run_terminal_for_actor` (its default answers unsupported,
    so a settled run publishes no `RunFailed`);
  - a `CoreExecutorPublicationHandle`: `publish_settled_run_terminal` (its
    default publishes nothing and answers unsupported);
  - a composed `RetainedJobSource`: `admission_committed`, routed to the
    source that confirmed the job (its default records nothing, so delivered
    consent notices stay owed);
  - a `RuntimeStore` decorator: `import_whole_blob_session` (its default
    answers `Unsupported`);
  - a `CompactionCommitCoordinator` wrapper: `authorize_committed_projection`
    (its default asks `authorize_projection`, which the runtime's coordinator
    refuses before a mob member's runtime is placed).

### Known limitations

- No native credential continuity witness: a host cannot prove later that a
  realm service secret or an OAuth credential is unchanged since an earlier
  call. The evidence is per call only.

- `meerkat-auth-core` (pre-registered MCP OAuth clients): a client profile
  does not pin the token endpoint. The secret goes to the token endpoint that
  the bound issuer's authorization server metadata names; under an `https`
  issuer that endpoint must use `https` too.

- `meerkat-auth-core`: a server that reports OAuth errors with HTTP 200 does
  not end a credential, for a pre-registered client as for Core's other OAuth
  refreshes: every use retries and fails with a typed error, and the
  credential's status can still read `Authorized`.

- `meerkat`: only a native host installs, replaces or removes a pre-registered
  MCP OAuth client profile (`HostAuthService`); no RPC, REST or SDK method
  does.

- `meerkat-core`: when the session's agent was rebuilt in the same process,
  consent moved into a resumed run is rebound only to the same durable
  execution, and that comparison has accepted limits: an MCP server is
  compared by its configured name, so a name re-pointed to another endpoint
  compares equal when the account does not name the endpoint, and an account
  the owner cannot state compares equal to another such account. A process
  restart still ends the consent, and the next call asks for fresh consent.

- `meerkat-core`: a notice receipt that commits after a resumed run's first
  boundary read the consent moved into it can let the model call the operation
  again first. That call asks for fresh consent once more, and approving it
  runs the operation again; the moved consent still runs once, at the run's
  next boundary.

- `meerkat-runtime`: the `RunFailed` that a run settled instead of resumed
  publishes (see Fixed) is not part of the settlement's commit. A crash in
  between, or a start whose tail repair leaves a tail standing, loses it, and
  no later start publishes it. A surface without the attachment's publication
  capability publishes none, and an archive, a retire, a destroy or a reset
  that ends a kept run publishes no run terminal.

- `meerkat-runtime`: a process-local completion waiter still fails
  `AuthorityUnavailable` when its registration adopts a terminal that a
  durable-tail recovery staged (see Changed), and an archive's own recovery
  leaves that terminal batch pending in the archived session.

- `meerkat-runtime`: rows that 0.9.5 wrote keep its behaviour. A run that
  0.9.5 started from a kept queued prompt, and that a crash cut before the
  upgrade, still has its inputs ended as `RequeueExpired` and is closed as
  interrupted by a start past the stop's max age, and a kept run that 0.9.5
  settled still reads as a terminal without a receipt.

- Three 0.9.5 known limitations that named the 0.9.6 line still apply, since
  this release carries fixes only: role-target admission and each flow step's
  choice of targets are checks the mob actor and the flow engine make over the
  mob machine's member facts; a channel-scoped `execution_identity`
  (gpt-live-1) is served for a mob member local to the JSON-RPC server only;
  and lifecycle disposal closes a channel opened under such an identity
  without the execution-identity authority's close. Each moves to a later
  release; the 0.9.5 notes give the details and workarounds.

- The optional live WebRTC path (`meerkat-live`'s `webrtc` feature) still
  carries RUSTSEC-2026-0387 and the unmaintained audiopus_sys
  (RUSTSEC-2026-0150), as the 0.9.5 Security notes describe; the port to
  webrtc 0.20 or later is still to come. Builds without that feature are
  unaffected.

## [0.9.5] - 2026-10-23

### Breaking

- `meerkat-runtime`, `meerkat-core`, `meerkat-machine-schema`,
  `meerkat-machine-kernels`: same-run resume after a restart changes the
  durable-tail recovery and MeerkatMachine vocabularies.
  `meerkat_runtime::recovery::DurableTailRecoveryOutcome` gains `Continue {
  candidate, run_id, receipt }`. The machine enums gain
  `DurableTailRecoveryClass::ContinuableCandidate`,
  `DurableTailRecoveryDisposition::ContinueRun` and
  `DurableTailRecoveryDisposition::OperatorRepairAndCommitInterrupted`,
  `RecoveredInputNormalizationReasonKind::ResumableRun`,
  `InputAbandonReason::ResumeRefused` (the `meerkat_machine::dsl` bridge copies
  and the catalog and kernel types). The session document vocabulary gains
  `RunIdCardinality::NoRunRows` and the `DurableTailRunCursor` type, and
  `SessionDocumentInput::ClassifyDurableTail` and
  `SessionDocumentMachineAuthority::classify_durable_tail` take `run_cursor`
  and `cursor_inputs_open`. `MeerkatMachineState` gains `resumable_run_id`;
  `MeerkatMachineInput` gains `MarkRunResumable`, `ResumeRun`,
  `ReleaseResumableRun`, `SettleResumableRun`, `SuspendRunForStop { run_id,
  durable_session }`, `ReplayAppliedRunContributor` and
  `AuthorizeOperatorDurableTailRepair`, and
  `NormalizeRecoveredInputLifecycle` gains `bound_run_resumable`;
  `MeerkatMachineEffect` gains `ResumableRunMarked`, `ResumedRunAuthorized`,
  `ResumableRunReleased`, `ResumableRunSettled` and `RunSuspendedForStop {
  run_id }`.
  The generated runtime kernel (`generated::meerkat`) adds the new transitions
  to `TransitionId`, appended last:
  `AuthorizeDurableTailRecoveryContinueIdle`,
  `AuthorizeDurableTailRecoveryRepairContinuableRetiredIdle`,
  `AuthorizeDurableTailRecoveryRepairContinuableRetiredRetired`,
  `AuthorizeDurableTailRecoveryHoldContinuableRetiredIdle`,
  `AuthorizeDurableTailRecoveryHoldContinuableRetiredRetired`,
  `MarkRunResumableInitializing`, `MarkRunResumableIdle`,
  `MarkRunResumableAttached`, `ResumeRunRunning`,
  `ReleaseResumableRunInitializing`, `ReleaseResumableRunIdle`,
  `ReleaseResumableRunAttached`, `ReleaseResumableRunRetired`,
  `ReleaseResumableRunStopped`, `SettleResumableRunInitializing`,
  `SettleResumableRunIdle`, `SettleResumableRunAttached`,
  `SettleResumableRunRetired`, `SettleResumableRunStopped`,
  `NormalizeRecoveredInputStagedResumableInitializing`,
  `NormalizeRecoveredInputStagedResumableIdle`,
  `NormalizeRecoveredInputStagedResumableAttached`,
  `NormalizeRecoveredInputStagedResumableRunning`,
  `NormalizeRecoveredInputStagedResumableRetired`,
  `NormalizeRecoveredInputStagedResumableStopped`,
  `NormalizeRecoveredInputAppliedResumableInitializing`,
  `NormalizeRecoveredInputAppliedResumableIdle`,
  `NormalizeRecoveredInputAppliedResumableAttached`,
  `NormalizeRecoveredInputAppliedResumableRunning`,
  `NormalizeRecoveredInputAppliedResumableRetired`,
  `NormalizeRecoveredInputAppliedResumableStopped`,
  `SuspendRunForStopRunningToIdle`, `SuspendRunForStopRunningToAttached`,
  `ReplayAppliedRunContributorIdle`, `ReplayAppliedRunContributorAttached`,
  `ReplayAppliedRunContributorRunning`, `ReplayAppliedRunContributorRetired`,
  `ReplayAppliedRunContributorStopped`,
  `ClassifyStopInputDispositionRetainResumableInitializing`,
  `ClassifyStopInputDispositionRetainResumableIdle`,
  `ClassifyStopInputDispositionRetainResumableAttached`,
  `ClassifyStopInputDispositionRetainResumableRunning`,
  `ClassifyStopInputDispositionRetainResumableRetired`,
  `ClassifyStopInputDispositionRetainResumableStopped`,
  `AuthorizeOperatorDurableTailRepairIdle`,
  `AuthorizeOperatorDurableTailRepairRetired`,
  `AuthorizeOperatorDurableTailRepairRefuseIdle`,
  `AuthorizeOperatorDurableTailRepairRefuseRetired`,
  `AuthorizeOperatorDurableTailRepairRefuseNonQuiescentInitializing`,
  `AuthorizeOperatorDurableTailRepairRefuseNonQuiescentAttached`,
  `AuthorizeOperatorDurableTailRepairRefuseNonQuiescentRunning`,
  `AuthorizeOperatorDurableTailRepairRefuseNonQuiescentStopped` and
  `AuthorizeOperatorDurableTailRepairRefuseNonQuiescentDestroyed`. Its
  `command_capabilities::CommandPlanKind` gains `AuthorizedResumedRun` ahead
  of `AuthorizedRuntimeLoopRunCommit`, so the variants after it change their
  implicit discriminants (`CommandPlanKind::*`); match them by variant name,
  not by numeric cast. The session document kernel's `TransitionId`
  (`generated::session_document`) gains `ClassifyDurableTailContinuable`,
  appended last.
  Behaviour: while a run is marked resumable, `Prepare` for any other run is
  refused and no queued batch is authorized.

- `meerkat-machine-kernels` (`generated::session_turn_admission`) and
  `meerkat-machine-schema` (`catalog::dsl::session_turn_admission`):
  `StartTurnExecutionKind` and `StartTurnDisposition` gain `ResumeRun`,
  appended last, so every 0.9.4 variant keeps its position. The enums are
  exhaustive, so a `match` outside the crate needs the arm. The kernel's
  `TransitionId` gains `ResolveDispositionResumeRun`, appended last.

- `meerkat-core`: `RuntimeExecutionKind` gains `ResumeRun`, the dispatch kind
  of a run a durable session left open and the runtime resumes. It is never an
  admission kind. `meerkat-contracts`: `WireRuntimeExecutionKind` gains
  `ResumeRun` (`"resume_run"`), mirroring the core kind. Both enums are
  exhaustive, so a `match` outside the crate needs the arm. The gate's finding
  for each: an added enum variant.

- `meerkat-runtime`: `meerkat_machine::dsl::RecoveredRuntimeExecutionKind`
  implements `TryFrom<RuntimeExecutionKind>`, with the error
  `DispatchOnlyExecutionKind`, instead of `From`. Recovering a stored input
  that carries the dispatch-only `ResumeRun` kind is refused as store
  corruption. Code that converted with `from` or `into` calls `try_from`.
  Declared by hand: the removed `From` impl may not be a gate finding.

- `meerkat-machine-schema`, `meerkat-mob`, `meerkat-machine-kernels`:
  MobMachine's `ResolveAutonomousShutdownMemberAction` input (the schema's
  and meerkat-mob's `MobMachineInput` variant and the kernel's input struct)
  gains the field `keeps_durable_run: bool`, appended last, so code that
  builds it literally must set it (`false` keeps the earlier behavior).
  `AutonomousShutdownMemberActionKind` (meerkat-machine-schema,
  meerkat-mob's `machines::mob_machine` and the kernel) gains
  `KeepForResume`, appended last; an exhaustive match needs the new arm. The
  kernel `generated::mob::TransitionId` gains
  `ResolveAutonomousShutdownMemberActionKeepForResumeRunning`,
  `ResolveAutonomousShutdownMemberActionKeepForResumeStopped` and
  `ResolveAutonomousShutdownMemberActionKeepForResumeCompleted`, appended
  last, so no existing implicit discriminant changes (see the default
  graceful Shutdown of a durable member, below).

- `meerkat-machine-kernels`: the kernel `generated::mob::TransitionId` gains
  `ObserveRuntimeDestroyedStopped`, `ObserveRuntimeDestroyedCompleted`,
  `AdmitDestroyMemberRetireRuntimeEndedRunning` and
  `AdmitDestroyMemberRetireRuntimeEndedStopped`, appended last, so no
  existing implicit discriminant changes (see Fixed, a member runtime
  destroyed outside the mob, and a mob whose member runtime ended outside
  it).

- `meerkat-core`: `AgentEvent` gains the variant `RunResumed { session_id,
  run_id, round, resume_point }`, wire type `run_resumed`, with the new enum
  `RunResumePointKind` (`tools_pending`, `awaiting_model`; non-exhaustive).
  A run resumed from its run cursor publishes it in place of `RunStarted`
  (see Added, per-round commits). `AgentEvent` is non-exhaustive, so a Rust
  match already has a wildcard arm; the published event catalog
  (`meerkat_contracts::KNOWN_AGENT_EVENT_TYPES`) lists the new type, and the
  generated SDK inventories with it. An SDK of this version surfaces the event
  as its unknown-event form; an older SDK refuses the unknown type, as for any
  newer contract.

- Behaviour-only (not measured by the gate): `meerkat-core`: a
  `SessionCheckpointer` whose `checkpoint_run` returns `Ok(None)` (no receipt)
  for a run's first round commit now fails that tool round before any of its
  tools runs: a round whose first commit is not durable dispatches nothing.
  Before, `Ok(None)` was accepted at every checkpoint. The session layer's
  checkpointer returns no receipt only for a session that has never committed
  a boundary, and runtime-backed sessions commit their first boundary at
  creation.

- The pending callback call carries its dedupe key (see Added, dedupe key
  delivery). `meerkat-core`: `PendingCallbackToolCall` gains the field
  `dedupe_key: Option<ToolCallDedupeKey>`, the struct variant
  `AgentError::CallbackPending` gains `dedupe_key:
  Option<Box<ToolCallDedupeKey>>`, and the struct variant
  `CoreApplyTerminal::CallbackPending` gains `dedupe_key:
  Option<ToolCallDedupeKey>`. `meerkat-runtime`: the struct variant
  `CompletionOutcome::CallbackPending` gains `dedupe_key:
  Option<ToolCallDedupeKey>`. `meerkat-mob`: the struct variants
  `MobError::CallbackPending` and `BoundedTurnFailure::CallbackPending` gain
  `dedupe_key: Option<Box<ToolCallDedupeKey>>`, so a host answering a
  member's callback from either sees the key, as the batch variants already
  carry it on each `PendingCallbackToolCall`. `meerkat-contracts`:
  `WirePendingToolCall` gains `dedupe_key: Option<ToolCallDedupeKey>`, and
  `WireCallbackPending::single` takes the key as its eighth argument. Rust
  code that builds these with struct literals names the new field
  (`dedupe_key: None` for a call outside an agent-loop round), and a pattern
  that lists every field adds it or `..`. On the wire the field is optional
  and omitted when absent, so readers that ignore unknown fields are
  unaffected. A pending callback call persisted with a dedupe key cannot be
  finalized after downgrading to a runtime that lacks the field: its stored
  candidate digest no longer verifies there. A row without a key keeps its
  bytes.

- `meerkat-mob`: `Profile` gains `durable: bool` (see Added, durable
  workers), and so do its wire forms `meerkat_contracts::WireMobProfile`,
  `MobProfileInput` and `PortableProfile`. A struct literal needs the field;
  `durable: false` keeps today's behaviour. Serde reads an omitted `durable`
  as false and writes it only when true, so a stored or sent ordinary profile
  keeps its bytes, and the adaptive `LayerDecision` schema leaves it out, so
  packs stay compatible across versions. The wire forms refuse unknown fields,
  so an older host refuses a profile that sets `durable`. A spawn of a durable
  profile on a mob whose member sessions do not outlive the process
  (`MobSessionService::keeps_durable_member_sessions`, see Added) is
  refused with the new `MobError::NonDurableService { member_id, profile }`,
  under the existing `CAPABILITY_UNAVAILABLE` wire code (structured data kind
  `mob_non_durable_service`).

- `meerkat-core::ProviderMeta` and `meerkat-contracts::WireProviderMeta` gain
  the `GeminiFunctionCall { provider_id, thought_signature }` variant,
  serialized with `provider: "gemini_function_call"` and required
  `provider_id`. Downstream exhaustive Rust matches and wire decoders must
  handle this metadata for provider-issued Gemini call IDs. Persisted
  transcripts using
  this metadata cannot be read after downgrading to a runtime or SDK that
  lacks the variant or its required `provider_id` field. The existing
  signature-only `Gemini` variant and Gemini's HTTP `functionCall.id` and
  `functionResponse.id` fields are unchanged. The new variant is declared
  between `Gemini` and `OpenAi`, so in both enums the implicit discriminants
  of `OpenAi`, `OpenAiResponse` and `OpenAiAssistantMessage` move up by one;
  their serialized `provider` tags are unchanged.

- `meerkat-schedule`: the occurrence lifecycle carries the admission evidence
  of an occurrence's receipt history (see Fixed, scheduled delivery after a
  lost executor). `OccurrenceLifecycleInput::ClassifyDue` and `Claim` gain the
  field `admission_evidence: AdmissionEvidence`, `ResolveTargetProbe` gains
  the field `redelivery: Option<ExistingDelivery>` (the redelivery the claim
  named, `None` for an ordinary claim), and the input gains the variants
  `ResolveReclaimExhausted` and `ResolveUnprovenLateNotAdmitted`.
  `OccurrenceLifecycleEffect` gains `DueReclaimExhausted`,
  `ReclaimedAfterAdmission` and `ReclaimedAfterUnprovenDispatch`.
  `OccurrenceDueAction` gains `ReclaimExhausted` and is now
  `#[non_exhaustive]`. `Occurrence::classify_due_action` takes the evidence
  as a second argument. The gate's findings: added enum variants, struct
  variant fields added, a method parameter count change, and an enum marked
  non-exhaustive. Code outside the crate that builds these inputs passes
  `AdmissionEvidence::None` and `redelivery: None`, the earlier behaviour,
  unless it derives the evidence with `AdmissionEvidence::from_receipt_stages`
  and the redelivery from the claim's effects. The variants after the new
  ones change their implicit discriminants (`OccurrenceLifecycleEffect::*`
  and `OccurrenceLifecycleInput::*`); match them by variant name, not by
  numeric cast. The persisted occurrence is unchanged (schema version 9).
- `meerkat-machine-kernels`: the generated occurrence machine
  (`generated::occurrence_lifecycle`) gains the same inputs and effects:
  `Input`, `InputKind` and `OccurrenceLifecycleInputVariant` gain
  `ResolveReclaimExhausted` and `ResolveUnprovenLateNotAdmitted`; `Effect`
  and `EffectKind` gain `DueReclaimExhausted`, `ReclaimedAfterAdmission` and
  `ReclaimedAfterUnprovenDispatch`; `TransitionId` gains
  `ClassifyDuePendingReclaimExhausted`, `ClaimPendingAfterAdmission`,
  `ClaimPendingAfterUnprovenDispatch`, `TargetProbeBusyExistingRedelivery`,
  `ReclaimExhaustedAfterAdmission`, `ReclaimExhaustedAfterUnprovenDispatch`,
  `UnprovenLateNotAdmittedFromClaimed` and
  `UnprovenLateNotAdmittedFromDispatching`. Every new variant is appended
  after the 0.9.4 ones, so the 0.9.4 variants keep their implicit
  discriminants (`EffectKind::*`, `InputKind::*`,
  `OccurrenceLifecycleInputVariant::*` and `TransitionId::*`) and their
  `PartialOrd` order. The input structs
  `ClassifyDue` and `Claim` gain the public field `admission_evidence`, and
  `ResolveTargetProbe` gains `redelivery` (struct literals need them).
- `meerkat-machine-schema` (`catalog::dsl::occurrence_lifecycle`): the
  occurrence machine's DSL enums gain the same variants and input fields
  (`OccurrenceLifecycleEffectVariant` and `OccurrenceLifecycleInputVariant`
  included), declared after the 0.9.4 ones, so the 0.9.4 variants keep their
  implicit discriminants and their `PartialOrd` order.

- `meerkat-contracts`: `SessionExternalEventParams` and `MobMemberSendParams`
  gain the field `idempotency_key: Option<String>`, and `MobMemberSendResult`
  gains `continuation: Option<WireContinuationReceipt>` (see Added). Code that
  builds them with struct literals sets the new fields; `None` keeps the
  earlier behaviour. The accept-input params that no method took are removed:
  `wire::runtime::SessionAcceptInputParams`, `WireRunPrimitive`,
  `WireStagedRunInput`, `WireConversationAppend` and
  `WireConversationAppendRole`. On the wire the key is optional: a server
  before 0.9.5 refuses it on `mob/member_send` (its params deny unknown
  fields) and drops it on `session/external_event` and the REST route, so the
  Python and TypeScript SDKs refuse a key against a server older than contract
  0.9.5.

- `meerkat-runtime`: the continuation admission index can release a
  reservation (see Fixed, continuations on a retired address).
  `ContinuationAdmissionTransition` gains the variant `Release`,
  `ContinuationAdmissionOutcome` gains the variant `Released`, and
  `ContinuationAdmissionTransition::next` answers
  `Option<ContinuationAdmissionEntry>` (`Holds(entry)`, or `Released` for a
  legal release) instead of `Option<ContinuationAdmission>`. A store that
  implements `RuntimeStore::transition_continuation_admission` itself
  removes the entry for `Released`, in the same transaction; a store that
  forwards the transition is unchanged.
- `meerkat-auth-core` (hosted MCP OAuth, #1808): `McpOAuthError` gains the
  variant `RemoteCustodyRequired { server_name }`, a refusal: an attempt
  started on a registered `https` redirect was completed without the host's
  retained attempt handle. The semver gate reports it as an enum variant
  added to an exhaustive enum; a match outside the crate needs the arm
  (surfaces map it to the reason `invalid_target` with the detail
  `remote_custody_required`). The enum stays exhaustive on purpose (the
  facade maps every variant to a reason with no wildcard arm), so every
  future variant is a declared break too. The text of `DisconnectRequired`
  now names its remedy: "disconnect it first: log it out, then log in
  again".
- `meerkat-contracts` (hosted MCP OAuth, #1808): `WireLoginStart` gains
  `host_attempt_handle: Option<String>`, `WireMcpLoginStart` gains
  `attempt_ref: Option<String>`, `LoginCompleteParams` gains
  `host_attempt_handle: Option<String>` and `iss: Option<String>`, and
  `WireAuthErrorData` and `WireAuthErrorBody` gain
  `detail: Option<WireAuthErrorDetail>`. The semver gate reports each as a
  field added to a constructible struct; struct literals pass `None` for the
  earlier behaviour. On the wire every new field is optional and omitted when
  absent, so loopback starts and completions and every existing error keep
  their exact JSON.
- `meerkat-machine-schema`, `meerkat-core` and `meerkat-machine-kernels`:
  `DurableHeadRelation` (the session document's DSL enum and its two
  generated copies) gains the variant `VerifiedRewriteDescendant`, appended
  after `Unverifiable`. All three are exhaustive, so a `match` on one adds the
  arm.

- Resumed provider switches (see Fixed, provider override on resume):
  `meerkat-core`'s `ConnectionTargetError` gains the variant
  `NoCredentialAccountRoute { provider, account }`; `meerkat`'s
  `LlmIdentityPreflightError` gains the variant
  `BindingSelection { source }`; and `meerkat-mob`'s
  `MaterializePreflightProbe::preflight_llm_identity` gains the parameter
  `resume_prior: Option<&SessionLlmIdentity>` (the resumed session's durable
  identity, `None` for a fresh member). Behaviour-only: a resume whose
  provider override changes the provider no longer restores the durable
  binding, also when the configuration now points that binding's name at the
  new provider; the new provider resolves its own route. A resumed
  self-hosted session whose build claims the model or the provider without
  naming a server follows the registry's server for its model, in the
  factory and in a mob member's merge alike, instead of the durable server.

- `meerkat-mob-mcp`: `MobMcpState::mob_list` returns each managed mob with
  its `MobLifecycleObservation` instead of its `MobState` (see Fixed, a
  listed mob whose actor has stopped); the phase is the observation's
  `phase`.

- `meerkat-contracts`: `MobStatusResult` gains the field
  `failure: Option<WireMobLifecycleFailure>`, so code that builds it as a
  struct literal sets `failure: None`. The wire stays additive: the field is
  left out when absent.

- `meerkat-auth-core` (bounded MCP OAuth network stages): `McpOAuthError`
  gains the variants `NetworkTimedOut { server_name, stage }` and
  `CommitUnsettled { server_name }`, appended last. `NetworkTimedOut`: a
  network stage of an MCP login got no answer within its bound
  (`McpOAuthNetworkStage`); nothing was published, a start admitted no
  attempt and a completion's attempt was retired, and
  `McpOAuthNetworkStage::code_sent` says whether the authorization code had
  been sent. `CommitUnsettled`: the credential commit consumed the attempt,
  or may have, and did not report within its observation bound, or its owner
  was lost, or it failed after the consume and could not restore the
  previous credential and lifecycle; whether the credential landed is
  unknown until the commit settles, and a later read of the stored
  credential reports it. It is never a success and never a clean failure.
  The semver gate reports each as an enum variant added to an exhaustive
  enum (`McpOAuthError` stays exhaustive, as above); a match outside the
  crate needs the arms. Surfaces map `NetworkTimedOut` to the reason
  `upstream_failure` with the detail `upstream_timeout` (the code had not
  been sent) or `upstream_timeout_after_code`, and `CommitUnsettled` to the
  new reason `commit_unsettled`.

- `meerkat-contracts` (bounded MCP OAuth network stages):
  `WireAuthErrorReason` gains `CommitUnsettled`, appended last; the semver
  gate reports it as an enum variant added to an exhaustive enum.
  `WireAuthErrorDetail`, new in this release (hosted MCP OAuth above),
  includes `UpstreamTimeout` and `UpstreamTimeoutAfterCode`. On the wire
  they are new values
  (`upstream_timeout`, `upstream_timeout_after_code`, `commit_unsettled`);
  SDK helpers built before them read them as absent.

- `meerkat-core` (bounded MCP OAuth network stages):
  `CredentialMutationError` gains the variant `RollbackFailed(String)`,
  appended last: a publication failed after it acquired the credential
  lifecycle, and restoring the previous credential and lifecycle failed too,
  so what is stored is unsettled. The commit paths of `meerkat-auth-core`
  (`save_tokens_and_publish_lifecycle`,
  `save_oauth_tokens_and_consume_browser_flow` and
  `save_oauth_tokens_and_consume_device_flow`) return it where they returned
  `AuthLifecycle` ("acquired lease rollback failed"). The semver gate reports
  it as an enum variant added to an exhaustive enum; a match outside the
  crate needs the arm. An MCP login completion now ends such a commit as
  `McpOAuthError::CommitUnsettled` (reason `commit_unsettled`), where it
  ended as `AuthLifecycle` (reason `infrastructure`). A connector login
  reports it as `ConnectorLoginError::CommitUnsettled` (below). A provider
  login's `HostAuthError::CredentialMutation` now carries `RollbackFailed`
  where it carried `AuthLifecycle`, with the reason `commit_unsettled`.

- `meerkat-auth-core` (unsettled credential commits): `ConnectorLoginError`
  gains the unit variant `CommitUnsettled`, appended last: a connector
  login's commit failed and could not restore the previous credential, or
  its owner ended after the attempt was consumed, so whether the credential
  landed is unknown. It carries no store text. The semver gate reports it as
  an enum variant added to an exhaustive enum; a match outside the crate
  needs the arm. Surfaces map it to the reason `commit_unsettled`.

- Behaviour-only (not measured by the gate): unsettled credential commits on
  every surface. A connector login whose commit owner ended before the
  consume is refused with `CredentialAccess` (`Pending`) and its attempt is
  retired, so nothing is published; after the consume it is
  `CommitUnsettled`, and a connector logout whose owner was lost is
  `CommitUnsettled` too, where all three were `AuthLifecycle`. A provider
  commit or logout whose rollback failed or whose owner was lost
  (`HostAuthError::CredentialMutation` with `RollbackFailed` or `Cancelled`)
  reports `commit_unsettled` where it reported `infrastructure`.
  `commit_unsettled` has one fixed public text, "the credential commit's
  outcome is unknown; read the status later", for every source; the detail
  stays in protected diagnostics. `auth/profile/create`,
  `auth/login/provision_api_key` and `POST /auth/profiles` answer a failed
  credential commit with a typed reason and a fixed text, where they put the
  store's own error text in the message and carried no reason; their codes
  are unchanged. `HostAuthService::mcp_status` now reports what a use of the
  stored credential would do, through the same rule
  (`McpOAuthAuthority::stored_credential_status`): a stored credential the
  use path refuses is `reauth_required` where it was `authorized`, and the
  read may restore the credential's lifecycle from its durable marker, as a
  use does. It never waits for the credential's lifecycle owner: while the
  owner is busy, the stored credential's own expiry decides.

- Behaviour-only (not measured by the gate): `meerkat-auth-core`:
  `auth_oauth::credential_http_client` and a required egress profile's
  credential client now bound every request: 30 s in total
  (`CREDENTIAL_REQUEST_TIMEOUT`) and 10 s to connect
  (`CREDENTIAL_CONNECT_TIMEOUT`). This covers every credential request Core
  sends with them, provider OAuth included (token, refresh, device code, and
  the code-assist setup requests). A token or device-code request that runs
  out of time reports `OAuthError::Timeout` where it reported
  `OAuthError::Network`; both stay transient for a refresh. The MCP
  transports' client (`same_origin_credential_http_client`) and the egress
  profile's ordinary and protected clients are unchanged: they carry tool
  calls and event streams.

- Behaviour-only (not measured by the gate): `meerkat-auth-core`:
  `McpOAuthAuthority` bounds each network stage of a start, a completion and
  a refresh (`McpOAuthNetworkBounds`), its account strategy's calls
  included: a host `McpOAuthAccountStrategy`'s `preflight` and
  `observe_account` futures are dropped at their stage bound. A confirmed
  retirement of an attempt (cancel by state or reference, a cancel handle, a
  logout) now also ends a completion of it already in flight, at once:
  `login_complete`, `login_complete_registered` and a pending loopback
  login's completion return `AttemptRetired` (the consuming `complete` with
  its close receipt). A completion observes its credential commit for a
  bounded time; one not admitted by then is retired and refused with
  `CredentialAccess` (`Pending`), and one past its consume is
  `CommitUnsettled`, where a lost commit owner was reported as
  `AuthLifecycle`. A well-known probe that timed out is a typed timeout, no
  longer an absent document. `McpOAuthPendingLogin::complete_until` keeps
  bounding only the callback wait with its deadline; the completion after
  delivery is now bounded too.

- A working directory for stdio MCP servers (see Added). `meerkat-core`:
  `McpStdioConfig` gains `cwd: Option<String>` (struct literals need the
  field; `None` is the earlier behaviour, and a configuration without it
  serializes unchanged), `McpConfigError` and `McpRealmPersistError` gain
  `Cwd(McpStdioCwdError)`, and `McpAttachmentTarget::Stdio` gains
  `cwd: Option<String>`. `meerkat-mcp`: `McpError` gains
  `WorkingDirectory(McpStdioCwdError)`. The semver gate reports a field added
  to a constructible struct, variants added to exhaustive enums and a field
  added to an enum struct variant; exhaustive matches need the new arms. A
  configuration, realm document or persisted profile that sets `cwd` is
  refused by binaries without the field (`McpStdioConfig` denies unknown
  fields), never run without it. The Python SDK's generated `McpStdioConfig`
  dataclass lists its optional fields alphabetically, so `cwd` now comes
  before `env` and `secret_env`: pass those by keyword.

- Behaviour-only (not measured by the gate): `meerkat-sqlite`:
  `watch::sqlite_watch_event_relevant`, and so the `Changed` ticks of
  `watch::start_sqlite_change_watch`, no longer count a connection's own
  open and close as a change: no event on the database's `-shm` file (the
  WAL index), and no creation, removal or metadata change of its `-wal`
  file. A write to the `-wal` (a commit), every event on the database file
  or on the directory itself, and an event that names no path still count.
  0.9.4 counted every event but an access on all three files.

- Behaviour-only (not measured by the gate): `meerkat-runtime`:
  `SqliteRuntimeStore::delivery_generation_reader` returns a reader on the
  fresh-open read path too, where 0.9.4 returned `None`. It keeps no
  connection, and answers a store notification from its last read while
  the database and its WAL stat as they did before that read
  (`DeliveryGenerationReader::read_on_notification`).
- `meerkat-contracts`: the mob destroy report is typed on the wire.
  `MobDestroyResult.destroy_report` changes from `serde_json::Value` to
  `WireMobDestroyReport`, and `MobLifecycleResult.destroy_report` from
  `Option<serde_json::Value>` to `Option<WireMobDestroyReport>` (see
  Added). The JSON value each surface sends is unchanged. Inside
  `destroy_report`, the members of the JSON-RPC `mob/destroy` and
  `mob/lifecycle` results and of the `@rkat/web` `Mob.lifecycle()` result now
  follow the report's field order, as the domain report serializes, instead
  of alphabetical order; the `mob_destroy_incomplete` data keeps its bytes.
  Code that read the field as a `Value` reads the struct's fields instead;
  code that builds a result converts a `meerkat_mob::MobDestroyReport` with
  `WireMobDestroyReport::from(&report)`.
- TypeScript and Web SDKs (not measured by the gate): `@rkat/sdk`'s
  `MeerkatClient.mobDestroy()` returns `destroyReport` as
  `WireMobDestroyReport` instead of `Record<string, unknown>`, and rejects a
  malformed report with `INVALID_RESPONSE`. `@rkat/web`'s `Mob.lifecycle()`
  rejects a refused action with a `MeerkatError` (`code`, `message`,
  `data`), as the other `Mob` methods do, instead of the runtime's JSON
  error string, and rejects a malformed destroy report.

- `meerkat-mob-mcp`: `HostJobSource::new` refuses a namespace in the
  Core-owned `meerkat.` prefix (for example the consent notices'
  `meerkat.consent`) with the new `HostJobSourceError::ReservedNamespace`, a
  new construction-time refusal for callers that declared one. No host
  source may own a reserved namespace.

- `meerkat-contracts`: `BridgeMaterializePayload` gains
  `report_adopted_first_turn: bool` and `BridgeMaterializedResponse` gains
  `adopted_first_turn: Option<BridgeAdoptedFirstTurn>` (see the protocol 7
  report under Added); `meerkat-mob`:
  `runtime::host_actor::MaterializedMemberRow` and
  `runtime::host_materialize::MaterializedBuildOutcome` gain
  `adopted_first_turn: Option<BridgeAdoptedFirstTurn>`, and
  `store::PlacedSpawnCommitRecord` gains `adopted_first_turn_started: bool`.
  Code that builds them with a struct literal sets the new field, normally
  to `false` or `None`.

- Behaviour-only (not measured by the gate): `meerkat-mob`: a resume spawn of
  an existing session whose first turn already started no longer delivers the
  spawn's `initial_message` (see Fixed). A caller that sent a message with a
  resume to give the member new work sends it after the resume.

- `meerkat-core`: `service::SessionBuildOptions` gains the field
  `prompt_context_fork_source: Option<PromptContextForkSource>`, and
  `meerkat`'s `AgentBuildConfig` gains the same field: the typed source
  member (and, when the controller knows it, the source session) of a
  prompt-context fork child, which the mob runtime sets on that child's
  create build. The standard build pipeline does not read it; a host's
  build hook may. Code that builds either type with a struct literal sets
  it, normally to `None`.

- `meerkat-core`: `SystemNoticeBlock` gains the variant
  `ForkBoundary(Box<fork_notice::ForkBoundaryNotice>)` (wire block type
  `fork_boundary`): the typed fork notice a fork child is given once,
  before its first input (see the behaviour entry below). Code that matches
  the enum exhaustively adds an arm for it. A 0.9.4 reader decodes the
  block as `Unknown` with its `summary`, so it still shows the model the
  notice text, and so does this release for a block holding a fork kind
  or reason a later release adds.

- `meerkat-contracts`: `BridgeMaterializePayload` gains
  `prompt_context_fork: Option<BridgePromptContextFork>`; `meerkat-mob`:
  `runtime::host_actor::MaterializedMemberRow` gains
  `prompt_context_fork_digest: Option<String>` and
  `runtime::host_materialize::MaterializeServingContext` gains
  `prompt_context_fork: Option<MaterializePromptContextFork>` (see the
  protocol 7 entry under Added). Code that builds them with a struct
  literal sets the new field, normally to `None`; a materialized row
  written before it reads as `None`.

- `meerkat-runtime`: `meerkat_machine_types::SupervisorBridgeCommandKind`
  gains the variants `HostFeatures` and `ReadMemberVisibleTools`, appended
  after `MemberOperatorRequest` (no other discriminant moves), for the
  protocol 7 commands of the same names. `HostFeatures` is admitted and
  served by the host daemon (`NotMemberAddressed`, served off the member
  drain); `ReadMemberVisibleTools` is admitted through the bound-supervisor
  ladder and served on the member drain. Exhaustive matches must handle
  both.

- Not measured by the gate (a wire change): `meerkat-core`:
  `ForkInstructionRefusal` gains `skills: Box<[SkillKey]>`, the skills a
  fork's source loaded with the built-in `load_skill` tool or, for a
  durable fork, was given as per-turn skill context (see the next
  entries), and `unreadable_skill_loads: u32`, the number of
  `load_skill` calls whose arguments name no skill. Each is serialized
  only when not empty or zero, and only a refusal that concerns
  loaded skills sets them; its message names only what the child would
  inherit. A decoder built from 0.9.4 denies unknown fields on this type
  and rejects a refusal that names either.

- Not measured by the gate (a behaviour change): `meerkat-mob`: a
  prompt-context fork (`MemberLaunchMode::Fork`, which
  `MobHandle::fork_helper` uses) gives the child only what the mob's fork
  instruction policy allows of its source's history, decided by each
  row's type (see Fixed):
  - the source's system prompt and host system context are never carried;
  - under the default `require_explicit_activation`, activated instruction
    bodies, skill bodies the source loaded with `load_skill` and
    host-injected context rows (per-turn memory recall) are not carried,
    and each `load_skill` result is replaced by a line naming the skill;
  - under `refuse`, a fork whose rendered rows hold an activation row or a
    `load_skill` result is refused with `MobError::ForkInstructionRefused`
    before anything is spawned;
  - under `reactivate_inherited`, each activated key's effective
    instruction, the skill bodies and the host-injected context rows are
    carried.
  A child created on this host gets the planned context as one typed
  injected-context row and a typed fork notice (`fork_boundary` block)
  before its first input, whoever starts that first turn, instead of a
  prefix of its first prompt; the notice names the source and, by name
  only, the instructions, skills and tools the child lost or gained. A
  child placed on a member host gets them the same way when its host
  serves prompt-context fork children (supervisor bridge protocol 7, see
  Added); toward a host of 0.9.4 or earlier it gets the context as a
  prompt prefix that ends with a `[fork_notice]:` line. A durable fork's
  child
  (`fork_member` and the forks built on it) gets the same notice, of kind
  `transcript`, at its first turn. The rendered rows fit a byte budget,
  newest first: half the child model's context window at four bytes per
  token, at most 256 KiB (256 KiB for a model the catalog does not know);
  the notice counts the older rows it left out. A fork whose newest row
  alone does not fit is refused before anything is spawned with the new
  `MobError::ForkContextTooLarge` (code `INVALID_PARAMS`, data kind
  `fork_context_too_large`).
