- The bundled SQLite is built without its three process-wide locks:
  allocator statistics, one page cache shared by every connection, and
  page-cache overflow statistics. Each put a mutex in front of every
  connection in the process, so concurrent sessions in one host queued on
  each other: sixteen threads that each opened their own database opened
  fewer connections per second together than one thread alone. The
  repository builds set `LIBSQLITE3_FLAGS` to
  `meerkat_sqlite::REQUIRED_LIBSQLITE3_FLAGS`
  (`-DSQLITE_DEFAULT_MEMSTATUS=0 -USQLITE_ENABLE_MEMORY_MANAGEMENT
  -DSQLITE_DISABLE_PAGECACHE_OVERFLOW_STATS`): Cargo through
  `.cargo/config.toml` (forced over a value in the environment) and Bazel
  through `MODULE.bazel`. Nothing Meerkat calls reads what the locks provided
  (SQLite's memory statistics, heap limits and `sqlite3_release_memory`). A
  build outside the repository (`cargo install rkat`, an application that
  embeds Meerkat) sets the variable itself; see "SQLite Lock Profile" in the
  deploying guide. Every host binary (`rkat`, `rkat-rpc`, `rkat-rest`,
  `rkat-mcp`, `rkat-mob-mcp`) turns allocator statistics off as the first
  statement of `main`, which removes that lock even without the variable.
- `meerkat-sqlite`: `ExclusiveFence` now holds the presence lock as well and
  creates `<file>.mpresence` next to each database it fences. `try_acquire`
  takes both locks or neither, and `acquire` takes the fence lock, then waits
  for the presence lock within the same deadline, so maintenance waits for
  kept connections to close.
- `meerkat-store`: the storage doctor's artifact sweep (`rkat storage
  doctor`) lists `*.mpresence` presence lock files as
  `maintenance-fence-lock` findings, as it lists the `*.mfence` fence lock
  files.
- A runtime delivery owner on a store other processes share reads the
  store's delivery generation through one kept connection instead of a
  verified open on every store tick (up to one tick per 10 ms on a busy
  store). In the ignored `bench_fresh_and_kept_generation_reads` test, in a
  release build on a shared 192-core host, a kept read took about 19
  microseconds and a fresh one about 500. The connection holds the
  database's presence lock and still takes the shared fence guard for each
  read; under the guard it checks that the path still names the file it
  opened and that the schema and the delivery domain's ledger row are
  unchanged, and opens again, verified, when they are not. The maintenance
  fence takes the presence lock after its fence lock, and the reader closes
  before its owner calls into the host, at its next read, which the fence
  refuses, or after `KEPT_DELIVERY_READER_IDLE` (1 second) without a read,
  so maintenance gets the database well inside `rkat storage migrate`'s
  default 10-second fence wait. Windows keeps the fresh-open read path
  because no CI lane runs the kept reader on Windows.
  Maintenance from an older binary takes only the fence lock and does not
  wait for a kept connection: run maintenance with the same release as the
  hosts.
- `meerkat-mob`: a mob Shutdown or Stop of a local member whose runtime
  registration is durability-degraded reports the member's run and run starts
  as `ReloadRequired`, where it failed or waited on the degraded registration.
  An autonomous member whose registration degrades after the stop held its run
  starts, so that the stop's cancel of its current run is refused, reports its
  run `ReloadRequired` and its run starts `Held`: that cancel was not
  dispatched. A degraded registration starts no run until a reload replaces
  it; a Shutdown's teardown discards it and unregisters the cold successor,
  and the `MobStop` a Stop staged first holds the reloaded registration until
  Resume. An autonomous member's stop skips its comms-drain abort and its run
  settlement for such a registration (the discard aborts and joins the drain
  itself). A Resume refuses typed (`MemberReloadRequired`, naming the member)
  while a member needs a durability reload, before anything moves; reload that
  member, then Resume. A reload while the mob is Stopped answers `Discarded`:
  its successor stays held, and the Resume completes its revival. Until its
  reload such a member starts no run, requests to it are refused typed the
  same way, and its member status and member list entry carry an error naming
  the reload. A Shutdown now holds every member's run starts and reports the
  first failure in roster order instead of stopping at it. On the wire,
  `stop_report` reports such a member with `run` and `starts`
  `reload_required`.

- `meerkat-runtime`: a fenced write whose `RuntimeStoreWriteFence` answers
  `Backoff` while the writer holds an async lock (the in-memory runtime
  store's fenced writes, and `MeerkatMachine`'s publication of a registered
  session) is tried again for up to 2 seconds before the `Backoff` is
  reported, with the lock released between attempts and each attempt
  re-reading what it writes. The trait's documentation now says
  `execute_if_current` never waits beyond its own I/O, so a caller that holds
  an async lock may call it provided it retries a `Backoff` the same way; a
  fence caller in another crate that holds an async lock should do so too.

### Fixed

- `meerkat-mob`: a member whose session's canonical head has moved past its
  committed runtime boundary respawns. A respawn reads the tool restrictions
  the member was spawned under before it retires anything; the persistent read
  materialized the session's transcript at the committed boundary, and the
  store refused it as a transcript revision conflict while a durable tail was
  ahead of that boundary or a turn was between its checkpoint and its
  boundary commit. The respawn, and the reset built on it, was refused and the
  member kept its old incarnation. HeadCanonical sessions now read the
  restrictions from the current boundary's metadata under one store snapshot,
  without the transcript.

- A live open refused because another live open on the same host was still
  being set up is now the typed, retryable
  `RealtimeSessionOpenProjectionError::Backpressured`, not an internal session
  error. A host admits live opens one at a time per process and queues none,
  and an open keeps that admission until its provider has acknowledged its
  seed: for a provider-brokered WebRTC channel (the provider answers the
  client's offer), through that offer and answer. A second open during that
  setup (two people starting voice, or a voice call and another live
  channel) was refused, and surfaces reported it as an internal failure the
  caller could not tell from a broken host.
  `rkat-rpc` `live/open` now answers it with the retryable `SessionBusy` code
  (-32002) and a member live host with `MemberLiveError::Unavailable`.
  Clients retry with backoff; the open succeeds once the other open's setup
  has finished.
- `meerkat-mob`: a Stop during a member's run no longer abandons that run's
  turn. A Stop leaves a turn-driven member's running turn to finish
  (`MemberStopRun::LeftRunning`), but it also cancelled every member
  session's checkpoint gate, so the run failed at its final checkpoint, on
  WholeBlob and HeadCanonical realms alike. The turn ended with an error
  ("turn abandoned"), the member's runtime was torn down, and the session
  kept nothing of the run although its tool calls had already run; Resume
  did not run the input again. The Stop now leaves the gates armed, and so
  does a failed Reset, which returns the mob to the same pause: the run
  finishes and commits while the mob is Stopped, and the member stays
  registered. A host that deletes a mob's storage after a Stop must Destroy
  the mob instead, since a run in flight at the Stop can still commit. The
  Stop watchdog no longer reports a `stop_checkpointer_cancel` stage.

- `meerkat-mob`: a mob restarts when one of its members has a durable tail
  ahead of the runtime boundary it last committed. A turn's durable rows can
  land after that boundary when a retirement cancels the turn mid-way, or when
  the process dies between the two commits. If that member's retirement was
  still pending, the next start restored the member's cleanup delivery by
  reading its session at the committed boundary; the
  store refused the read as a transcript revision conflict, and the whole mob
  stopped before admitting any command. The restore now settles the tail
  first, through the store-owned recovery the resume path runs (a proven
  continuation is adopted), and then reads the session.

- `meerkat-session`: a member retires, respawns or resets when its retirement
  cancels a turn at the turn's boundary. A turn cancelled after its durable
  rows landed commits no boundary, so the session's canonical head stayed
  ahead of the runtime boundary while this process still hosted the member's
  live session. Every read of the session was refused as a transcript
  revision conflict, and the retirement, or the respawn or destructive reset
  built on it, stopped after it had durably started. A read of a hosted live
  session that still conflicts after its retries now settles that tail
  through the store-owned recovery a restart runs (a proven continuation is
  adopted; a held or refused tail is left intact), and then reads again.

- `meerkat-mob`: a mob Stop or Shutdown no longer fails with an internal error
  when a member's runtime unregister is past its final transition, for
  example when the member's own runtime loop unregisters it as the Stop
  reaches it: its store finalization still in flight, its outcome unknown, or
  a failed finalization left the registration for the next unregister. Such a
  registration refuses every lifecycle mutation, and its runtime loop has
  already exited. The stop now reports the member's run `NoRun` and its run
  starts `Held`: the registration starts no run until the unregister removes
  it, and the `MobStop` a Stop staged first holds any registration that
  replaces it until Resume. A Resume's release of that member is answered the
  same way, and a Shutdown's teardown joins or retries the unregister as for
  any member. For a placed member, the member's host answers a supervisor's
  bridged hold the same way (`RunStartsHeld` with no run) and its release
  with `Ack`, and a restore of a Stopped mob in the same process stages the
  member's hold without failing. `MeerkatMachine::hold_run_starts` and
  `release_run_starts` refuse such a registration typed
  (`UnregisterFinalizationOutcomeUnknown` while the final transition is
  staged, `ValidationFailed` as the teardown-only anchor) instead of
  `Internal`, and `MeerkatMachine::unregister_owed` reports the state.

- `meerkat-mob-mcp`: after a restart, the session that created a mob with
  the agent mob tools manages it again. A session's persisted mob operator
  authority binds no mob, so the manage grant its create returned was gone
  after a restart; the agent mob tools now re-derive it, for the incarnation
  the mob runs at, from the mob's creation record, while the session may
  still create mobs. The record proves it only for the session's own create:
  `MobProvenance::OperatorSession` naming the session, and
  `MobProvenance::OperatorMember` only while the session is still the bridge
  session of the recorded member at the recorded generation in the recorded
  parent incarnation. A mob a host created for a session
  (`MobMcpState::mob_create_definition_with_owner_bridge_session`, recorded
  as `Session` or `Member`) is owned by that session, but that create
  granted the session nothing, so it gets no grant. Nothing else is granted
  either: `Host`, `Ambiguous` and `Unrecorded` records, another session, a
  later generation of the creating member, and a session whose operator
  removed its create capability get no grant.
- `meerkat-store`: the SQLite session store lays out a whole-blob session
  whose transcript graph retired its oldest occurrences, which every session
  compacted more often than `history_retained_rewrites` (default 4) has. It
  refused such a session typed before. The realm's one-time migration of a
  blob row, the standalone WholeBlob conversion's seeding and read-only head
  synthesis now write or derive the rows the store keeps after retiring the
  same occurrences incrementally: the retired base as a
  `session_transcript_retirements` row and rewrite rows for the retained
  generations only, and the synthesized head is the head the migration
  writes. A host that reads such a session's head at every committed
  boundary, like a persistent Meta gateway without a roster, no longer stops
  accepting work for a member after its fifth compaction. The in-memory store
  still refuses such a session typed.
- A governed realm no longer refuses every input of a host whose model key
  comes from the environment (`OPENAI_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and the
  other provider and `RKAT_*` keys, with no realm binding configured, or none
  that resolves) (`meerkat-runtime`, `meerkat-core`). Stock `rkat` in a
  governed realm, and any host that installs native work authorization,
  answered such input `controller credential is not currently usable` before
  any model request: governed admission required an authorized credential
  lease, and the env-var default route never has one, by design, since it is
  the host process's own key and not a durable identity. Admission now holds
  no lease for that route, as for an explicitly authless one, and publishes or
  synthesizes none. The route is recognized from the selection the provider
  factory pins (no recorded auth binding, the `env_default` credential,
  `ControllerModelSelection::uses_synthetic_env_default_credential`), and, as
  for an authless route, the live selected client must still report exactly
  that selection. Every other governed check still applies, and ungoverned
  hosts, which never held a lease, are unchanged. In a governed realm, the
  env-key route, including the factory's fallback to it when a configured
  binding cannot be resolved (for example a logged-out OAuth binding), now
  reaches controller authorization instead of being refused at admission: a
  stock controller grant admits it only if one of its `--route` keys is that
  route, and a grant that names only the configured routes refuses it with a
  typed policy refusal.
- A command sent to a mob while its actor is exiting after a shutdown now
  settles instead of going unanswered (`meerkat-mob`). The actor dropped its
  command channel without waiting for a send that had already reserved
  capacity, so a command written just after that drop stayed queued, with
  its reply sender, for as long as any handle to the mob lived: an unbounded
  caller waited forever, and `MobMcpState::close_admission` or `stand_down`
  called right after shutting a managed mob down waited out its deadline and
  reported "admission close not answered before the deadline". The exiting
  actor now closes the channel and receives until it is empty, after it has
  dropped itself, so such a command is dropped and its caller sees the reply
  channel close. A caller that observes `ActorCommandChannelClosed` still
  does so only after the actor has quiesced and dropped. Pre-existing in
  0.9.2 and 0.9.3.
- A grant resolution read inside an enclosing observation of the grant
  publication that meets an owner change published during the resolution
  is now that observation's stale read, as for any other concurrent owner
  change, instead of an unavailable grant authority. A grant-backed
  operation preparation refuses it as
  `OperationRefusalKind::ReprepareRequired` and rebuilds once, for the
  work's own grant and for the contributor ceilings of work that names
  other originals (a helper's source); controller admission refuses it as
  `ReprepareRequired`, which the runtime driver reports as
  `RuntimeDriverError::ControllerReadinessUnavailable` with reason
  `ControllerReadinessFailure::PolicyChanged`. A review read, which reads
  its material once by design, is not rebuilt: when the stock governed
  realm's review mandate or
  a contributor ceiling meets such a change, the review now refuses as
  stale (`ToolError::AuthorizationRefused` with `ReprepareRequired`)
  instead of reporting an unavailable review context, and a fresh attempt
  reads it again. The per-agent grant check of a configured MCP attachment
  (`AgentInstallationGrant`) reports such a change while it reads the
  agent's lineage as `McpAttachmentRefusal::NotCurrent`, as it already did
  for one published after the read, instead of `Unavailable`. A poisoned
  publication still answers `Unavailable` and is never retried. Failed
  durable grant custody and a clock failure still answer `Unavailable`,
  except that one the resolution meets while an owner change publishes is
  discarded with that stale read; a preparation's one rebuild then answers
  `Unavailable` if the failure persists. A standalone
  `LocalGrantAuthority::resolve_lineage` still reports a concurrent change
  as `GrantRefusal::Unavailable`.
- Stores no longer refuse to open with "schema domain ... has no ledger row
  but already owns objects" when another process creates the same schema
  domain at that moment (the 0.9.3 known issue "First concurrent durable
  delivery"). The open-time check now reads the schema ledger and the
  catalog in one snapshot, so a domain created concurrently is seen whole or
  not at all. Two processes racing their first durable delivery write
  (`runtime-delivery`) hit this most often. A durable delivery read also
  decides from the version its own check verified whether that domain
  exists and which of its tables to read, so a domain stamped after the read
  opened, possibly by a newer binary, is checked before it is read.
- A job delivery whose projection into the runtime inbox failed is retried
  on the delivery owner's next wake of any kind. While it keeps failing,
  each further retry waits for twice as many wakes (up to 64), so a busy
  runtime does not retry it on every wake; it is never retried by itself
  or in a loop. Before, only a job commit or a delivery generation change
  retried it, so it could stay pending until the process restarted. This
  was the retry half of the 0.9.3 known issue "First concurrent durable
  delivery".
- `meerkat-sqlite`: starting a SQLite change watch no longer waits for the
  operating system to register file notifications. On macOS, FSEvents
  registration held the first mob storage open for over 30 seconds, with
  the process-wide mob observer registry locked, so every other mob storage
  open waited too. The bounded sweep worker now starts first, and the
  registration runs on a thread of its own: `SqliteChangeWatch::registration`
  reports where it stands (`SqliteWatchRegistration`). Stopping a watch
  cancels a registration still running without waiting for it: its thread
  discards its result when the platform call returns, and is never
  detached. It stays with the watch and, once the watch is dropped, with
  the process (`meerkat_sqlite::watch::retained_registrations`). A mob
  observer drain counts such registrations
  (`SqliteMobObserverDrainReport::retained_registrations`). This covers
  `MobStorage::persistent`, `SqliteMobStores::open`, arming a runtime
  delivery owner and the multi-process hosting check. At most 64
  registrations run at once in a process, so a long FSEvents stall cannot
  use up its threads: a watch started while 64 are pending runs on its
  sweep alone for the rest of its life and logs one warning.
- `meerkat-sqlite`: a change watch whose notification registration fails
  (at an inotify instance or watch limit, for example) keeps its sweep.
  Before, the watch did not start at all, and a mob event observer then ran
  with no cross-process catch-up.
- `meerkat-sqlite`: registering a change watch's notifications no longer
  aborts the process when notify's inotify event-loop thread could not
  start (the process at its thread limit). notify 8.2.0 ignores that failed
  spawn, then panics in `watch()` and again in its `Drop` while the first
  panic unwinds. The registration now contains the panic, leaks that
  watcher instead of dropping it, and leaves the watch on its sweep.
- The `meerkat-contracts`, `meerkat-runtime` and `rkat` packages build their
  tests standalone. From rkat 0.8.1, meerkat-runtime 0.8.11 and
  meerkat-contracts 0.8.26 through 0.9.3, their tests embedded files from
  outside their own package, which no published package contains, so
  `cargo test` in the unpacked published crate failed to compile
  (meerkat-runtime's with the `sqlite-store` feature, meerkat-contracts'
  with `schema`). rkat's mobpack help-versus-docs contract test embedded the
  repository's `docs/`, and from 0.8.43 rkat's binary tests also embedded
  meerkat-runtime's released-realm `config.toml`. meerkat-runtime's tests
  embedded meerkat-core's synthetic 0.8.10 recovery-migration session, and
  meerkat-contracts' tests meerkat-core's compiled-policy v1 fixtures. Each
  crate now embeds its own byte-identical copy, pinned to the original's
  SHA-256. The mobpack help test still reads `docs/`, so it stays out of the
  rkat package and runs in the repository only.
- A request a mob's actor answers while a Shutdown drains its own work is
  refused with the new `MobError::ShutdownInProgress`, no longer with
  `MobError::ActorCommandChannelClosed`, which a caller could not tell from
  an exited actor: `MobHandle::stop` reported the mob gone while its Shutdown
  could still fail and leave the actor serving, and the actor's own recovery
  retries stopped. A retry now runs on the actor once its Shutdown fails, and
  finds the channel closed once it finishes. The `meerkat-mob-mcp`
  stand-down counts a shutting-down mob's admission as closed, and
  `MobHandle::revoke_forked_participant_with_recovery` revokes through its
  recovery transport while the source mob shuts down, as both did when the
  drain answered with a closed channel.
- The recovery of a durable placed lifecycle intent stops once the mob's
  admission is closed. A Reset intent, which the Closing state refuses, was
  retried every 2 s with a warning for the rest of the actor's life after a
  stand-down or a failed Shutdown. The intent stays recorded, and the next
  start drives it again.
- `MobHandle::shutdown` closes the mob's admission, as its contract says
  ("After this, no more commands are accepted"). The actor closes it on its
  serialized admission path when it admits the Shutdown, before any teardown
  step, with the new `MobAdmissionCloseReason::Shutdown` (appended to the
  `#[non_exhaustive]` enum; it displays as "shutdown"); an earlier close keeps
  its reason. Before, admission closed only through `close_if_idle`, the last
  owner's release or `close_admission`: after a Shutdown, `acquire_owner`
  handed out an owner lease on an actor that would take no further command,
  and `admission_closed()` stayed `None`, so an embedding host that treats a
  closed mob as gone kept treating the shut-down mob as live. A Shutdown that
  fails after its admission leaves admission closed; Stop, Shutdown and
  Destroy stay available. A Stop, the resumable pause, leaves admission open.
- `MobHandle::destroy` closes the mob's admission once the destroy is
  admitted (its durable destroy marker is written, by this attempt or an
  earlier one), before any destroy cleanup, with the new
  `MobAdmissionCloseReason::Destroyed` (it displays as "destroyed"); an
  earlier close keeps its reason. Before, a destroyed mob's actor exited with
  admission open, so `acquire_owner` still handed out owner leases and
  `admission_closed()` stayed `None`. A destroy left incomplete after its
  admission keeps admission closed; retrying the destroy stays available. A
  mob restored with the durable marker starts with admission closed, before
  `MobBuilder::resume` returns its handle, so nothing is spawned into it, and
  no owner lease is granted, while its destroy is unfinished.
- A durability fail-stop (a durable mutation whose outcome stayed uncertain,
  or a durable recovery that fails before the actor admits a command) closes
  the mob's admission before the actor exits (a mutation's fail-stop before it
  quiesces), with the new `MobAdmissionCloseReason::DurabilityFailStop` (it
  displays as "durability fail-stop"); an earlier close keeps its reason.
- A lost mob actor task (one that ends without its loop returning, as on a
  panic or an abort) closes the mob's admission from its spawn wrapper,
  before the task is reported lost, with the new
  `MobAdmissionCloseReason::ActorLost` (it displays as "actor lost"); an
  earlier close keeps its reason. Before, a lost actor left admission open,
  so `acquire_owner` still handed out owner leases and `admission_closed()`
  stayed `None`.
- A composition dispatch failure at a loop boundary (a structural routing
  failure, which stops the mob's actor) closes the mob's admission before the
  actor stops, with the new `MobAdmissionCloseReason::DispatchFailed` (it
  displays as "dispatch failure"); an earlier close keeps its reason. Before,
  the actor stopped with admission open, so `acquire_owner` still handed out
  owner leases and `admission_closed()` stayed `None`. With the closes above,
  no mob actor exit leaves admission open.
- `meerkat-runtime`: in-memory runtime store execution custody no longer
  refuses with `RuntimeStoreExecutionCustodyError::Busy` because its counter
  lock was briefly held, for example while a claim released on another
  thread (a dropped machine's ops worker) updated the counters. An acquire or
  upgrade now waits for that update, so `Busy` means only a real governed or
  shared conflict; a poisoned owner is still `Unavailable` (#1736).
- `meerkat-runtime`: live channel custody and playback-readiness reads
  (`MeerkatMachine::validate_live_channel_custody_by_pending_receipt`,
  `validate_live_channel_custody_by_activation_receipt`,
  `validate_live_playback_owner_readiness` and
  `validate_live_active_playback_owner_readiness`, and the facade's
  `validate_experimental_live_channel_custody*`) answer from one machine
  snapshot. An activation, revocation or close that commits during the read
  no longer fails it with `ValidationFailed` ("receipt is not current"): the
  read answers the phase its snapshot holds, and the next read answers the
  committed one. Four generated machine invariants pin the stage and
  activation records every custody answer reads (#1606).
- `make check-rust-release-packaging` no longer checks an archive left by an
  earlier run. With a persistent `CARGO_TARGET_DIR`, each crate's
  `package/` directory kept the `.crate` files of earlier runs, so a crate
  whose `cargo package` wrote no archive at the workspace version was
  checked (license texts, internal requirements, the facade link smoke)
  against an earlier run's archive. Each package job now removes its
  crate's earlier archives first, and such a crate fails as a missing
  archive. `scripts/test-release-packaging-isolation.sh` reruns the check
  over a persistent target with one crate writing no archive. Release
  tooling only.
- A mob that was reset and then re-spawned a member under an identity it had
  before the reset resumes after a restart. Resume replays the events after
  the last `MobReset`, and that replay required each identity's first
  generation there to be 0, so a re-spawn that continued the identity's
  generation failed the resume with an internal error. The replay now
  accepts any ascending generation (`RecoverRosterMember`,
  `RecoverRosterMemberReset` and `RecoverCommittedPlacedSpawn`), and a stored
  `MemberReset` must ascend from its previous generation instead of being its
  exact successor. Identity member target resolution follows the same rule.
- A mob member re-spawned after a mob reset and a restart no longer reuses a
  generation its pre-reset incarnation already had. Resume seeds the MobMachine
  only from the events after the last `MobReset`, so an identity that epoch had
  not seen started again at generation 0, with the runtime id and member
  address of its pre-reset incarnation; without the restart it got the next
  generation. Resume now first recovers every identity's highest generation
  from the whole event log, every reset epoch included, into
  `identity_generation_highwater`, then seals that window; a sealed machine
  refuses the recovery signal, and a recovery never lowers a recorded value.
  Minting (every spawn opener and membership commit, and
  `ComputeRespawnGeneration`) reads one past the larger of the retained
  generation and the high-water, and the shell no longer decides that an
  identity is fresh: every spawn takes its generation from the machine. A
  store whose last epoch already reused a generation still resumes, and that
  identity's next spawn goes above the high-water. The invariant
  `next_generation_above_highwater` is model-checked by a bounded TLC audit
  (`specs/machines/mob_machine/generation_highwater_audit.sh`, lane shard
  audits-c). It also reaches both replay histories above, refuses three
  seeded defects, and checks that restoring the exact-successor replay rule
  makes those histories unreachable.
- Work that names an original whose admission its source owner has not
  settled yet is no longer refused as malformed or denied
  (`meerkat-runtime`). Native admission of input that names such a
  contributor, `require_source_original_live` and a retained resume report
  `ControllerReadinessUnavailable` with `OriginalAdmissionPending`; operation
  authorization of work that names it, the further originals of a helper
  admission or child issuance, and the controller-grant mutation check report
  it unavailable, and none of them waits. A retained resume therefore stays
  retryable until the owner settles the original, instead of being refused
  for good. A cancelled original is still refused, and the controller-grant
  mutation check no longer counts such a contributor as unreferenced.
- The `web_search` tool's native search call now reads its stop reason
  (#1887). A search the provider refused or filtered, one whose context window
  filled and a cancelled one come back `failed`, naming the stop reason, with
  no answer, evidence or native events: the refusal text is no longer reported
  as a `completed` (or `unavailable`) answer.
- A Gemini prompt blocked before any candidate (`promptFeedback.blockReason`
  and so no `finishReason`) now ends the response as a content filter
  (#1888). The run fails as `content_filtered` after one provider call,
  instead of being retried as an incomplete response and failing as
  `ProviderError(IncompleteResponse)`. Every block reason reads this way,
  `OTHER` and one the adapter does not know included: a blocked prompt is
  blocked again on every retry. The raw block reason and the blocked safety
  categories now reach the caller as the typed reason's provider detail, so a
  `SAFETY` block and a `BLOCKLIST` block can be told apart, of the prompt or
  of a candidate.
- An OpenAI refusal is no longer committed as the answer. A Responses
  `refusal` output part, streamed (`response.refusal.delta`/`.done`) or in the
  terminal response, and a Chat Completions `delta.refusal` end the response
  as a refusal: the run fails `content_filtered` with stop `refusal`, and the
  refusal text travels as the provider detail, never as answer text. The
  refusal wins over text and tool calls in the same response. A refused
  OpenAI native search now comes back from the `web_search` tool `failed`
  (#1887), as the Anthropic and Gemini ones do.
- An Anthropic refusal now carries its `stop_details` (policy category and
  explanation) as the provider detail. Its terminal waits for `message_stop`,
  so `stop_details` is read wherever the stream puts it: inside the
  `message_delta` delta, beside that delta, or on `message_stop`. When more
  than one carries it, the `message_delta` wins (inside its delta, then
  beside it), and `message_stop` only fills in a detail it lacked. A refusal
  whose stream is cut after its stop still ends as a refusal, with whatever
  detail was seen.
- A native web search cut at its output cap (`max_tokens`) or paused by the
  provider's server-tool loop (`pause_turn`) keeps its status and answer and
  now says, in its `error`, that the answer may be incomplete (#1887).
- `meerkat-session`: the last-resort compaction source (user requests only)
  no longer claims to keep every user request. Its note says it carries the
  newest N of the M requests, and the completion reports the same counts.
- A model request of the agent loop no longer returns to the controller with
  an `operation_refused` notice, or fails the turn, because an owner change
  was still in progress on its work's own publication. An owner that holds a
  change across its storage commit outlasted both built-in rebuilds, the
  preparation's and the request's own. On such a `ReprepareRequired` refusal
  the request now waits for the change to complete, then rebuilds under the
  same operation without spending its own rebuild. The wait is bounded: one
  wall-clock deadline per model call, set at its first wait to 2 s or to the
  remaining run budget if that is less, so the rebuilds in between count
  against it; at most 3 such free rebuilds per call; and a free rebuild only
  once no change is in progress. Past those bounds the refusal takes its
  ordinary path (one rebuild, then the controller feedback request), as does
  any other refusal kind and a refusal while the work's own publication has
  no change in progress. The run budget is checked after every wait, so a
  turn whose budget runs out during one ends with the time-budget terminal,
  not a refusal. Each refused attempt keeps its own audit record, and a
  `debug` event `meerkat::authz::owner_change_wait` (operation id,
  `waited_ms`, `settled`) marks each wait.
- The same bounded wait covers the other operations that rebuild after a
  `ReprepareRequired` refusal. A governed tool dispatch waits at its prepared
  entry and again at its body entry, and when the call-level execution
  policy gate stages the call again after its own awaits (dispatch admission,
  consequence policy), inside the tool's timeout. At the body entry the review
  check point runs on the decision checked after the wait; a reviewed tool whose
  decision changed meanwhile is reviewed once more (see below) and no review
  is reused. The `web_search` tool's helper model request waits within the
  call's remaining tool time and asks again under the same delegate
  operation. A compaction summary waits within the same
  bounds, and past them the refusal still fails its compaction. When the
  body entry or the gate's staging waits out a change after recording its
  `Entry` record, it records another for the decision checked after the
  wait. The gate's check point also runs on the decision checked after its
  wait, but the gate's own code already ran: a reviewed tool whose decision
  changed while the gate waited settles as `review_unsatisfied`
  (`context_changed`) and is not reviewed again. A streaming tool's gate
  wait also counts against its inactivity window, and past that window the
  call ends as the tool's inactivity timeout. The debug event names the
  site (`model_request`, `compaction_summary`, `tool_dispatch`,
  `tool_entry`, `tool_policy_entry`, `web_search_delegate`).
- A governed helper admission fence and a helper child issuance answer
  `Unavailable` instead of `Denied` when their check refuses to rebuild
  (`ReprepareRequired`), on the prepared path and on the dispatch path alike:
  under the owner-change exclusion they cannot wait, and a refusal to rebuild
  is no verdict on the operation, so a later attempt may succeed. A denial
  and malformed facts stay `Denied`.
- A model-reviewed (R2) tool call no longer fails with `review_unsatisfied`
  (`context_changed`) when one owner publication change lands during its
  review, at its verdict's commit, or at the dispatch's own entry staging
  before the tool's dispatcher runs. When the operation is still permitted at
  R2 with the same review material, the fenced dispatch re-prepares it and
  reviews it once more from the start, as a second review attempt for the
  same `tool_call_id`; the earlier verdict is never used. Deciding to review
  once more reads the successor's review material once
  (`review_operation_context`), so an owner sees one more read per
  superseded call; when the material is unchanged, that read is the one the
  second attempt is shown. A review observer can therefore see a
  `ContextChanged` retirement followed by that second attempt: a host must
  not treat the retirement as the call's final outcome.
  At most one re-review runs per call, only after an allow or a reviewer
  failure, and only with enough tool time left for a whole review deadline.
  A second change, a denial or escalation, an expired review, a changed tier
  (human consent included), changed or unreadable review material, and a
  change once the tool's dispatcher is running still settle as before. An
  owner change still in progress when the verdict is checked is now waited
  out (within the attempt's own review deadline, 2 s at most) instead of
  settling at once as changed authority; past that bound it settles as
  before. The re-review adds no record type: the audit shows a second
  `ReviewAttemptStarted` after the successor's `Prepared` record, and a
  change at the entry staging also leaves that staging's `Entry` record
  twice. Per tool call the waits stay bounded: at most 3 wait states (the
  dispatch's preparation, and each review attempt's, which every staging of
  that attempt shares), 9 free rebuilds and 6 s of waiting, inside the
  tool's timeout.
- `MobBuilder::resume` no longer fails when a host refuses the registration
  of a member the boot recreates on a fresh session, as it does when the
  session service keeps no durable sessions (`meerkat-mob`). The refusal
  failed the whole resume with the host's error, so the mob did not come
  back after a restart. Now only that member is Broken, with the typed
  refusal (`MobError::MemberRegistrationRefused`, shown in
  `MobMemberSnapshot::registration_refusal`), as a member restored from its
  durable session is; the other members resume. The refused member can be
  retired, and stays Broken until an explicit repair. Any other failure to
  recreate a member still fails the resume. Pre-existing in 0.9.3 and
  earlier.
- `meerkat-contracts`: the `tool_config_changed` entry of
  `WireEvent.known_payloads` in `artifacts/schemas/events.json` is generated
  from the typed payload. The hand-written entry required a `status` field
  that the event has never carried (its status is `status_info`), so every
  real `tool_config_changed` event failed validation against it. It now
  accepts the events the runtime serializes, including those stored by
  0.9.3 and earlier and served with their `persisted` bit.
- Creating a persistent `MeerkatMachine` over one store no longer waits for
  another store's OAuth flow rehydration (`meerkat-runtime`). The
  process-wide provider-auth authority cache held one lock while it built a
  store's authority, which rehydrates that store's OAuth flows (a store read,
  and a write back when flows were persisted), so every machine creation in
  the process queued behind the slowest store. Each store key now has its own
  slot: the cache lock covers only the slot lookup, and machines over one
  store still wait for and share one authority, rehydrated once.
- `@rkat/sdk`: a Node process that calls `MeerkatClient.close()` now exits
  as soon as it has nothing else to do, instead of about 5 seconds later.
  `close()` waits up to 5 seconds for the `rkat-rpc` child to exit before
  it kills the child with SIGKILL, and the timer for that wait kept running
  when the child exited first. It is now cancelled; a child that does not
  exit within 5 seconds is still killed as before. `close()` also settles on
  the child's exit instead of on its output pipes closing: a process the
  child started that still held those pipes made `close()` wait the full
  5 seconds after the child had exited, or wait forever after the SIGKILL.
  Requests waiting on a child that exits by itself, a crash for instance,
  likewise fail with `PROCESS_EXITED` at most about a second after the
  exit, even when such a process still holds the pipes; before, they and
  every request sent after the exit waited for the pipes to close, possibly
  forever. After a protocol error (a reply line that is not JSON), the client
  now stops the child the way `close()` does, and a later `close()` returns
  once that child has exited: a child that ignores SIGTERM is killed after 5
  seconds instead of being left running, and a process the child started can
  no longer keep the caller's process alive through the child's pipes.
  Pre-existing since 0.6.0; the protocol-error case since 0.7.0.
- Python SDK: requests waiting on an `rkat-rpc` child that exits by
  itself, a crash for instance, now fail with `CONNECTION_CLOSED` and the
  child's stderr tail at most about a second after the exit, even when a
  process the child started still holds the child's output pipes; before,
  they and every request sent after the exit waited for those pipes to
  close, possibly forever. `MeerkatClient.close()` likewise returns once
  the child has exited, and lets go of such pipes: on Python 3.11 and
  3.12, and on 3.13 and 3.14 before the fix for CPython issue 119710,
  `asyncio`'s `Process.wait()` returns only once the child's pipes have
  closed, so `close()` waited 5 seconds for a child that had already
  exited. Pre-existing since 0.3.0.
- `meerkat-openai`: on public GPT Live, a delegation result held behind the
  user's unanswered question no longer leaves the voice model believing the
  work is still in progress (#1820). Meerkat holds a result while the user's
  latest utterance is unanswered, so the model answers that first; the
  model's only fact about the delegation was then its in-progress
  instruction, so "is it done yet?" got "Not yet" while the finished result
  waited behind that very question. A held result now sends a notice at
  once, always ahead of the result itself, on the instructions lane and
  bound to its delegation: the work has
  finished, its result has not reached the model yet, and the model may say
  it has just finished but must not state, guess or imply the outcome until
  the result arrives. The notice carries no result content and promises no
  timing, the result is still released only by the existing triggers, later
  "still running" lines stop naming that delegation, and the result's cue
  no longer tells the model that anything it said earlier was said before
  the work was done. A finished delegation whose result the runtime cannot
  deliver yet (while another result holds the channel's one result slot, or
  while results wait for the provider to acknowledge a concurrent
  historical summary) gets the same notice: the machine authorizes it
  once, as the narration kind `FinishedPending`, until the result is handed
  to delivery, and the broker sends it
  (`PublicLiveBrokerSession::append_delegation_finished_notice`) unless a
  result of that delegation has already reached the session. While the
  model is speaking, that notice waits until its response ends or the user
  takes the floor (an instructions append mid-answer can cut the answer
  off), and it is withdrawn, never sent, if the result reaches the session
  first.
- A session forked with RPC `session/fork_at` or `session/fork_replace` can
  now run a turn (`meerkat-session`). The fork committed the child with its
  source's session metadata but without the build state a cold resume
  requires, so the child's first `turn/start` failed with `INTERNAL_ERROR`
  "turn abandoned: persisted session <id> is missing session build state".
  Every durable fork (`fork_at`, `fork_replace`, and the mob member,
  turn-boundary and planned-identity forks) now commits a child build state
  derived from the source's. The session configuration is carried: output
  schema, hook overrides, budget limits, callback tool definitions, comms
  settings, application context, additional instructions, and the shell and
  tool call timeouts. The source's shell environment (`shell_env`), its MCP
  attachment requests and its mob operator authority are not: the source
  keeps its `shell_env` when it resumes, and MCP servers are attached to the
  child itself. A source with session metadata but no build state cannot
  give a child that runs, so every fork entry point now refuses it before
  committing anything (`INVALID_PARAMS`, data kind
  `fork_source_build_state_missing` with the `source_session_id`). A child
  forked by 0.9.3 or earlier that never ran a turn still fails `turn/start`
  with the error above, because it has no build state to derive one from:
  fork its source again instead.
- RPC transcript edits (`session/fork_at`, `session/fork_replace`,
  `session/rewrite_transcript`, `session/update_system_prompt` and
  `session/restore_transcript_revision`) on an idle persisted session no
  longer answer `SESSION_BUSY` ("session ... is active") after the RPC server
  restarts (`meerkat-rpc`). The edit now registers the session with the
  server's runtime before it asks for the busy verdict, so a session with a
  running turn or pending input is still refused with `SESSION_BUSY`. A
  session whose durability needs a reload now answers the runtime's typed
  refusal ("durability reload required") instead of `SESSION_BUSY`, and a
  session another process hosts answers its typed hosting refusal.
- `meerkat-openai`, `meerkat-live`, `meerkat` and `meerkat-rpc`: an OpenAI
  realtime response that ends without completing is now a typed failure, not
  a finished turn (#1883). A `response.done` with status `failed`,
  `in_progress`, or `incomplete` for a reason other than `max_output_tokens`
  or `content_filter` used to surface as a completed turn with stop reason
  `end_turn`, so the session committed the failed response's partial text as
  an ordinary assistant reply, and a failed response without usage closed the
  whole live channel. It now surfaces as the `turn_failed` observation with
  the typed status; the provider's reason, code and message are diagnostics
  only. The observation is not terminal: the channel stays open, the next
  turn proceeds, and Meerkat sends no cancel. Both projection sinks commit
  nothing of the failed response: they record `AssistantTurnFailed`, which
  discards everything the response staged on every lane, and drop its
  display-text buffer, so a barge-in after the failure never targets it. A
  WebRTC peer stops playing the audio still queued for the failed response,
  as it does for an interrupted one. A playback terminal waiting on the failed
  response settles at the failure.
  The response's usage is charged to the session and the budget when the
  provider reported it; when it did not, the session event stream carries
  `turn_usage_accounting_unmeasured` and no counter advances. A failed
  response is not retried automatically: the client receives the typed
  failure and decides whether to ask again. The `max_output_tokens`,
  `content_filter` and cancellation mappings are unchanged. SDKs older than
  this release do not know the `turn_failed` observation or the
  `assistant_turn_failed` transcript event, and a decoder that validates the
  observation type rejects them; upgrade the SDK with the server.
- `rkat` builds without its default features
  (`cargo check -p rkat --no-default-features`). Five helpers named types
  and methods that exist only with `session-store` and failed to compile
  without it: the ungoverned `bind_stock_prompt`, the governed-realm MCP
  server lookup (`persistence_is_governed`, `GovernedMcpServers`,
  `governed_configured_mcp_servers`) and the runtime-backed service builder
  that waits for MCP servers. They are now gated on `session-store`, and a
  build without it no longer warns about the session code it leaves out.
  Pre-existing in 0.9.3.
- A mob Shutdown's runtime teardown, and the settlement it reports,
  unregister a member whose runtime registration is durability-degraded
  (`meerkat-mob`). A failed boundary commit leaves the session
  `ReloadRequired`, and its exited runtime loop can keep the session's
  mutation fence, which only the runtime's reload-required discard releases.
  The teardown's exact unregister admission waited on that fence, so the
  member was reported `UnregisterPending` and stayed registered until the
  process exited. The teardown and the settlement now run the discard first,
  as retire and destroy do, and unregister the cold successor it publishes.
  An unregister coordinator admitted before the session degraded still waits
  on the fence; its settlement stays pending, bounded by each call's
  deadline.
- A pending member unregister that a mob Shutdown reported no longer
  unregisters a registration that a later owner took over (`meerkat-mob`,
  `meerkat-runtime`). When Shutdown's deadline passed before a member's
  exact unregister was admitted, its settlement admitted that unregister
  later through the member's exact registration witness. A later owner can
  take a registration over in place under the same witness: a mob
  reconstructed in-process over the same stores prepares its members'
  bindings on the registrations the old incarnation left, a
  `register_session` reuses a registration as it is, an executor
  registration takes over a registration's live runtime loop as it is, and
  an executor attachment or actor materialization adopts a registration
  without a runtime loop. The settlement then unregistered the later
  owner's live registration, or ran the reload-required discard on it once
  it degraded.
  It also followed whatever registration of the session was current once
  its discard returned, which a later owner could already have replaced.
  The runtime now stamps a registration's use at every adoption, Shutdown
  reads it when it hands the member's registration back, and the settlement
  starts the discard or the unregister only while that use is unchanged,
  reporting `MemberUnregisterState::HandedOver` otherwise. It follows only
  the successor its discard returns as published.
- The runtime's reload-required discard disposes of a durability-degraded
  registration that no runtime loop holds (`meerkat-runtime`). It required
  the exact teardown handoff of the registration's runtime loop, so a
  registration that never had a loop, or whose loop's teardown had already
  completed, was refused until a repair nothing could perform: the exact
  unregister is refused too while the session is degraded (the durability
  gate refuses its first durable write), so a mob Shutdown reported that
  member `UnregisterPending` for good, and a later owner's executor
  registration on the session was refused. When no runtime loop can hold
  the registration's mutation fence (no pending or committed attachment and
  no runtime-loop teardown slot), the discard now takes the fence itself and
  publishes the durability-ready cold successor, which the exact unregister
  then settles, and a later owner's executor registration cold-reloads such
  a registration as it does one whose loop handed its executor back. A
  registration whose runtime loop is still attached keeps its fence until
  that loop hands it back, and the discard waits for that handoff, as
  before.
- A peer message or request steered into a running turn was shown to the
  model for one request and then lost (`meerkat-runtime`,
  `meerkat-machine-schema`):
  the machine classified it request-only, so it was consumed when it was
  injected, never written to the transcript, missing from every later request
  of the run and from history, and no `peer_content_ingested` event was
  published for it. Text-only prompt steers, external-event steers and local
  flow-step steers lost the same way. They now take the durable in-turn path
  (see Breaking): one transcript row, committed with the run, recovered by
  exactly one follow-up turn when its image is discarded or the process stops
  mid-run. Pre-existing in 0.9.2 and 0.9.3.
- `reply_to_peer` can answer a peer message that joined the running turn
  (`meerkat-core`, `meerkat-runtime`, `meerkat-comms`). The turn's reply
  capabilities came only from the deliveries that started it, so a message
  delivered into the running turn was refused with `no_reply_capability`, or
  with `unknown_reply_to` for its id. The durable in-turn delivery now adds
  the message's reply capability to the running turn, and the message's
  notice shows the `Delivery ID` that `reply_to` takes. When the selected id
  matches deliveries of two different senders in one turn, the tool refuses
  with `ambiguous_reply`, names each sender and sends nothing; before, it
  answered the first. Pre-existing in 0.9.3.
- A mob destroy whose member's boundary commit fails while the destroy
  waits on that member's ingress detach now reloads the member, retries its
  retirement once, and names it in `reloaded_members`. It answered
  `MobDestroyError::Incomplete`; 0.9.3 listed this as a known limitation.
- A wait for a session's durability-ready mutation gate now ends with the
  typed `RuntimeDriverError::RecoveryRepairBlocked` as soon as the session's
  durability degrades, even while another holder keeps the gate. The exited
  runtime loop of a member whose boundary commit failed keeps the gate until
  a reload, so such a wait lasted until the member was reloaded. This
  includes the run-start hold a mob Shutdown takes on each member. An
  unregister that waits for the gate before it stages its final unregister
  also ends typed and releases its teardown coordinator, so the
  reload-required discard can run.
- The other waits for a session's mutation gate that serve live work now end
  the same way instead of waiting for a holder of the gate once the session's
  durability degrades: an exact-run interrupt and its reconciliation, the
  recover and destroy control commands (`RuntimeControlPlaneError::StoreError`
  carrying the refusal, as their durability-ready wait answers), a comms abort
  (an abort of every session aborts the others, then answers the typed
  refusal naming the sessions it skipped),
  unregistering or retiring an executor attachment, an explicit stop and its
  post-stop fence, installing an unregister coordinator, closing an idle
  registration, input admission, the return to the gate after a boundary
  callback, a member effect, the admitted-original read
  (`AdmittedOriginalRefusal::Unavailable`), registering an executor over an
  existing entry, and the runless terminal publication task. A session that
  has already degraded refuses such a wait whenever another holder keeps the
  gate. Waits that run only once the degraded holder has released the gate
  (the reload-required discard) or before any runtime loop exists keep
  waiting.
- Reads of a session's runtime state that take no mutation gate (whether it
  has active inputs, which a mob's close-if-idle and last-owner release ask;
  a runtime wake; whether a run input awaits its boundary; a stopped run's
  contributor terminal; an input's terminal completion) and a member's
  tracked-input cancel waited behind a boundary commit or run
  terminalization that holds the session's driver. Past its deadline such a
  commit holds the driver until the store answers, so once the session
  degrades they answer without it: the active-input read answers busy, an
  input's terminal completion refuses with the new, retryable
  `RuntimeDriverError::InputTerminalNotYetReadable` (the enum is
  `#[non_exhaustive]`), the contributor terminal is unknown, and the others
  refuse with the typed, retryable `RecoveryRepairBlocked`.
- A boundary commit whose store never answered (a stalled disk or a hung
  network filesystem, for example) kept the session's mutation gate for
  good, so every later wait for the gate waited for it, a mob destroy's
  retirement of the member and a force cancel of it included. The commit's
  declared deadline now degrades the session (see Changed), those waits end
  typed, and a reload replaces the registration once the store has answered.
- An input admission whose store write never answered kept the session's
  mutation gate and driver until it did, so every later wait for the gate
  waited for the store: the session's next admission, its next run and a
  reload of it. The admission now waits for its write only as long as the
  store's declared commit outcome deadline (120 s for the SQLite store).
  Past it, the admission refuses with the retryable
  `RuntimeDriverError::RecoveryRepairBlocked`, naming the input, and the
  session needs a reload (`runtime_admission_deadline`), so those waits end
  typed. The write keeps running and keeps the gate until the store answers,
  so the input may still be admitted: resubmit it with the same idempotency
  key, or read it after the reload. A reload refuses with the same
  retryable error until the store answers, then replaces the registration
  from durable truth. Sessions without durable state, and stores that
  declare no deadline (the in-memory store), admit as before.
- A scheduled mob delivery whose redelivery found the delivery already failed
  (`meerkat-mob-mcp`) recorded the occurrence `completed`. It now records
  `delivery_failed` with the delivery's failure class.

- A continuation or detached-job delivery owed to a mob member is no longer
  delivered to the member of the same identity in a mob destroyed and
  created again under the same id (`meerkat-mob`). A member's delivery
  address named the mob id, the identity and the generation only, and the
  new mob's generations start over, so the new member served the rows owed
  to the old one. The address now names the mob incarnation too
  (`rt:mob-member:{mob}:{incarnation}:{identity}:{generation}`): the
  address of a destroyed mob's member resolves as retired, and its rows
  strand (`ContinuationStatus::Stranded` with `OwnerRetired`). A handle
  kept from the destroyed mob, such as the one a fork_off or council
  completion that ends after the destroy submits through, submits nothing:
  `MobHandle::submit_continuation` and `submit_retained_continuation` answer
  `OwnerRetired` (a destroy and a create again that both complete between
  that check and the commit are not caught). An address minted before 0.9.4
  names no mob incarnation, and only a mob created before 0.9.4, whose
  incarnation was assigned at its first 0.9.4 resume, serves it; so rows
  owed before the upgrade to a mob that was destroyed and created again
  before the upgrade still reach the member of the same identity. A
  continuation key submitted again for a member after its mob was created
  again still replays its first receipt, bound to the old member's address.
- On macOS a stdio MCP server's close now settles as soon as the server has
  exited, as on Linux (`meerkat-mcp`). The close could not see the server's
  exit there, so every close waited out the whole EOF grace (5 s by default),
  sent SIGTERM, waited the TERM grace (3 s) and sent SIGKILL, even to a
  server that had already exited. A failed connect, a removal, a reload, a
  session end and a host shutdown each took about 8 s per stdio server; a
  server that failed its setup stayed pending for that long, and a live add,
  reload or restore of the same server was refused meanwhile. The close now
  checks the server's exit on macOS without reaping it, as it does on Linux
  (a non-blocking `waitid` with `WNOWAIT`; only an exit counts, not a stop).
  Other platforms without that check keep their graces as before.
  Pre-existing since 0.9.0.

- An intent-managed identity on SQLite mob storage could stay in `Backoff`
  indefinitely on a host with slow disk writes. The identity runtime write
  fence gave up at once while a convergence status write committed, and every
  retry met the next status write. The fence now waits up to 2 seconds for the
  mob database's write lock when the SQLite runtime store calls it, and the
  in-memory runtime store and the session publication retry it for up to 2
  seconds with their locks released.
- An intent-managed identity could stay in `Backoff` for good after its
  member retirement ran past the budget its reconcile pass gave it (30
  seconds), as on slow storage with many identities adopting at once, or
  failed at a stage after it had durably started (a storage or host error).
  Once the retirement had durably started the member read as recovering,
  which identity reconciliation only waits on, and nothing finished the
  retirement. Identity reconciliation now owns a retirement it started until
  it settles: it runs under the lifecycle hang guard, a shutdown interrupts
  it instead of waiting, and a failure after the durable start settles as
  stuck and is re-driven on the identity's next backoff pass (250 ms
  doubling, at most 60 s apart), so the identity converges once the error
  clears. A stopped mob re-drives it when it is resumed. Every re-drive of a
  stuck retirement (this one, a mob resume or
  `MobHandle::redrive_retirement`) now keeps a host's refusal of the
  member's registration, so a member its host refused at a restart is
  retired on the refused member's path again, as its first attempt was.
- An intent-managed identity (`meerkat-mob`) whose lease the previous process
  still held when the mob restarted converges once that lease expires, at
  most 30 s after the previous process last renewed it. Nothing woke the
  identity when the lease expired, so it stayed in `AwaitLease` until the
  slow safety scan, about five minutes later. Reconciliation now schedules
  its next attempt for the observed expiry, or re-checks after a second when
  no expiry can be read.
- `meerkat-mob`: a stale runtime route no longer ends the mob's actor. A
  restart could leave a runtime-retire route queued for a member whose
  retirement had already finished; when the member's runtime refused it, the
  machine rejected the refusal's feedback and the whole mob stopped
  answering. A refused route that names a runtime the mob no longer runs is
  now dropped with a warning, and a refusal for a member the mob still runs
  stays queued while the mob is `Stopped` and is handled after it resumes.
- A fork child of a member or session with activated host instructions no
  longer commits only to fail its first turn ("forked session must explicitly
  activate inherited instruction keys"). `fork_off`, council participants, the
  other self-starting forks and the RPC forks now either carry the source's
  effective activations into the child (`reactivate_inherited`) or are refused,
  typed, before commit. Council crash recovery verifies a planned child's
  re-activation rows exactly and measures its prefix without them.
- Generated TLA+ models now evaluate ordering comparisons between optional
  values. The renderer wrote MobMachine's member progress guards
  (`get_copied(id) <= Some(observed_at_ms)` and its `>` twin) as a plain `<=`
  or `>` between option records, which TLC cannot evaluate, so any MobMachine
  run with members stopped at the first state where a member progress
  observation could fire: the deep profile stopped after nine states, before
  any member transition was checked. Such comparisons now render with Rust's
  `Option` order (`None` below every `Some`, two `Some`s by their values)
  through `OptionLt` / `OptionLe`, which a model defines only when it uses
  them, with ASSUMEs that re-check the order on every TLC run. The operators
  branch with `IF`, not `\/`, because TLC evaluates every disjunct of an
  action-level `\/`. The Rust kernel already applied this order; only the
  models of MobMachine and the two compositions that embed it change.
  A TLC audit (`specs/machines/mob_machine/member_lifecycle_audit.sh`, lane
  shard audits-b) now model-checks the member lifecycle around those guards,
  over the whole reachable space of its domains, which no generated profile
  checks to the end: roster recovery and
  reset, session binding (fresh, replacing, already current), progress
  observations, the local retire arms and the RetireMember signal, the
  runtime retirement and archive observations, the resume path's replay
  arms, stop and resume, and the recovery of an archived identity's next
  incarnation. Every one of those arms must fire, a member's recorded
  observation time never decreases, and the audit fails when a progress arm
  loses its guard or the guard is rendered as a plain `<=` again.
- MobMachine closes two latent gaps in its roster replay arms
  (`meerkat-machine-schema`, `meerkat-mob`); no shell path feeds either
  sequence.
  - A replayed peer-only retirement start is refused for a runtime whose
    retirement already records a session. Replayed over a releasing
    retirement in flight, whose binding is already gone, the start removed
    the recorded session while that session's ingress detach was still
    pending, which broke the generated invariant that every pending detach
    keeps its session. The resume path replays at most one start per
    incarnation into freshly recovered state.
  - A replayed Retired record that names the identity's current runtime
    with another generation now matches no arm. The stale-incarnation arm
    took it and pruned that runtime's state while the identity still mapped
    to it, which broke the generated invariant that an identity held for a
    respawn maps to no runtime or to a Retiring one. A consistent record
    cannot carry that pairing: a runtime id names its generation. The arm
    now takes only an identity that maps to no runtime and whose recorded
    generation differs, so it no longer overlaps the current-runtime and
    remapped-identity arms, which keep taking every record they took
    before.
  The member lifecycle audit, which now drives every replay arm, fails on
  either gap.
- A respawned member no longer starts from its predecessor's execution-health
  record (`meerkat-machine-schema`, `meerkat-mob`). MobMachine kept each
  identity's run state, in-flight work, progress token, last observation,
  last progress time and event, and health class across incarnations, because
  no arm removed them: until the new incarnation's session answered an
  execution snapshot, its status reported the predecessor's in-flight work and
  last progress time, and a first snapshot equal to the predecessor's last one
  read as unchanged at the predecessor's progress time. Every arm that mints an
  incarnation (spawn commit, placed and roster recovery, roster reset) now
  clears that record, so a new incarnation's progress clock starts at its
  first observation.
- An idle close no longer counts a retired member's last observed work
  (`meerkat-mob`). `close_if_idle` and the latched close after the last owner
  releases summed the in-flight work of every identity's last execution
  observation, retired ones included, so a member whose last status read saw
  work in flight and that then retired kept the mob busy for its life:
  admission never closed idle, and `MobBusy` reported runs that did not exist.
  Only identities with a current incarnation count now. Pre-existing in 0.9.3.
- After a restart, a placed member no longer shows its predecessor's kickoff
  (`meerkat-mob`). The startup replay applies kickoff updates per identity and
  installs the current placed incarnation from its committed carrier only after
  the whole event pass, so the kickoff phase and error of an earlier
  incarnation of the same identity (a failed kickoff, for example) carried
  over to a placed incarnation that had no kickoff of its own, although the
  live spawn commit had cleared them. The replay now clears the identity's
  kickoff where that incarnation's spawn event sits; the incarnation's own
  kickoff updates follow it and still replay. Pre-existing in 0.9.3.
- GPT Live: the transcript rows a channel's transport already holds when a
  running member turn ends (the user's finalized speech, the assistant's
  spoken segments) now all commit at that turn's boundary, before a member
  turn queued behind them starts. Each row took the session's turn boundary
  on its own, and the member's next queued turn was already waiting for it
  behind the first row, so while member turns ran back to back (a typed
  message, a second delegation) the backlog drained one row per turn: the
  persisted transcript fell further behind the conversation with every turn,
  and speech said before a typed message landed after that message's
  answer, so the turn answering it did not see it. The transport now holds
  the boundary across the rows it already has, for at most 64 rows or about
  a second at a time, so a queued turn waits at most that long for them.
  WebSocket and WebRTC live channels hold it the same way across their
  consecutive transcript rows (see `docs/guides/realtime.mdx`). (#1821)
- Voice audio on WebSocket and WebRTC live channels no longer pauses while
  another turn runs on the same session. The transport applied each
  transcript row to the session before it forwarded anything behind it, and a
  row waits for a running turn, so the assistant's voice (and on WebSocket
  the user's microphone audio too) stopped until that turn ended and then
  arrived in a burst. The rows now wait in an ordered queue off the media
  path and commit in arrival order once the turn ends; on WebRTC an
  interruption stops the queued output audio at once.
- A persisted mob whose resume is refused at restore no longer fails the
  whole restore of `MobMcpState` (`meerkat-mob-mcp`). One such store, for
  example one whose creation record disagrees with its log
  (`MobError::IncarnationInconsistent`), made every mob verb fail after a
  restart, and no mob of the host came back. That mob is now left
  unrestored, its store kept as found, and the other mobs restore. A lookup
  of its id, and a create of that id, answer its refusal:
  `IncarnationInconsistent` and `IncarnationDestroyed` keep their variants,
  and any other refusal answers `MobError::Internal` with its message. Its
  stored roster still counts for the provenance a session's create
  records: a create by a session that roster names, or while it cannot be
  read, is refused with `MobError::ProvenanceUnavailable` naming that mob.
  A child mob that a member of that mob created still resumes while its
  owner session is live, although its parent mob does not run. The sweep
  of empty stores at restore keeps a store whose log is empty while its
  creation record is not finalized (the log lost the `MobCreated` that
  record names): it is left unrestored the same way, under the record's
  mob, answering `IncarnationInconsistent` (`RecordWithoutCreation`). An
  empty store with no creation record, or one a finished destroy
  finalized, is still removed. A transport or persistence fault, and a
  store that names no mob, still fail the restore, so the next mob verb
  tries it again. Pre-existing in 0.9.3 and earlier.
- A session whose last turn an earlier release committed but never
  finalized, such as a member stopped at a compaction in 0.9.2 or 0.9.3,
  now finalizes that turn's result at its next start and accepts work
  again (`meerkat-runtime`). Its completion receipt row still carries the
  earlier release's `stored_input_state_version` (6), and the SQLite
  store's exact input-state batch compare-and-swap compared those bytes
  with this release's encoding of the same row, so every start failed with
  "terminal completion finalization lost the exact durable CAS" and the
  session refused all work. The same mismatch blocked the other exact
  terminal rewrites of such rows (payload retirement, interaction terminal
  outbox adoption, finalization and publication receipt). The store now
  compares a row an earlier release wrote as this release encodes the
  typed row it reads, and writes the replacement in the current encoding.
  A row in the current encoding is still compared byte for byte, and a row
  whose content changed is still stale.
- `MobBuilder::resume` finishes a Stop that an earlier process durably
  began and never finished before it hands the mob back (`meerkat-mob`).
  A mob whose last process ended in the middle of a Stop (for example a
  shutdown that waited on a member stuck at a compaction in an earlier
  release) resumed as Running, and its recovery finished the Stop in the
  background a moment later. A host that reads the phase right after the
  resume to decide whether to lift a stopped mob read Running and never
  lifted it: the mob stayed Stopped, every send to a member was refused
  with `invalid state transition: Stopped -> Running`, and the next
  shutdown failed on the Stop of a stopped mob. The resume now waits, up
  to 5 s, for the first attempt at that Stop, so the handle it returns is
  Stopped and the host lifts it as it lifts a completed Stop. An
  interrupted Complete is finished the same way, so the handle reads
  Completed. An attempt that is refused, or still running when the wait
  ends (a Stop held on a member or on a placed completion), goes on in the
  background as before; a host that must see the phase such a slow Stop
  leaves waits for its `MobStopped` itself.
- `meerkat-mob`: a respawned local member keeps the restrictions it was
  spawned under. `MobHandle::respawn` and the `mob_respawn` tool built the
  successor from the member's profile alone, so a member spawned under its
  spawner's tool ceiling, deny list or launch policy came back without them.
  The successor now keeps the predecessor's launch tool access policy and
  inherited visibility ceiling, as its session recorded them, intersected with
  the successor's own and never widened. It keeps the auth binding the
  predecessor's session recorded only when its own spec names none and its
  profile resolves to the provider that binding was recorded for; a successor
  re-profiled to another provider (or to one that cannot be told) selects its
  own binding, as a fresh spawn does. For a member with a local session, the
  successor's profile and provider are resolved before anything is retired. A
  respawn whose predecessor's restrictions cannot be established, whose
  successor profile cannot be resolved, or whose member changes while they are
  read, is refused before anything is retired, and the member is kept. A
  recorded binding that has since been removed from the realm configuration,
  or re-pointed to another provider, is not validated before retirement: the
  successor's build then fails after the predecessor is retired
  (`MobRespawnError::SpawnAfterRetireWithCause`). Name a binding in a spawn
  customizer, or retire and spawn. A peer-only member whose generation was
  never bound to a local session carries no session restrictions; its
  successor keeps the launch policy and ceiling its own spec inherits. Placed
  members are unchanged.

- `meerkat-runtime`: a session with compaction history no longer refuses its
  next transcript rewrite after its runtime moves to the head-canonical
  profile (a SQLite realm opened with `SqliteRuntimeStore::new_head_canonical`,
  or a standalone WholeBlob database converted with
  `SqliteRuntimeStore::convert_standalone_whole_blob_in_place`). The
  conversion recorded the runtime's boundary with a different row commitment
  from the session's stored head, so the first rewrite after a restart, such
  as the next compaction, was refused ("previous transcript revision ... did
  not match commit parent ..."), and a converted Meta gateway with a
  compacted member failed to start. A conversion now records the stored
  head, and opening a store that an earlier build converted repairs each
  affected runtime record in place. Pre-existing in 0.9.3.
- `meerkat-runtime`: revoking a controller grant no longer answers
  `Unavailable` once the runtime store holds a mob member's runtime with its
  mob binding, as it does after a restart recovers the members. The custody
  scan took that binding, which names the mob runtime the member's session
  runtime serves, for a lifecycle stored under another runtime's id. A
  session runtime may now name its mob runtime; any other runtime must still
  name itself. Pre-existing since 0.8.52.

- `meerkat-core`: a session that holds inline video compacts, and a
  compacted 0.9.3 session that holds inline video converts to the
  head-canonical profile. Video has no blob form, so ordinary appends always
  kept its bytes in the session's rows, but a transcript rewrite refused
  rows with inline video as if they were images that had to move to the blob
  store first. A live head-canonical session that had received an inline
  video could never compact again ("post-rewrite live tail carries inline
  media"), and the conversion of a compacted 0.9.3 session with inline video
  (`SqliteRuntimeStore::convert_standalone_whole_blob_in_place`, and the Meta
  storage migration that runs it) was refused ("compact rewrite delta carries
  inline media"). Rewrites and the conversion now keep inline video as row
  content, byte for byte; inline images still move to the blob store before
  they become rows.

- `meerkat-runtime`: a compacted 0.9.3 session that holds inline images
  converts to the head-canonical profile. Its WholeBlob body keeps those
  images inline in its transcript graph (the anchor, rewrite replacements and
  parent advances, across user messages, tool results and comms notices), and
  the conversion refused it ("compact rewrite delta carries inline media").
  `SqliteRuntimeStore::convert_standalone_whole_blob_in_place_with_media` now
  first stores every such image in the realm blob store under its content
  address, then seeds the session with those images as blob references; the
  transcript revision and the rewrite commits stay the body's, and the
  WholeBlob body is kept as it was. A crash during or between the two steps
  leaves each runtime converted or untouched, and running the conversion again
  finishes the rest.

- `meerkat-runtime`: a SQLite realm that holds such a session, in a runtime's
  WholeBlob body or as the session store's legacy blob row, opens on the
  head-canonical profile. Its activation refused the session the same way,
  so the realm did not open. `SqliteRuntimeStore::new_head_canonical_with_media`
  first stores the images in the realm blob store, then lays the session out
  with them as blob references; the body and the blob row are kept as they
  were, and an open stopped after storing the images finishes on the next one.
  The SQLite session store's own activation of such a legacy session
  (`IncrementalSessionStore::activate_head_canonical_store_with_staged_images`,
  after `stage_legacy_inline_images`) crosses it the same way, and one whose
  images were not staged refuses the whole activation, writing nothing.
- `meerkat-core`: a session whose realtime projection holds a transcript
  segment converts to the head-canonical profile, and a session that took a
  live image reopens after a compaction or another transcript rewrite. The
  conversion of a 0.9.3 session (the session store's crossing, the store-wide
  activation, the realm open and the standalone conversion, and the Meta
  storage migration that runs the first two) and every transcript rewrite or
  recovery rebase write the realtime projection as one snapshot event, whose
  items key their text, staged content and image fingerprints by content
