    falling back to the workspace on anything the scoping cannot read.
  - The TLC audits run in three shards instead of two, xtask's unit tests
    (5-7 minutes) run in a lane of their own, and a `governance-gates` job
    runs the typed governance gates (`rmat-audit`, `seam-inventory`,
    `runtime-authority-bypass`, `machine-authority-docs-gate`) when machine
    authority or a dogma document changes.
  - The pre-push hook no longer runs the changed-path ratchets, the machine
    codegen drift check, the canonical TLC lane or the deterministic workspace
    test gate (they are manual hooks; CI runs each before merge or on the push
    a release tag requires green, except the gate's lib tests under the
    workspace's unified features, which only nightly's workspace unit lane
    runs: the push runs every member's lib tests with that member's own
    features), skips the release contract tests CI already runs on every pull
    request, and runs its two slow harness contracts only when a push changes
    what they exercise.
  - The `CI gate`'s pull-request budgets drop to 1080 s of lane execution and
    1200 s push-to-terminal (runner queue still excluded), from 1500 s and
    2700 s.
  - A push to `main` now diffs against the last main commit whose CI run
    completed green with its attestation instead of the push's payload base,
    so the changes of a cancelled, superseded or failed main run still run the
    push-only lanes; it plans the whole workspace when no such commit is
    found, when the push carries more than one commit (the finder runs from
    HEAD's first parent only when that parent is the push's payload base), or
    when the finder's answer is not a full sha of an ancestor of HEAD.
- A push to `main` runs the payload base's own copy of
  `scripts/ci-push-plan-base.mjs`, which decides the push's diff base, so a
  pushed commit cannot change that decision for its own push; without that
  copy the push plans the whole workspace. CI only.
- **Every third-party GitHub Action is pinned to a commit SHA, and Renovate
  no longer automerges action updates.** Each `uses:` in `.github/`
  workflows and composite actions (release and reusable workflows included)
  names the full commit its tag or branch resolved to, with the ref in a
  trailing comment; Renovate keeps them current
  (`helpers:pinGitHubActionDigests`), proposes new action versions in a
  group of their own a week after their release, holds a digest update (a
  tag that now names another commit) for approval on the dependency
  dashboard, and never automerges one. `scripts/ci-action-pins.mjs` (in
  `make path-classifier-selftest`) fails on an unpinned third-party action
  and on any spelling of a `uses` key it cannot read (quoted, in a flow
  mapping, its value on the next line) or any key whose name a line cannot
  show (an explicit `?` key, an alias, an escape in a quoted key), naming
  its file and line, and on a Renovate configuration that could automerge
  an action update, including automerge set outside packageRules
  (`vulnerabilityAlerts`, an update type's settings), release its digest
  updates from approval, or automerge what a regex manager
  (`customManagers`) pins: the container digests and the sccache release,
  which Renovate proposes a week after their release, in a group of their
  own, and never automerges. The pinned
  `dtolnay/rust-toolchain` commit is that of its `1.94.1` branch, which
  installs that toolchain; the trailing comment names it. The release jobs
  whose checkout can be an older tag (a recovery dispatch) run their setup
  action, Rust or BuildBuddy, and the scripts it runs from a checkout of
  the workflow's own commit, so an older tag's setup action never runs,
  and the Rust setup installs the channel the checked-out tree names when
  it differs. The BuildBuddy release validation, which runs the actions of
  the tree it checks out, refuses a release tag; the github-hosted backend
  validates one. CI only.
- **A release tag no longer restores a Bazel repository cache another run
  could have saved.** The tag's full BuildBuddy graph (`buildbuddy.yml`
  with `repository_cache: "false"`) restores none, and the dispatch-only
  release checks (`release-binaries-check.yml`, `release-turbo-s.yml`)
  restore it without saving, so no dispatch writes the cache scope tags
  read. The release doctor now reads the reusable workflows a tag run calls,
  with the caller's inputs, and fails on a call it cannot read, on any tag
  restore of that cache, and on any dispatch-like run that saves it. CI
  only.
- **The nightly full BuildBuddy graph no longer passes every repository
  secret.** `nightly.yml` calls `buildbuddy.yml` with exactly the secrets
  that workflow declares instead of `secrets: inherit`, and the release
  doctor's token check now fails on `secrets: inherit` in any workflow of
  the repository, not only `release.yml`. CI only.
- `.github/CODEOWNERS` names the maintainer as the owner of `.github/`,
  `renovate.json`, `Makefile` and `scripts/` explicitly, so the CI, release
  and dependency-update configuration keeps that owner if the default
  owner changes. Repository configuration only.
- **A dispatch saves no cache that a tag-trusted run restores.** `ci.yml`
  (which writes the exact-tree attestation), `release-semver-readiness.yml`
  (the semver attestation) and `release-binaries-check.yml` save no cache
  on a `workflow_dispatch` run, and the release doctor fails on a
  dispatch-like run that saves a cache in any workflow whose runs a tag
  trusts or that checks out a ref its inputs choose. The semver readiness
  and release binaries checks no longer cache `~/.cargo/bin`. CI only.
- **Release runs restore no GitHub Actions cache.** The release
  validation, binary, Web SDK and semver baseline jobs run no rust-cache
  step, on a tag or on a dispatch (a prebuild or a recovery): nothing on
  main saves their keys. `build-windows-cross` restores the Windows SDK
  cache only for a caller that saves it, which release.yml does not, and
  the BuildBuddy release jobs pass `repository-cache: "false"`. The
  semver gate's dispatch measurement keeps its cache, which the readiness
  workflow's push to main saves. Only a re-run of the same tag loses a
  warm cache. The release doctor fails on any cache a release job would
  restore, on any event. CI only.
- **Only push and schedule runs set the CI sccache client to write its
  bucket.** Every other run, pull requests from this repository included,
  runs it read-only (`SCCACHE_GCS_RW_MODE=READ_ONLY`), and the lanes no
  longer install sccache through sccache-action, so no step exports the
  job's Actions cache token to their run steps. Both stop short of a
  credential: the read-only mode is a client-side setting, and any later
  step of a lane that authenticated to GCS can read the credentials file
  `SCCACHE_GCS_KEY_PATH` names, whose bearer is the job's Actions runtime
  token (the runner sets `ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN` to the same
  token). That token reaches the Actions caches, which no release job
  restores. The release doctor checks the mode and the install. CI only.
- **CI installs a pinned sccache release.** The CI lanes' setup
  (`.github/actions/setup-sccache-ci`) downloads the sccache v0.18.0
  tarball itself and checks it against a pinned sha256, instead of
  installing through `mozilla-actions/sccache-action`, which checks a
  download only against the `.sha256` file of the same release. Every
  remaining sccache-action step (nightly, `cargo.yml` and the dense Mob
  topology workflow, which use the GitHub Actions cache backend the action
  sets up) names the release it installs (`version: v0.18.0`) instead of
  taking the newest one when the job runs. Renovate proposes new releases
  through a regex manager; the setup's sha256 must change with the
  version, or its install fails. `scripts/ci-action-pins.mjs` fails on an
  sccache-action step without an exact release, and the release doctor on
  a CI setup that installs through the action or skips the sha256 check.
  CI only.
- **The Linux release build image is pinned by digest.**
  `buildpack-deps:bullseye` (the release workflow's Linux build container
  and the Bazel x86_64 and arm64 execution platforms) is named by its
  multi-arch index digest, which a Renovate regex manager keeps current.
  `scripts/ci-action-pins.mjs` refuses a `docker://` action, a
  `container:` or `image:` value, or a Bazel `docker://` reference without
  a digest, with one named exception: the self-hosted CI image, whose
  registry is private. CI and release builds only.
- The BuildBuddy edge-lane detector (`scripts/buildbuddy-edge-changes`)
  matched crate paths without their `crates/` prefix, so a crate change
  selected none of the WASM, SDK, minimal or feature-matrix edge lanes it
  should; it now does, and its WASM list gains the five crates the web
  runtime's dependencies reach that it lacked (authorization contracts,
  capabilities, jobs, models, workgraph). A self-test in
  `make path-classifier-selftest` fails when that list drifts from cargo
  metadata. `make buildbuddy-doctor` reads the mixed
  fast/non-fast routing and the `oai-rt-rs` pin without pinning a target
  list or a crate version. CI only.
- **CI starts its long rows first.** The Clippy, main unit, closure-tests
  and feature-check lanes run in two waves: the rows that took 8 minutes or
  more on a green run (`scripts/ci-row-durations.json`, regenerated with
  `scripts/ci-row-durations.mjs`), and rows never measured, start right
  after the change classification; the shorter rows, and the short lanes,
  wait for a `stagger` job (30 seconds on a push, none on a pull request).
  The account's hosted runners take about 40 jobs at a time and pick queued
  jobs in no reliable order, so a long row picked late set the run's wall
  time; a simulation of the two whole-workspace main pushes before this
  change puts such a push at about 18 minutes instead of about 24, with no
  other run on the account. The `CI gate` counts a two-wave lane as run
  when every wave that holds rows succeeded (and main unit coverage when
  each of its packed waves and archived lanes that holds rows succeeded),
  and requires the `stagger` job; the pull-request lane budget adds the
  stagger job's run time to the lanes that wait for it and leaves its
  runner queue out, as for every lane. CI only.
- A push to `main` or a `release/**` branch runs no separate unit lane. The
  rows a pull request's unit lane would run for the same change (its
  shards, with the same `-p` sets, and its feature suites) run verbatim in
  the main unit lane, which ran the same tests again in other shards; the
  rest of the workspace is packed around them. The plan names them
  (`unit_rows_on_main`), the `CI gate` requires the main unit lane in their
  place, and the exact-tree attestation records their count, which
  release-projection evidence accepts for the skipped unit lane. A
  whole-workspace push runs 13 fewer jobs. Each unit row runs only the
  target kinds its packages have (`--bins` for the binary-only rkat and
  surface-build-fixtures, which a push runs in rows of their own). CI only.
- Clippy refuses the APIs that start a process: the new workspace
  `clippy.toml` disallows `std::process::Command::new`,
  `tokio::process::Command::new`, `CommandExt::exec`, the `libc` `fork`,
  `vfork`, `clone`, `exec*`, `posix_spawn*`, `system` and `popen` functions,
  `nix::unistd::fork` and `exec*`, and `webbrowser::open*`, including when a
  call goes through an aliased import or a re-export the source test cannot
  see. Shipped code allows the lint only at the launch sites
  `crates/meerkat/tests/host_launch_sites.rs` lists, once per launch
  expression, and that test now checks it, so `SITES` stays the one list;
  each host launch exemption keeps its one fixed-program constructor. Test
  code, the `xtask` developer tooling and the examples allow the lint for
  themselves. The test also fails when anything turns the lint off in bulk:
  a second Clippy configuration file (a crate's own `clippy.toml` or
  `.clippy.toml` would replace the root one for that crate), a `warnings`,
  `clippy::all` or `clippy::style` allow or expect in shipped code, a Cargo
  manifest entry for the lint or an allow of its group, or a Cargo
  configuration file in the tree (`.cargo/config.toml`) whose `rustflags`
  allow the lint, its groups or `warnings` or cap lint levels, or whose
  `[env]` sets `CLIPPY_CONF_DIR` or `CLIPPY_ARGS`. A run whose environment
  sets those variables or such `RUSTFLAGS`, or a Cargo configuration outside
  the checkout, is outside the test; the repository's lanes and CI set none.
- **CI runs the tests that read a changed doc.** A change to a file that
  belongs to no crate (docs, skills, `CHANGELOG.md`, specs, fixtures) now
  adds the exact targets that read it to the integration lane, as listed
  in `scripts/ci-non-rust-readers.json`: on a pull request, unless the
  reader compiles meerkat-mob (then on the push, named in the plan); on a
  push without a main unit lane, for the lib, bin and example targets; and
  on every push for a test target that needs features the push's
  closure-tests rows do not build (xtask's machine-authority contracts,
  the GPT Live replay suite). For a reader in library code a pull request
  runs the lib and bins and leaves its test targets to the push's
  closure-tests rows, as for a code change; the nested-Cargo canary tests
  run only there. The plan names what a pull request leaves to the push.
  A reader that needs live-provider credentials runs in no CI lane, and
  the plan and the `CI gate` name it. Before, a docs-only pull request ran
  none of them and a docs-only push never ran rkat's doc-example test. A
  crate's in-crate documentation that it compiles in (the
  `skills/*/SKILL.md` files) is now a build input of that crate, and the
  authority-language check of `xtask machine-check-drift` runs on the live
  docs in an xtask library test, so a docs pull request runs it too. The
  inventory's guard fails a reader whose named test the reader's features
  compile out (meerkat-store's 0.8.10 corpus test needs `sqlite`, not a
  default feature of the crate). CI only.
- **The live gate skips xtask changes.** `scripts/live-gate-changed` no
  longer counts a change under `crates/xtask/` as live-relevant: no live
  gate target compiles or runs xtask, so a pull request that changes only
  xtask passes the gate without running the GPT Live scenarios. CI only.
- Release: before it builds the Python and TypeScript SDK packages,
  `publish_registries` waits for the release's complete binary manifest
  (`scripts/release-await-binary-manifest`: up to 150 minutes on a tag run,
  usually no time with a prebuild, a failed API call counting as "not yet";
  a package recovery needs the manifest already published), verifies each
  `rkat-rpc` archive's build attestation, stamps the pinned digests into both
  SDKs and refuses to publish a package that does not pin exactly them for
  its version. The job's token gains `attestations: read`, and its timeout is
  240 minutes, up from 180. Crate publication and the publication SLO do not
  wait for it.

### Deprecated

- `meerkat::open_system_browser`
  (`meerkat_auth_core::mcp_oauth::open_system_browser`) and
  `McpOAuthPendingLogin::launch_system_browser`, which name no host judgement:
  a host that confines its agents' launches and called them would run a
  browser opener a confined process planted on `PATH`. Use
  `open_system_browser_guarded` with the host's launch guard, or
  `open_system_browser_trusting`, and pass it to
  `McpOAuthPendingLogin::launch_browser`. Their behaviour is unchanged.

### Fixed

- A mob member's failed provisioning cleanup no longer deadlocks with a
  concurrent raw unregister of the same session (`meerkat-mob`). An owned
  actor transaction (a member create or revival whose create failed after
  the session service published its actor, or one cancelled after that)
  rolled its prepared materialization back while still holding the
  session's turn-finalization boundary. That rollback takes the session's
  live lifecycle lease, which a concurrent
  `MeerkatMachine::unregister_session` saga holds into its surface cleanup,
  and that cleanup waits for the boundary. The cleanup now discards the
  exact live actor under the boundary, releases it, and then rolls back
  through the ordinary path, in the saga's own lock order. If a raw
  unregister removes the registration while the boundary is released, or
  the session id is registered again, the rollback leaves it alone. The
  host materializer's rollbacks before any actor is published keep the
  boundary, since no surface cleanup waits on it there. Debug builds assert
  that no actor is published at those points; release builds check it too,
  and refuse such a rollback with a typed
  `MaterializeServeError::UnrecordedSessionCleanup`, which fail-stops the
  serving actor, instead of risking the deadlock. (#1814)
- A member force cancel (`MobHandle::force_cancel_member`, `mob/force_cancel`,
  the `force_cancel_member` tool) and `mob/cancel_all_work` no longer fail
  with an internal error ("cancelling the current run of '...' failed:
  Interrupt outcome is not settled ...") when the member's run crosses a
  boundary while the cancel is delivered. The runtime has recorded the
  cancel for that exact run by then, and the run ends at its next boundary;
  without live delivery the run's work continues until the runtime next
  observes a boundary (for a service that reports none, the turn's end).
  The verb now succeeds, as a member stop already did: its success means
  the cancel is recorded. The same holds when the member's session service
  does not support the live boundary cancel
  (`SessionService::cancel_after_boundary`): the runtime has recorded the
  cancel first, and the verbs report it instead of an internal error.
  `MeerkatMachine::cancel_after_boundary_run_if_current` also reports
  `InterruptDispatchOutcomeUnknown` rather than a bare `Internal` for the
  other failures that follow the recorded cancel (its effect projection, the
  withdrawal of its dispatch), so the verbs report the recorded cancel there
  too. This was the intermittent
  `member_creation_some_origin_authority_matrix` failure in meerkat-mob's
  tests.
- A mob Stop no longer holds up every later mob command for one session wait
  per member. It cancelled every member session's checkpoint gate, then held
  every member's run starts, one member after another, and each of those
  steps can wait on that member's session: an in-flight checkpoint save holds
  its gate, and a running turn's commit holds the session's mutation gate. A
  Stop of a large busy mob blocked its actor for seconds. Both phases now run
  concurrently per member (run-start holds 32 at a time) and keep their order
  (every hold before any interrupt); a failed Stop still reports its first
  failure in roster order. Every member that can be held is now held even
  when another member's hold fails (before, the members after the first
  failure were not held), and a failed Stop now releases every member's
  hold again (before, they stayed held), except while the actor is
  fail-stopping for cold recovery, where cold replay decides. After a
  failed Stop the mob stays Running and input queued before the Stop runs,
  but the Stop's lifecycle intent stays pending: new member input is
  refused with `LifecycleOperationPending { intent: "stop" }` until a
  retried Stop completes and the mob is resumed, or a Reset takes the
  intent over (Resume alone does not clear it: it resumes only a Stopped
  mob). The actor's inline-step watchdog now names each Stop stage
  (`stop_checkpointer_cancel`, `stop_run_start_holds`, and so on) in its
  `stage_timings_ms`.
- The fork_off re-link after a restart no longer only logs a failed
  retirement of a child whose settled outcome retires it (its own turn
  failed, or it ran past its `max_run`). It retries the retirement for up to
  about ten seconds, in that child's own settlement, and reports the result
  typed (`ChildRetirement`) in each report and outcome; a child whose
  retirement still fails is reported `Failed`, logged, and retired by the
  next pass (a restart, or `MobMcpState::relink_restored_fork_children`).
  (#1391)
- Destroying a mob no longer hangs when one of its members lost a boundary
  commit: the commit failed after the member's run consumed its input in
  memory, so the member's runtime requires a durability reload. The member's
  exited runtime loop keeps the session's mutation gate until a reload
  releases it, and the destroy waited on that gate in the member's ingress
  detach forever, because nothing performed the reload. The destroy now
  reloads such a member first, as retirement already did: its runtime is
  replaced by one recovered from the durable store, where the consumed input
  is pending again, and the member's retirement records that input as
  abandoned (`Retired`) instead of losing it with the in-memory run. The
  reload runs before the destroy writes anything, and again just before each
  member's ingress detach. A reload that fails or overruns the member retire
  budget makes the destroy a typed `MobDestroyError::Incomplete` whose report
  names the member and the reload error. When that happens before the destroy
  started, the destroy has written nothing and can be retried, but the
  members it reloaded before the failing one stay reloaded (their degraded
  shells were replaced and their consumed inputs are pending again), and the
  report lists them in `reloaded_members`. (#1222)
- Agent schedule tools no longer keep a stopped schedule host's session and
  mob hosts alive. `SharedScheduleTargetAdapter` now owns the create-time
  identity-target probe it attaches and the `ScheduleService` holds it
  weakly, so the schedule tools in a factory builder's
  `default_schedule_tools` slot, which the session service owns, no longer
  keep the session service and the mob state alive once the schedule host
  has stopped, and a mob store's `drain_observers` no longer needs that slot
  cleared. An embedder that tears these down while its process keeps running
  drops the 0.9.2 teardown step: `spawn_schedule_host`, the runtime-backed
  schedule host spawners, `SharedScheduleTargetAdapter::new`,
  `set_default_schedule_tools`, `FactoryAgentBuilder::default_schedule_tools`
  and the scheduling guide now say so. A schedule host started after
  teardown for the same service judges identity targets itself (see
  Breaking), and store-only schedule tool calls (get, list, pause and the
  rest) keep working after teardown.
- The first fire of a materialize-on-demand schedule completes, in every
  schedule host (a stock-governed realm refuses the fire before it
  materializes a session; see Security). After the dispatch materialized its
  session, the schedule
  driver synced the in-flight occurrence's target to the newly bound session,
  and generated occurrence authority refused that sync while the occurrence
  was dispatching: the driver tick failed, and the occurrence never completed
  and was retried after each lease expiry. A dispatching occurrence now
  records the session its dispatch materialized, once; rebinding it stays
  refused.
- `rkat-rpc`'s schedule host delivers a scheduled prompt or event to the
  session its fire has just materialized. That session is staged until its
  first turn, and the delivery read its keep-alive policy from the persisted
  session, so every materialize-on-demand fire failed as `transport_error`
  ("session not found"). The policy now comes from the staged session, as it
  does for `turn/start`.
- One failing delivery no longer holds back the rest of a schedule driver
  tick. When handling one claimed occurrence failed with an error (for
  example, a delivery adapter returned a dispatch inconsistent with its
  occurrence), a `ScheduleDriver` tick returned that error at once. Every
  occurrence the tick had claimed after it stayed claimed and undelivered
  until its lease expired (60 seconds in the schedule host), then fired late
  or misfired. The tick now handles every occurrence it claimed, unless the
  claim scan breaks the store contract, which still fails the tick at once.
  It returns the first handling error, or that contract violation, and logs
  every error it does not return, so the schedule host still records the
  failed tick.
- A read of runtime delivery state no longer creates the state directory or
  an empty runtime store. The SQLite runtime store's delivery reads (delivery
  authorities and inbox records, continuation key bindings and admissions,
  and the delivery generation) opened a create-capable connection, so a read
  over a store whose file or directory was gone (a released, moved or removed
  state directory, read by a delivery owner or a health tick that outlived
  it) re-created the directory and an empty `runtime.sqlite`. They now open
  an existing file without create and answer "not provisioned" when it is
  missing, unless another holder's maintenance fence covers the missing file
  (an archive by rename), which still fails typed; among delivery
  operations, only a write creates the store. No schema change.
- Detached callback tools work in ordinary RPC turns. A callback tool
  registered with `execution.mode: "detached"` refused every call with
  "requires runtime-owned interaction lineage" unless the turn carried a
  transient turn context: a plain `turn/start`, the first turn of a
  deferred session, the immediate turn of `session/create` and a mob
  member's `mob/turn_start` gave the turn no interaction. Such a call now
  queues its job. A turn that merges inputs of several interactions, or
  whose input names none (for example a flow step without a correlation
  id), still refuses typed, and the refusal now says so.
- A detached job a mob member's session submitted delivered its
  notifications and terminal to that session's runtime, and an
  explicit-resume repoint moves the member to a successor session without
  migrating delivery rows, so after a repoint they stranded on the
  superseded session (#1790). The job store the persistence bundle hands
  producers (`PersistenceBundle::producer_job_store`, which the RPC host and
  the runtime-backed surfaces use) now records the delivery address of the
  member whose current session submits a job
  (`rt:member:{mob}:{identity}:{generation}`, as the host's continuation
  resolver reports it) as the job's origin member (`JobSpec::origin_member_id`),
  and the delivery owner applies such a job's rows in the session serving the
  member when they are delivered; other sessions' subscriptions are
  unchanged. A replay of the same call from the superseded session joins the
  admitted job: the callback and shell producers adopt its origin member. A
  member respawned under its identity is a new generation that never receives
  an earlier generation's rows, which stay pending. Jobs submitted before
  0.9.3, and jobs of sessions no member serves, keep their session's
  address; a replay keeps what its admitted job recorded. A host that builds
  its own job producers from `PersistenceBundle::job_store()` keeps session
  addressing; give them `producer_job_store()` for member addressing.
- An Anthropic `pause_turn` stop (a server-tool loop reached its iteration
  limit) is reported as `pause_turn` instead of `end_turn`. The paused turn
  commits like an end of turn, even when it holds only server-tool blocks, and
  its `server_tool_use` blocks go back to the provider as history with the
  next request. That replay has been checked against a stub server only, not
  against the live API (#1881). Recovery of a durable tail left by a shutdown
  race classifies a tail that ends in a `pause_turn` turn as `Ambiguous` and
  holds it, as it does a `max_tokens` tail. Before, such a tail read as
  `end_turn` and could be recovered as a completed run.
- A tool call whose streamed input a refusal or a filled context window cut
  off now ends the Anthropic stream with that stop reason instead of a stream
  parse error. Under any other stop reason a tool input that does not parse
  still fails the response as before.
- `rkat mob deploy --surface rpc` now builds from the deploy config, as the
  default `cli` surface does. The deploy flags (`--model`,
  `--max-total-tokens`, `--max-duration`, `--max-tool-calls`) and the pack's
  deploy defaults (`max_tokens`, `[models]`, `[budget]`, `[compaction]`)
  apply, as defaults, to every member and session the RPC host builds, and
  to its model resolution and model hot-swaps; an explicit `session/create`
  or mob spawn parameter replaces them for that session. A flag wins over the
  realm config, which wins over the pack default. The host used to build from
  the realm's config documents alone (a known issue since 0.9.1). The deploy
  values are not
  written to the realm document: `config/get` and `config/set` on the host
  still read and write the realm's own document. The host now also refuses
  to start when the realm declares multi-process hosting its stores cannot
  provide, as the `cli` surface already did (see Breaking).
- `rkat mcp login` refusals now name the server and the remedy. A server
  without an account selection is refused before any credential store or
  network effect, with the server's scope and the `rkat mcp remove` and
  `rkat mcp add` commands for each choice. A `discover` (or
  `--oauth-account`) server whose authorization server publishes no usable
  OpenID Connect UserInfo is still refused before client registration with
  nothing stored, and the refusal now says so, says to retry first when the
  issuer could not be reached (one typed reason covers both), and names
  `unverified` as the deliberate alternative and what it means; it never
  switches the server to `unverified`. An account other than the selected
  one is refused naming the server, and for a `discover` server how to bind
  another account. A slot holding a credential the login may not replace is
  refused with the real way to disconnect it (RPC `auth/logout` with the MCP
  target, or the SDK `auth_mcp_logout` / `authMcpLogout` helpers; `rkat` has
  no disconnect command). The printed commands single-quote the server name
  and URL, so a URL with `?` or `&` pastes as shown. A successful login says
  whether the account was bound by discovery, and an unverified login says
  it carries no account verification.
- `rkat run --mcp-auth interactive` logs in to `discover` and `unverified`
  servers when they first require OAuth. The CLI's in-session login refused
  every server without an `oauth_account`, unlike `rkat mcp login`; only a
  server without any account selection is refused now. An in-session login
  prints the same one-line outcome as `rkat mcp login` on stderr, including
  that an unverified credential carries no account verification.
- The `McpOAuthError::AccountSelectionRequired` text (shown by RPC and REST
  for the `account_selection_required` reason) now names both ways to
  select: "MCP OAuth interactive login requires an account selection:
  oauth_account (a provider subject ID) or oauth_account_selection (discover
  or unverified)". It said an explicit expected account was required.
- The quickstart, the MCP examples and the embedded `mcp-server-setup` skill
  showed `rkat mcp add <name> --url <url>` followed by `rkat mcp login
  <name>`, which that refusal stops; they now pass
  `--oauth-account-selection discover`.
- The MCP reference said MCP OAuth credentials are stored per installation,
  not per realm. Since 0.9 each realm has its own credential slot in the
  host's token store (the slot key includes the realm the host serves), as
  the CLI reference and the 0.9 migration notes say; the reference now says
  so.
- Guarded config writes over one state root take turns. Every store
  declared with its realm chain (`FileConfigStore::with_realm_chain`, as the
  stock hosts' stores are, and `SdkConfigStore::with_realm_document`) holds
  an exclusive advisory lock on the state root's composition lock file from
  before it reads its own document, through its composition check, to after
  its write, in one process and across processes. A check that reads
  another document can then never read one another writer is about to
  replace, so two writes that each pass alone cannot combine into a
  composition neither checked. In 0.9.2 each write was checked alone (the
  0.9.2 known limitation). A host on another state root takes another
  lock; a write to the user document also composes each realm it states as
  if that realm had no document (below), so none of its checks depends on a
  document only another state root holds. `rkat realm create`, `delete` and
  `prune` do not take the lock: a delete or prune that races a write naming
  the realm as a parent leaves that realm with a missing parent, which does
  not compose. An NFS mount that keeps locks on each machine (`nolock`,
  `local_lock=flock`) does not carry the lock between machines.
- A write to the user document checks each realm the user document states a
  section for both with that realm's own document from the writing host's
  state root and as if the realm had none. Several state roots can share one
  user document, and on one that holds no document for a realm, that realm
  takes the user document's section for it. In 0.9.2 the check composed such
  a realm only from the writing host's state root (the 0.9.2 known
  limitation), so a write there could, for example, remove the
  `parent = "global"` edge of `[realm.team]` that put the user document's
  `[governance]` on `team`'s chain wherever `team` has no document. A stated
  realm whose chain resolves on no such state root, before or after the
  write, composes nothing there and does not refuse it. One whose chain
  resolves there only after the write (removing a stale `[realm.team]
  parent = "org"` where `org` has no document, say) is refused with an
  error naming the realm on a state root without its own document and the
  remedy, editing the user document by hand: such roots refuse to compose
  the realm before the write, and would compose it from the user document
  alone after it.
- `rkat` hides a client secret typed at its terminal where neither
  `/bin/stty` nor `/usr/bin/stty` exists (NixOS): terminal control
  (`HostLaunchExemption::terminal_control`) falls back to the `stty` the
  launch's `PATH` finds, which under a host that confines its launches holds
  no relative directory and no directory a confined process could change. In
  0.9.2 it ran `/bin/stty` regardless, so on such a host `rkat` refused to
  read a secret typed at the terminal (the 0.9.2 known limitation).
- `meerkat` built without its `session-store` feature (its default feature
  set included) no longer warns that `ConsentAwareJobSource` is never
  constructed. The crate-private consent-aware job source is now compiled
  only with the session-store runtime delivery host that builds it.
- A governed web_search helper whose owner rates its model request R2 or R3
  now gives the model the same typed review feedback as any other tool:
  `review_unavailable` with kind `unsupported_entry` (R2) or
  `review_unsatisfied` with kind `human_consent_required` (R3), carrying only
  that `kind`. The request still settles at its model entry with nothing
  sent, but the Anthropic, OpenAI and Gemini web_search executors
  (`AnthropicWebSearchExecutor`, `OpenAiWebSearchExecutor`,
  `GeminiWebSearchExecutor`) dropped the typed settlement at their provider
  seam and returned `LlmError::OperationAuthorizationUnavailable`, so the
  model saw `operation_authorization_unavailable` (as the 0.9.2 notes
  described). They now return `LlmError::OperationReviewRefused`, which the
  builtin web_search tool already reports as review feedback. web_search
  gains no review support: its review entry stays unsupported and the
  installed reviewer is never asked. An owner that cannot decide the helper
  still gives `operation_authorization_unavailable`.
- The live host gives the live model the same typed review feedback when a
  session fails a live tool call with a model request's settled review (R2
  `unsupported_entry`, R3 `human_consent_required`, carried in the
  authority-unavailable model error's details).
  `LiveToolDispatchError::from_session_error` classified every such error as
  `ToolError::OperationAuthorizationUnavailable`; it now decodes the
  settlement with core's `AgentError::operation_review_refusal` and gives
  `ToolError::ReviewUnavailable` or `ToolError::ReviewUnsatisfied`. Plain
  authority unavailability, and a review detail that does not decode, still
  give `operation_authorization_unavailable`.
- `LiveToolDispatchError::from_session_error` now also classifies a model
  failure that its session reports with settlement diagnostics. Core keeps
  such a failure inside `AgentError::WithSettlementFailures`, and the
  classifier matched only an unwrapped model error, so a settled review,
  authority unavailability or observation unavailability with diagnostics
  fell through to `LiveToolDispatchError::Session` (code `AGENT_ERROR`) and
  reached the live model as a prose tool error. The classifier now reads the
  primary error: a settled review and authority unavailability give the same
  typed tool feedback as without diagnostics, and the diagnostics travel in
  the live tool result's `settlement_failures`; observation unavailability
  leaves the tool feedback path as
  `LiveAdapterHostError::OperationObservationUnavailable` carrying them. An
  operation refusal keeps its classification and is never read as review
  feedback, also when its details carry a review.
- A GPT Live barge-in duck (`live/assistant_playback_hint`) over an answer now
  ends once the user has been quiet for 1.6 s, the floor guard's release
  length, even while the answer is still talking. Since 0.8.51 every duck
  waited for a 600 ms gap in the assistant's output after the user went quiet,
  so an answer that started into the user's speech and never paused stayed
  muted until it ended: in Turbo S S107 the duck ran from 3289 ms to 19205 ms
  over a 12.8 s answer, and the user heard none of it. The broker now keys the
  restore on what the duck covers, by onset order on the provider audio clock
  (gpt-live-1 output frames carry no response id). A burst the assistant was
  voicing when the user started speaking is the one the user interrupted: it
  keeps the 0.8.51 rule (once the user is quiet, ducked to its next 600 ms
  output pause or its end, so the stale tail of Turbo S S103 R3 stays silent),
  and it ends at its first 600 ms pause. Audio after that pause, and any
  response that starts into or after the user's speech, is an answer and
  restores on the user's quiet, mid-sentence if need be. So does an answer
  that follows an early yield within the 1.6 s that would end the interrupted
  response, and one that follows a user onset within 1.6 s of an answer that
  had ended at least 600 ms before. The duck still holds while the user
  speaks, and pauses inside the user's speech (under 1.6 s) never restore it.
  By design, an answer spoken entirely while the user is still talking stays
  ducked to its end (Turbo S S106): the user held the floor for all of it.
- Live channels: rows a close took behind a running member turn (the user's
  finalized speech, the assistant's spoken segments) are no longer dropped
  when the close's deferred settlement gives up because the member turn ended
  with an error or its ten-minute hang guard elapsed. The rows it still holds
  are applied in arrival order at the next point each can land, with no
  further deadline; the settlement's outcome and its recorded deferral are
  unchanged. (#1821)
- Live channels: a row deferred to a close that the session then refuses for
  a reason other than a held turn boundary is no longer dropped silently. A
  warning and a `live_transcript_row_unrecorded` runtime notice in the
  session's transcript record that it was not recorded, naming the channel,
  the row kind, its provider item id, its position among the rows the close
  held and the refusal class, never the row's content. (#1821)
- Live channels: a close takes the rows the transport deferred to it only once
  it has committed, so a close that fails before that leaves them deferred on
  the channel for its retry; a close that cannot record its deferred
  settlement still applies its rows at the boundary; and a row its settlement
  applies after settling playback, finding the channel released again while a
  member turn holds the boundary, waits for the boundary instead of being
  reported as unrecorded. (#1821)
- A deferred playback release replayed after its channel closed no longer
  fails on the closed channel's playback segment: its speech commits and the
  release succeeds (it was reported as refused although recorded). (#1821)
- Live channels: a closed channel that replays two spoken segments of one
  provider turn, both of whose output starts waited behind a member turn, no
  longer reports the second segment's output start as unrecorded while its
  release commits that speech. A refused output start is not reported while
  later rows among the rows the close held settle its provider item's speech:
  a playback terminal such as that release, a playback completion or
  truncation, or the item's final transcript or spoken transcript deltas
  whose response then completes normally (not cancelled, not a tool call)
  with no barge-in interrupt discarding them first. The session applies those
  rows by its usual rules, or refuses one and it is reported itself. Text
  whose response does not complete that way among those rows is not
  recorded, so the start is still reported. (#1821)
- GPT Live: speech whose output start waited behind a running member turn
  when the channel closed is committed under its generated output instead of
  being abandoned with its captions retracted. The segment's release follows
  its start to the close, and the close keeps the channel's generated outputs
  addressable until its deferred settlement has replayed both. (#1821)
- An idle session recovered after an abrupt host stop records its typed
  interrupted-run notice at attach even when its runtime loop checks for
  owed notices before the attachment hands them over. The attach woke the
  loop when it published and handed the notices to the session just after;
  the loop runs on its own runtime, so it could spend that wake on a check
  that found nothing and wait for the next input (the notice still reached
  the model on that turn). The attachment now wakes the exact attached loop
  again after the hand-off. `tool_process_custody_restart` forces that order
  with two test-support gates (meerkat-runtime
  `MeerkatMachine::arm_attachment_interrupted_notice_handoff_test_hook` and
  `MeerkatMachine::arm_runtime_loop_after_empty_interrupted_notice_check_test_hook`,
  doc-hidden). (#1696)
- The same notice is recorded at attach when the attachment replaces a
  predecessor whose queued inputs it fences. Fencing them left the
  replacement no queued work, so it published without waking its loop and
  skipped the wake after the hand-off as well; the hand-off now wakes the
  exact attached loop whenever it hands notices over.
- A host started where its thread limit (a container pids limit,
  `RLIMIT_NPROC`) is below its CPU count failed with only "failed to spawn
  the rkat-rpc main thread: Resource temporarily unavailable (os error 11)"
  (#1799). Tokio launches one worker per CPU and silently queues the ones it
  cannot spawn, so the main thread was the first refusal anyone saw. The
  error now names the worker count and where it came from, the cgroup
  `pids.max` and `RLIMIT_NPROC` that Linux reports, the variable to lower
  (the one that set the count, else `RKAT_WORKER_THREADS`), and, when
  `RKAT_WORKER_STACK_BYTES` overrode the stack, its size, since mapping an
  oversized stack fails with the same EAGAIN. A fatal error whose chain holds
  an `std::io::Error` of kind `WouldBlock` (EAGAIN) now ends with a `hint:`
  line naming the usual causes and the variable that set the worker count,
  in `rkat`, `rkat-rpc`, `rkat-rest`, `rkat-mcp` and `rkat-mob-mcp`.
- The push-only exact-selection lanes count this release's new cases: the
  Linux positive confinement lane expects seven MCP supported-native tests
  (the stdio stderr-tail case is new) and the governed JSONL lane expects
  five tests (the two schedule-composition cases are new). CI only.

### Known limitations

- An in-process sender that holds a peer request id can tell from its send
  result whether this session holds that request for another peer (dropped) or
  does not hold it (admitted, then refused); the id is only ever sent to the
  addressee, so a sender that holds it already sees the exchange.
- A member whose boundary commit fails while the destroy is already waiting
  on that member's ingress detach still holds the destroy: the detach waits
  on the session's mutation gate before it can see that the runtime needs a
  reload.
- `MobHandle::force_cancel_member` cannot cancel a member whose runtime
  requires a durability reload: it fails with the runtime's repair-blocked
  error. Retiring the member, or destroying the mob, reloads it first.
- No governed runtime runs scheduled agent work yet, whether it is a
  stock-governed realm or an embedder's native grant configuration (a
  `NativeGrantWorkConfiguration` installed with
  `MeerkatMachine::persistent_with_local_grant_authorization`). Such a
  runtime admits only work bound to an authenticated original, and a
  schedule fire carries none, so no fire runs outside a mandate. In a
  stock-governed realm rkat and rkat-rpc refuse every fire as
  `schedule_mandate_unavailable` without materializing a session. Any other
  host on a governed runtime whose schedule service records no
  commissioning agent (`ScheduleService::new`, or
  `PersistenceBundle::schedule_service()` outside a stock-governed realm)
  still materializes the fire's session and then fails the fire late: the
  fire never runs, and its failure class names the step that refused it,
  not the missing mandate.
- A mob member repointed between applying a job delivery row in one session
  and acknowledging it can see the row applied again in the successor
  session: each session keeps its own idempotency ledger. Continuation rows
  already have the same window.
- A background shell job's terminal, which the job applies itself, still lands
  in the session that ran it, not in the session now serving the member that
  submitted it (#1790).
- A run that stops with `pause_turn` ends there: Meerkat does not yet continue
  a paused turn automatically (#1881).
- A context-window stop fails the run; the loop does not compact and retry the
  turn (#1882).
- An Anthropic stream that carries no stop reason at all (a proxy may omit it)
  still ends as `end_turn`: a missing reason is not an unknown one.
- A Chat Completions stream that ends without a `finish_reason` also still ends
  as `end_turn`, and a tool call it streamed without a `tool_calls` (or
  `function_call`) finish is dropped, not run.
- The OpenAI realtime session adapter (live channels) still reports a failed
  response, or an incomplete one with an unknown reason, as `end_turn` (#1883).
- The `web_search` tool's native search call does not read its stop reason: a
  search the provider refused or filtered comes back as `completed` (or
  `unavailable`) with the refusal text as its answer (#1887).
- A Gemini prompt blocked before any candidate (`promptFeedback.blockReason`,
  no `finishReason`) still fails as an incomplete response, retried and then
  failing the run as `ProviderError(IncompleteResponse)`, instead of as
  `content_filtered` (#1888).
- Disabled Anthropic thinking is not live-verified in this release: which
  models accept it comes from Anthropic's per-model thinking table. Claude
  Opus 5 and Haiku 5.5 accept it only at `high` effort or below, and a
  request that sets no effort relies on their documented default efforts
  (`high` and `medium`); set the effort explicitly at `high` or below on
  those two models to be certain.
- Live transcript rows commit one at a time, in arrival order, and each waits
  for the session's turn boundary. While a member turn runs (for example
  voice-delegated work in the existing member), later rows wait behind it, so
  the persisted transcript can lag the conversation by up to that turn's
  length (see `docs/guides/realtime.mdx`). (#1821)
- When the member turn's boundary frees while a channel close is still
  settling, a later live row can commit ahead of an earlier row the close
  holds for its settlement. No row is lost; only their order in the
  transcript can differ from the conversation. (#1821)
- Rows a channel close holds for replay after its deferred settlement gave up
  are held in memory only: they are lost if the process exits before the next
  boundary lets them land. Durable staging is planned. (#1821)
- A row the transport cannot hand to its closing channel because the channel
  is already gone from the host is dropped with a warning only. The shipped
  close order keeps the channel reachable until the close has taken its rows,
  so this needs a close out of that order. (#1821)
- A member turn that ends with an error after it staged its final checkpoint
  leaves that checkpoint staged until the runtime recovers it, and while it is
  staged the store can refuse ordinary live writes to the session. A row a
  channel close replays in that window can then go unrecorded: it is reported
  with a warning, and its `live_transcript_row_unrecorded` notice can be
  refused the same way. (#1821)
- For a refused live output start a channel close replays: text of its item
  that arrives after its response's completion is recorded at once, yet the
  start is still reported, so that notice over-reports. A refused
  completion's own notice names no item or response, so the text it would
  have recorded cannot be attributed from the notice. Staged text is also
  recorded only after the item before it in the transcript, so text whose
  earlier item has not landed waits while its start is not reported; if that
  item never lands, the text is lost without a notice. (#1821)
- GPT Live barge-in duck: without a response id the broker cannot tell a
  resumed interrupted response from a new answer. If the interrupted response
  pauses for 600 ms or more while the user is still talking and then resumes,
  or the user starts speaking inside a 600 ms to 1.6 s pause of a response
  that then resumes, the resumed audio counts as an answer: it stays ducked
  while the user speaks and is restored once the user has been quiet for
  1.6 s, mid-sentence if need be.

## [0.9.2] - 2026-10-16

### Breaking

- Per-model stream-inactivity windows (see Added) add the public
  `stream_inactivity_timeout_secs: Option<u64>` field to the following
  constructible Rust structs; struct literals must set it (`None` keeps the
  global window):
  - `meerkat_core::model_profile::capabilities::ModelCapabilities::stream_inactivity_timeout_secs`
  - `meerkat_core::model_profile::ModelProfile::stream_inactivity_timeout_secs`
  - `meerkat_core::config::SelfHostedModelConfig::stream_inactivity_timeout_secs`

  `ModelProfile` and `SelfHostedModelConfig` omit the field when it is unset,
  so existing documents keep their bytes.
- Behaviour-only (not measured by the gate): a model fallback switch
  (`AgentLlmFallbackSwitch`) whose `target_profile` witness was not judged
  for the target identity's own binding
  (`ModelProfileWitness::judged_for_identity`) is refused with
  `AgentError::ConfigError`; the activation used to replace it with the
  model row's profile. A custom `AgentLlmClient` that proposes fallbacks to
  targets that name a binding must mint their witnesses with
  `ModelRegistry::profile_witness_for_identity`.
- Builtin web_search target and delegated hosted search (see Added).
  `meerkat-authorization`: `grant_policy::operation_grant_target` takes the
  operation's `&PreparedAuthorizationBinding` instead of its
  `&OperationAuthorizationFacts`: a delegated hosted search selects its own
  route's lineage from its binding, where the facts alone would select the
  base. Callers pass the binding they already hold.
  `meerkat-authorization-contracts`: `AuthorizationAuditObservation` gains
  `delegate_attribution: Option<AuditDelegateAttribution>` (struct literals
  add `delegate_attribution: None`). No exhaustive public enum gains a
  variant: `ToolOperationTarget` and `GrantTarget` are non-exhaustive.
  Persisted format (not measured by the gate; the stored version is
  unchanged): `GrantTarget`'s new `BuiltinToolOperation { operation }` and
  `DelegatedHostedSearch { route, capability }` are ordered after every
  earlier target kind, so existing selections keep their order and
  canonical bytes. A binary without this change cannot read a work
  association whose targeted selection names one of them, nor an input row
  whose audit holds a delegate attribution. Every governed web_search helper
  decision records one, under any grant basis, so this reaches every
  governed session that ran web_search. 0.9.1 treats such input rows as
  corrupt and recovery skips them; drain governed work before downgrading.
  Associations and rows that use neither are unchanged.
- Behaviour-only (not measured by the gate): the builtin web_search call's
  plan now carries a `ToolOperationTarget::BuiltinOperation` target under
  every grant basis, a single `GrantLineage` included. A host policy owner
  that refuses operation targets it does not map now refuses web_search
  where it used to allow it; this fails closed, and mapping the target
  restores it.
- Behaviour-only (not measured by the gate): under a targeted grant basis
  the builtin web_search call selects only its `BuiltinToolOperation`
  lineage and its helper's model request only its `DelegatedHostedSearch`
  lineage, never the base, so a host that admitted the helper's inference
  under the base now sees Denied until it selects the delegate (a single
  `GrantLineage` basis is unchanged). A governed web_search whose context
  does not carry the dispatch's own prepared call is refused as malformed
  facts before its helper runs. A stock realm with a per-target selection
  refuses web_search as Denied (no lineage is selected for it) instead of
  Unavailable; a legacy single stock grant still leaves it Unavailable. A
  web_search plan is refused at dispatch as `ExecutionOwnerChanged` when it
  reaches another composite dispatcher that registered web_search as its
  own builtin, when the same composite replaced a
  builtin registration after resolving it, or when another owner (such as
  an external tool) now holds the name: a plan that carries the composite's
  builtin witness runs only on that builtin.
- Behaviour-only (not measured by the gate): comms and `memory_search`
  operations carry typed operation targets (see Added). Under a targeted
  grant basis (`WorkAuthorityBasis::TargetedGrantLineages`) each resolves
  only the lineage selected for its own target and is denied without one;
  the base lineage no longer covers them. A stock realm issues no peer,
  peer-directory or memory grant, so its per-target selections now deny
  these operations at the grant owner, where the stock policy used to
  report them unmapped (`operation_authorization_unavailable`).
- Behaviour-only (not measured by the gate): a comms tool call whose
  addressee cannot be determined (arguments that do not parse as the tool's
  input, or a `reply_to_peer` that selects no single delivery of the turn)
  now fails at execution-plan resolution with `invalid_arguments` and the
  handler's own reason, where it failed at dispatch with `execution_failed`.
- Behaviour-only (not measured by the gate): under governed work the comms
  tools and `memory_search` run only when the dispatch's prepared
  authorization names exactly the typed target they are about to reach (the
  peer a delivery reaches, the peer directory, or the read of the memory
  scope searched). A wrapper that forwards their `dispatch_with_context` but
  resolves its own plan without that target (which a base lineage would
  cover), or with another one, is now refused with `authorization_refused`
  (malformed facts) before any delivery or memory read. Forward
  `resolve_execution_plan` and `dispatch_resolved_with_context` to the
  owning dispatcher instead. A context that carries work authorization
  without its prepared check, or the reverse, is malformed for them (as for
  `ToolDispatchContext::check_tool_authorization`), never ungoverned.
  Ungoverned dispatch is unchanged.
- Behaviour-only (not measured by the gate): under governed work the fenced
  tool dispatch (`dispatch_tool_execution_plan_fenced`, which the agent
  loop uses) refuses, before preparation, a plan for a tool whose root
  catalog provenance is comms or memory unless every operation target it
  carries is of that owner's kind (a peer delivery or the peer directory
  for comms, a memory operation for memory) and it carries one, with
  `authorization_refused` (malformed facts). Another owner's target, such
  as the bundle target a registered Rust bundle attaches to a plan that
  names none, does not stand in for it. Such a plan comes from a wrapper
  that does not forward `resolve_execution_plan` to the owner and may also
  drop the dispatch context, where the owner could no longer check its
  target. This includes the deprecated
  `SendTool` and `PeersTool` builtins (see Deprecated).
- Behaviour-only (not measured by the gate): the comms dispatchers
  (`CommsToolSurface`, `CommsToolDispatcher`, `DynCommsToolDispatcher`) and
  `MemorySearchDispatcher` own their execution plans: their
  `dispatch_resolved_with_context` refuses, as unavailable
  (`ExecutionOwnerChanged`), a plan they did not resolve themselves for
  exactly the call's current target and binding. A wrapper that forwards
  `dispatch_resolved_with_context` to them but resolves its own plan (does
  not forward `resolve_execution_plan`) no longer runs these tools; forward
  both.
- Behaviour-only (not measured by the gate): a host `OperationPolicyOwner`
  now reads an owner-produced target for the comms tools and
  `memory_search`: `single_tool_operation_target` returns
  `Some(PeerSend { .. })`, `Some(PeerDirectoryRead)` or
  `Some(MemoryOperation { .. })` where it returned `None`. An owner that
  mapped these tools in its target-less arm (for example by tool name) no
  longer reaches that arm for them; map the new targets instead.
- Persisted format (not measured by the gate): a work association whose
  targeted selection names a `peer`, `peer_directory` or `memory` target
  cannot be read by a binary without this change (such as 0.9.1), and
  neither can a `prepared` authorization audit record of any operation of
  such work, which embeds the work's whole authority basis
  (`AuditPolicyRead::operation_authorities`). Such a binary fails to decode
  the record with an unknown-variant error naming the target kind; it never
  reads it as another target. Associations and audit records that name none
  of them are unchanged.
- Audit entries name their boundary (see Added). `meerkat-core`:
  `OperationObservation::Entry` is now `Entry(OperationEntryBoundary)`
  instead of a unit variant, so a match needs `Entry(_)` or a boundary, and
  `PreparedOperationCheck::observe_entry` takes the observing boundary,
  `observe_entry(boundary: OperationEntryBoundary)`; a custom model
  transport (for example an `LlmClient::stream_prepared` fixture) passes
  `OperationEntryBoundary::ModelRequest`.
  `meerkat-authorization-contracts`: `AuditObservation::Entry` is now the
  struct variant `Entry { boundary: Option<OperationEntryBoundary> }`
  instead of a unit variant, so a match needs `Entry { .. }`. Persisted
  audit records (not measured by the gate): a new entry record adds the
  boundary (`{"kind": "entry", "boundary": "tool_effect"}`); a record
  written before decodes with `boundary: None` and re-encodes unchanged,
  and a reader built before this change ignores the field and still decodes
  the record as an entry. `SafeAuditObservation::EntryAttempt` is unchanged.
- `meerkat-core`: `SessionBuildOptions` and `SessionBuildState` gain
  `shell_timeout_secs: Option<NonZeroU64>`, and `meerkat`'s
  `AgentBuildConfig` gains the same field (see Fixed: MCP
  `builtin_config.shell_timeout_secs`). Struct-literal constructors must add
  it; `None` keeps the previous behaviour. `SessionBuildState` skips it when
  unset, so stored sessions keep their bytes.
- `meerkat-core`: `ToolUnavailableReason` gains `CallbackRouteUnclaimed` (see
  Added: `mob/claim_callback_route`). The enum is not `#[non_exhaustive]`;
  exhaustive matches must add the variant.
- Behaviour-only (not measured by the gate): `meerkat-mob`'s
  `MobProvisioner::start_turn` for a runtime-backed member resolves at the
  admitted input's terminal, not at an execution attempt the runtime
  retries, so a turn whose retry succeeds returns success (see Fixed). The
  wait checks every 120 s that the input's session is still progressing,
  and a retried input counts as parked, ending the call with the failed
  attempt, only when at a check no run holds it, it gained no attempt since
  the last check, and its session has no running turn. A retry queued
  behind another run of the session keeps waiting; a session that ran other
  inputs during the period but is idle at the check, with the retry still
  queued, counts as parked.
- Behaviour-only (not measured by the gate): `meerkat-rpc` answers a turn or
  event its session's runtime refuses to admit with the refusal's typed
  JSON-RPC code instead of `-32603` (see Fixed), and its not-ready refusal
  reads "the session runtime is <state> and does not admit this request"
  instead of "runtime not ready for llm reconfiguration: <state>".
- Behaviour-only (not measured by the gate): a config write that changes a
  realm's own parent edge is refused (`confinement_administration_required`,
  or invalid params when the new edge does not resolve) when the realm would
  compose a different `[confinement]`, and a section one config document
  states for another realm no longer replaces that realm's own edge (see
  Fixed). Re-parent such a realm by editing its document as its host.
- `meerkat_core::service::SessionBuildOptions` and `meerkat::AgentBuildConfig`
  have a new `refused_mcp_servers` field (`Vec<McpServerRefusal>`); a struct
  literal must add it (or use `..Default::default()` or
  `AgentBuildConfig::new`).
- `meerkat::HostMcpTargetRefusal` has a new variant `Refused { server_name,
  refusal }` (an MCP auth target only an untrusted `mcp.toml` defines; see
  Fixed); an exhaustive match must handle it.
- `meerkat_llm_core::provider_runtime::ProviderAuthError` has a new variant
  `HostLaunchRefused { exemption, refusal }` (a credential command a
  confined process could change; see Fixed); an exhaustive match must handle
  it.
- `meerkat_rest::AppState` has a new public field `host_confinement`
  (`meerkat::HostConfinement`); a struct literal must add it
  (`HostConfinement::trusted_host()` keeps the previous behaviour).
- Behaviour-only (not measured by the gate): a config write that changes the
  realm sections of a realm's own document (its parent edge, or a
  `[realm.global]` section) is also refused with
  `governance_administration_required` when the realm would compose a
  different `[governance]` (see Fixed).
- Behaviour-only (not measured by the gate): a realm whose ancestor's own
  config document is missing no longer composes (a missing parent), and
  `rkat realm delete` and `rkat realm prune` keep a realm another realm's
  document names as its parent, `--force` included (see Fixed).
- Behaviour-only (not measured by the gate): under a host that confines
  `mcp_stdio`, a stdio skill source runs confined (its program by absolute
  path, only its configured environment, from the kind's working
  directory), and under a host that confines every launch kind, a
  credential command or Git skill cache a confined process could change is
  refused. See Changed and Fixed.
- `meerkat_core::ConfigError` has a new variant `CompositionAdministration
  { administered, change, composer }`: a config write that changes realm
  sections so that a realm would compose a different `[confinement]` or
  `[governance]` (see Fixed). Refusals of changed realm sections use it
  instead of `ConfinementAdministration` and `GovernanceAdministration`; an
  exhaustive match must handle it. `ConfigError::administered_section`
  gives the section of all three.
- Behaviour-only (not measured by the gate): a credential command without
  `cwd` runs from the user's home directory on every host, not from the
  host's working directory, and a credential command the host refuses ends
  its binding's resolution with `HostLaunchRefused` instead of falling back
  to the next credential (see Fixed).
- Behaviour-only (not measured by the gate): a write to the user document
  that changes its realm sections is refused too when another realm would
  compose a different `[confinement]` or `[governance]` afterwards, such as
  removing or adding `[realm.global]` when the user document states
  `[governance]` (see Fixed).
- Behaviour-only (not measured by the gate): under a host that confines
  any launch kind, the programs the host runs as itself (credential
  commands, `git` for Git skill repositories, the browser opener, `stty`,
  `wasm-pack`) no longer inherit the variables that make a program load
  code or startup options from elsewhere (`LD_*`, `DYLD_*`, `PYTHON*`,
  `NODE_OPTIONS`, `NODE_PATH`, `PERL5LIB`, `PERL5OPT`, `RUBYLIB`, `RUBYOPT`,
  `BASH_ENV`, `ENV`, `GIT_DIR`, `GIT_WORK_TREE`, `GIT_EXEC_PATH` and the
  like), and lose the paths a confined process could change from the
  others; a credential command that needs such a variable states it in its
  own `env` (see Fixed). A host that confines no launch kind runs them with
  its environment as before.
- `meerkat_core::ConfigError` has a new variant
  `CredentialCommandAdministration { realm, profile }`: a config write that
  adds a credential command or changes what one runs (see Fixed); an
  exhaustive match must handle it. `ConfigError::administered_section`
  gives it as `Confinement`.
- Behaviour-only (not measured by the gate): a config write that adds a
  credential command, or changes its program, arguments, environment or
  working directory, is refused with `confinement_administration_required`
  on every config write surface; the host edits the document instead (see
  Fixed).

### Security

- Cargo.lock moves quinn-proto from 0.11.14 to 0.11.19, clearing
  RUSTSEC-2026-0185, RUSTSEC-2026-0338, RUSTSEC-2026-0339, RUSTSEC-2026-0340
  and RUSTSEC-2026-0342. No build compiled it: it is reachable only through
  reqwest's weak `quinn` feature, which nothing enables
  (`cargo tree --workspace --all-features --target all -i quinn-proto` is
  empty), but lockfile scanners flagged it. Lockfile only; the new version
  also locks the unused rand_pcg 0.10.2.

### Added

- `meerkat_core::model_profile::capabilities::ModelCapabilities::gemini_provider_tag_rejection`
  says why a Gemini catalog row refuses the thinking level of a
  `GeminiProviderTag` (see Fixed), and
  `meerkat_core::lifecycle::run_primitive::GeminiThinkingLevel::as_effort_level`
  names a Gemini thinking level in the catalog's `EffortLevel` vocabulary.
- `meerkat_core::ModelRegistry::profile_witness_for_identity` mints a
  `ModelProfileWitness` for an identity as its binding's backend serves it,
  and `ModelProfileWitness::judged_for_identity` says whether a witness was
  judged for exactly that identity, binding included (see Fixed).
- Per-model stream-inactivity windows. A model's profile can carry its own
  watchdog window: the catalog sets one where the provider documents
  responses that can stay silent for minutes (`gemini-4-argon`, 900 s per
  Google's 15-minute client-timeout guidance; `gpt-5.5-pro`, 7200 s, its call
  timeout, since its requests can run for minutes without streaming), and a
  self-hosted model can declare `stream_inactivity_timeout_secs` (for example
  for a long prefill; config validation refuses a window below 60 s,
  `meerkat_core::MIN_MODEL_STREAM_INACTIVITY_TIMEOUT`, twice the 30 s
  post-finish trailer wait of the OpenAI-compatible client, so the watchdog
  cannot race that wait). The window is resolved for each LLM call like
  `call_timeout`: an explicit `[retry] stream_inactivity_timeout` (a duration,
  or `"disabled"`) wins, then the current model's window, then the built-in
  300 s, so a model change or fallback uses the new model's window. The 300 s
  window used to apply to every model. Rust embedders get the provided
  `ModelOperationalDefaultsResolver::stream_inactivity_timeout_for` (default
  `None`) and `AgentBuilder::with_stream_inactivity_timeout_override`.
- `meerkat-mob-mcp`: `MobMcpState::set_before_create` installs a
  `MobBeforeCreate` hook that admits or refuses every mob the state creates
  (an agent's `mob_create`, the implicit delegation mob, a temporary council,
  a host's definition or mobpack create) before anything of the mob exists.
  It gets a `MobCreateRequest` built by the create path itself: the mob id,
  the owner bridge session (`None` only for a host's own create) and whether
  the mob is that session's implicit delegation mob, which counts only under
  the id derived from the session. The hook fails closed: a refusal or a
  panic refuses the create with an error `MobMcpState::is_create_refusal`
  recognizes, carrying the reason in its message and structured data (`kind`
  `MOB_CREATE_REFUSED_KIND`). Restoring a persisted mob never asks it, and
  neither does a handle a host registers itself with `mob_insert_handle` or
  `try_mob_insert_handle`.
- Governed builtin web_search: a typed operation target for the call and a
  delegated hosted-search lineage for its helper. The composite dispatcher
  states `ToolOperationTarget::BuiltinOperation { operation:
  BuiltinToolOperation::WebSearch }` for the web_search builtin it
  registered (the tool declares it through `BuiltinTool::builtin_operation`;
  tools without a declaration keep their plans) and revalidates it at
  dispatch against its exact registration: another composite that
  registered web_search as its own builtin, another owner
  key, a plan resolved before the composite replaced its web_search
  executor (even with an identical schema), or a plan whose name another
  owner now holds is `ExecutionOwnerChanged`, and no executor runs. This
  rejects stale, wrong-owner and tampered plans within trusted Rust
  composition; witness constructors are public, so it is not cryptographic
  resistance to hostile in-process Rust code. A tool
  merely named web_search (a host dispatcher's, a registered bundle's or an
  undeclared builtin) has no such target unless its owner states it itself,
  which an in-process dispatcher can. The
  helper's own model request is the typed delegate of exactly that call:
  `ToolDispatchContext::tool_delegate_attribution(call,
  ToolDelegateRole::HostedSearchInference)` mints a `ToolDelegateAttribution`
  only from the dispatch's own prepared call (matched by identity) whose plan
  carries that target, `LlmRequestAuthorization::for_tool_delegate` carries
  it, and `PreparedAuthorizationBinding::delegate_attribution` exposes it to
  owners. The delegate binds only an inference with exactly one hosted search
  capability (`WebSearch`, or `GoogleSearch` for a Gemini helper) and no live
  channel, under the call's work, execution scope, run and context revision
  with a fresh operation id, and never moves to another run. One
  attribution can prepare helper requests until its run ends; each is its
  own operation and needs its own current lineage. Under a
  targeted basis `operation_grant_target` selects
  `GrantTarget::BuiltinToolOperation { operation }` for the call and
  `GrantTarget::DelegatedHostedSearch { route, capability }` for the helper,
  where `route` is the helper's own `ControllerRouteKey`; the work and every
  original (named contributors and further originals) use the same
  selector, with their current ceilings and the earliest expiry. Choosing
  a target erases no restriction: hosts issue the target lineages and every
  contributor's ceiling with the original time, operation (including
  read-only, which is an action set: `ExecutionRestrictions` has no
  read-only flag), resource-domain and private-data restrictions, and a
  typed public-search target or read-only declaration does not mean private
  information cannot leave. The
  attribution grants, inherits and exempts nothing: it keys the selection
  and the protected audit record (`AuditDelegateAttribution {
  parent_operation_id, role }`), which also records the helper's own
  decision and authorization refusal before its provider send. A helper
  rated R2 or R3 settles at its model entry as `unsupported_entry` or
  `human_consent_required` whether or not a reviewer exists, and nothing
  is sent; the model sees it as `operation_authorization_unavailable`
  feedback, and no audit row records that review refusal (a limit of every
  model request). Behaviour contract:
  revoking the call's own lineage refuses later calls but does not cancel
  an invocation that already entered, which may still make its authorized
  helper request (the helper passes its own work, contributor, route,
  capability and entry checks and inherits nothing of the call); revoking
  the helper's or a contributor's lineage before the helper's send prevents
  it. Neither undoes a provider effect or ends the run on a local refusal.
  `ResolvedToolExecutionPlan::single_operation_target` states the one-target
  rule `grant_policy::single_tool_operation_target` now forwards to, and
  `ServerToolKind` derives `PartialOrd`, `Ord` and `Hash`. Stock issues no
  grant for either target and leaves both unmapped: stock is unsupported for
  this route, not stock coverage of web_search. Limit: operation review of
  web_search is an unsupported slice, not review coverage. It has no
  reviewed entry point, so a review its owner requires settles as local
  feedback and the search never runs: R2 is `reviewer_missing` without a
  reviewer and `unsupported_entry` with one; R3 is `human_consent_required`
  without a human consent route and `unsupported_entry` with one.
- Typed catalog mode and visibility query. `meerkat_core::ToolCatalogView`
  (with `ToolCatalogViewEntry` and `ToolCatalogVisibility`: `Visible`,
  `Deferred` or `Hidden`) reports how a live session's next model request
  projects its tool catalog: the catalog mode it takes (deferred only when
  the exact catalog selects it and a catalog control plane exists or may be
  composed), sources still connecting, whether a staged visibility change
  waits for the next boundary, and for each catalog entry its deferral
  eligibility (with its typed source owner), callability and visibility to
  the model. It is read without changing anything, by the rules each
  model-call boundary applies; the boundary now computes its control and
  deferred names through the same projection. `Agent::tool_catalog_view`,
  `SessionAgent::tool_catalog_view` (defaulted to `None`),
  `EphemeralSessionService::tool_catalog_view`,
  `PersistentSessionService::tool_catalog_view` and
  `MobSessionService::tool_catalog_view` (defaulted to `Ok(None)`) expose it
  beside the existing tool-scope snapshot queries. Like those siblings it
  is not exposed over JSON-RPC or REST. A host that attaches a
  deferred-eligible operation can ask whether the session defers it instead
  of inferring that from the operation's source kind.
- Typed boundary identity on authorization audit entries. Several
  boundaries can record the entry of one operation (each staging point on a
  tool call's dispatch chain, then its effect), and each now names itself
  with the new `meerkat_core::OperationEntryBoundary`: `ToolDispatch` (the
  root dispatch or an adapter staging the call), `ToolExecutionPolicy` (the
  call-level execution policy gate), `ToolEffect` (the owning leaf's entry
  immediately before its effect or transport handoff), `McpResourceRead`,
  `McpAttachment`, `ModelRequest`, `ContextAppend` and `ReviewContextRead`.
  The new `ToolDispatchContext::observe_tool_entry_at` stages a tool entry
  at a named boundary; `observe_tool_entry` keeps its signature and names
  `ToolDispatch`.
- Typed grant targets for peer (comms) and memory operations.
  `meerkat-core`: `ToolOperationTarget` gains `PeerSend { peer, kind }` (one
  delivery to exactly one peer, by its canonical `PeerId`),
  `PeerDirectoryRead` (a read of the session's own trusted-peer directory)
  and `MemoryOperation { scope, operation }`, with the new `PeerSendKind`
  (`Message`, `Request`, `Response`), `MemoryOperation` (`Read`, `Write`,
  `Delete`, `Propose`) and `MemoryScopeRef` (`Session { session_id }`,
  `Host { owner, scope }`, with `is_named()`), and
  `MemorySearchScope::scope_ref()`. `SessionId` implements `PartialOrd` and
  `Ord`. The default plans of the comms tools carry these targets:
  `CommsToolSurface` (meerkat-tools) and `CommsToolDispatcher` and
  `DynCommsToolDispatcher` (meerkat-comms), through the new
  `meerkat_comms::CommsExecutionAuthority` and
  `meerkat_comms::comms_tool_operation_target`, attach the peer each
  delivery reaches (the `peer_id` of `send_message`, `send_request` and
  `send_response`; for `reply_to_peer`, the sender of the turn's peer
  message it selects) and the peer directory for `peers`.
  `MemorySearchDispatcher` attaches a `Read` of the session memory it
  searches. Each owner revalidates its own target at dispatch, so a plan
  resolved for one peer never delivers to another, and under governed work
  each runs only when the prepared authorization names exactly that target,
  through the new `ToolDispatchContext::require_authorized_operation_target`
  (for any owner whose effect a typed target selects) and
  `CommsExecutionAuthority::require_authorized_target`. These guarantees
  hold when every wrapper between the root dispatcher and the owner
  forwards `resolve_execution_plan` and `dispatch_resolved_with_context`
  with its context; the fenced dispatch refuses a governed comms or memory
  plan that carries no target of its owner's kind.
  `meerkat-authorization-contracts`: `GrantTarget` gains `Peer { peer }`,
  `PeerDirectory` and `Memory { scope }`, and `meerkat-authorization`'s
  `operation_grant_target` selects them on the normal targeted grant path:
  one lineage per peer, per memory scope and for the peer directory, never a
  wildcard and never the base. An embedding host maps the typed facts to its
  own actions and selects one grant per target. The peer targets cover only
  the five comms tools (`send_message`, `reply_to_peer`, `send_request` and
  `send_response` select `Peer`, and `peers` selects `PeerDirectory`).
  Other tools that reach agents, such as `delegate`, `council`,
  `mob_spawn_member` and a mob member's calls up to its mob's operator,
  carry no peer target and stay on the work's base lineage, which a `Peer`
  lineage neither widens nor narrows. A `send_response` delivery's
  addressee is the caller's assertion: the runtime checks that its request
  id names a request this session received and can still answer, but
